## Primewise detection of torsion

[Open item](item-lem-author-c5b0693f4fc3-top-torsion-primewise) · level 0

### Statement
An abelian group $M$ is torsion-free if multiplication by every prime is injective.

### Facts & Assumptions
[F1] Torsion means annihilation by some positive integer, as in [math:def-annihilator-and-torsion-of-a-module](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-annihilator-and-torsion-of-a-module).

### Proof
**Given:** $M$ satisfying the stated injectivity.

**Goal:** Show every torsion element is zero.

1.1 For $nx=0$ with $n>0$, factor $n$ into primes. Multiplication by $n$ is the composition of the corresponding injective prime multiplication maps, hence is injective (the empty composition for $n=1$ is the identity). [given]

2.1 Thus $nx=0$ implies $x=0$, as required. [F1, step 1.1] ∎

## Finite projective modules are finitely presented

[Open item](item-lem-author-3af31ead36fb-finite-projective-presentation) · level 0

### Statement
Let $A$ be a commutative unital ring and $P$ a finite projective $A$-module. Then $P$ is finitely presented: there is an exact sequence $A^m\to A^n\to P\to0$ with $m,n$ finite. Here finite projective means finitely generated and having the lifting property through surjective module maps.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative unital ring $A$ and a finite projective $A$-module $P$.

**Goal:** Construct a finite presentation of $P$.

### Proof

1.1 Choose finitely many generators of $P$ and let $q:A^n\to P$ be the resulting surjection. Projectivity lifts the identity of $P$ through $q$, giving a section $s:P\to A^n$. Thus $A^n=s(P)\oplus\ker q$. [given, choose, construct]

2.1 The projection $A^n\to\ker q$ maps the standard basis to a finite generating set of $\ker q$. Mapping a finite free module onto that kernel and composing with its inclusion in $A^n$ gives the required presentation. [step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Dimension of the maximal spectrum

[Open item](item-lem-author-3af31ead36fb-max-spectrum-dimension) · level 0

### Statement
Let $A$ be a nonzero noetherian commutative ring of finite Krull dimension $d$. Its maximal spectrum $\Omega$, the set of maximal ideals with the topology induced from $\operatorname{Spec}A$, is noetherian and has topological dimension at most $d$. Krull dimension is the supremum of the lengths of strict chains of prime ideals; topological dimension is the supremum of the lengths of strict chains of irreducible closed subsets.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonzero noetherian commutative ring $A$ of finite Krull dimension $d$.

**Goal:** Establish the noetherian and dimension assertions for $\Omega$.

### Proof

1.1 The closed sets of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ are the sets $V(I)$ of primes containing an ideal $I$. An ascending chain of ideals stabilizes because $A$ is noetherian, so descending chains of closed sets stabilize. Every subspace of a noetherian topological space is noetherian: the closures in the ambient space of a descending chain of subspace-closed sets stabilize, and intersection with the subspace recovers each set. [given, construct]

2.1 The ambient closures of a strict chain of irreducible closed subsets of $\Omega$ form a strict chain of irreducible closed subsets of $\operatorname{Spec}A$: closure preserves irreducibility, and intersection with $\Omega$ recovers each member. Each irreducible closed subset of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is $V(\mathfrak p)$ for a prime $\mathfrak p$: if $V(I)$ is irreducible, its radical is prime, since $ab$ in the radical implies $V(I)\subseteq V(a)\cup V(b)$. Inclusion of such closed sets reverses inclusion of primes. Hence every chain has length at most $d$. [given, step 1.1, construct] ∎

### Statement

Suppose that for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, the localization $M_{\mathfrak m}$ has a free direct summand of rank greater than $e$. Then $M\cong A\oplus M'$ for some $A$-module $M'$. ## Cylinder and zero section of a smooth affine surface

[Open item](item-lem-author-f08c343a07fc-local-cylinder-geometry) · level 0

### Statement
Assume AC. If $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ is a nonempty smooth affine surface over a field $k$, then $Y=\operatorname{Spec}A[t]=X\times_k\mathbb A^1_k$ is a smooth affine threefold. Projection $p:Y\to X$ and the zero section $s:X\to Y$ satisfy $p s=\operatorname{id}_X$, and therefore $s^*p^*E\cong E$ for every vector bundle $E$.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data and hypotheses in the statement.

**Goal:** Establish the stated conclusion.

[F1] A noetherian finite-dimensional ring gains exactly one dimension on adjoining a variable. [math:thm-dimension-of-a-polynomial-ring-over-a-noetherian-ring](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-dimension-of-a-polynomial-ring-over-a-noetherian-ring)

[F2] Smooth morphisms are stable under base change and composition. [math:thm-smooth-morphisms-stable-base-change-composition](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-smooth-morphisms-stable-base-change-composition)

[F3] The finite presentation $k[t]$ has one variable and no equations; its empty Jacobian minor is $1$. Under AC, the relative Jacobian criterion applied with this presentation proves that $\mathbb A^1_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth. [math:thm-jacobian-criterion-smooth-morphism](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-jacobian-criterion-smooth-morphism) The meaning of smooth is fixed in [math:def-smooth-morphism-schemes](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-smooth-morphism-schemes).

### Proof

1.1 The smooth finite-type coordinate ring $A$ is noetherian, and the surface has dimension two. By [F1], $A[t]$ has dimension three. Its finite type over $k$ is immediate from generators for $A$ and $t$. The map $p$ is a base change of the smooth affine line by [F3]; composition with the smooth map $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ makes $Y$ smooth by [F2]. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 The homomorphisms $A\to A[t]$ and $A[t]\to A$, $t\mapsto0$, compose to the identity. Hence $p s=\operatorname{id}_X$. Pullback of sheaves is functorial up to its canonical isomorphism, so $s^*p^*E\cong E$. [construct, step 1.1] ∎

## Vanishing end groups kill the middle obstruction group

[Open item](item-lem-author-9b282fc59773-zero-obstruction-extension) · level 0

### Statement
Let $A,H,D$ be abelian groups and $f:A\to H$, $g:H\to D$ homomorphisms exact at $H$, meaning $\operatorname{im}f=\ker g$. If $A$ and $D$ are zero groups, then $H$ is a zero group. Every nonempty set that is a surjective image of the underlying set of $H$ then has exactly one element. No injectivity of $f$ or surjectivity of $g$ is required.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The groups, exactness, and vanishing assumptions in the Statement.

**Goal:** Prove the zero-group and singleton assertions.

### Proof
1.1 Since $D$ has only its identity element, every $h\in H$ satisfies $g(h)=0$, hence $\ker g=H$. Since $A$ has only its identity and $f$ preserves identity, $\operatorname{im}f=\{0\}$. Exactness gives $H=\ker g=\operatorname{im}f=\{0\}$. [given, algebra]

2.1 A function from the one-element underlying set of $H$ has image consisting of its single value. If it is surjective onto a nonempty set, that set equals this image and is a singleton. [step 1.1, given] ∎


## Reindexing a chain complex cohomologically

[Open item](item-lem-author-91088613574d-chain-cochain) · level 0

### Statement
Let C be a chain complex of abelian groups, with differential d from $C_n$ to $C_{n-1}$. Define the cochain complex $C^\vee$ by $(C^\vee)^q$ = $C_{-q}$, with differential d in each degree. Then $H^q(C^\vee)$ is canonically $H_{-q}(C)$.

A chain complex has consecutive differentials whose composite is zero; its homology is the kernel modulo the image. A cochain complex is defined analogously, with differential increasing degree, and its cohomology is the corresponding kernel modulo image.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A chain complex C and an integer q.

**Goal:** Identify the cohomology of its reindexing with its homology.

### Proof
1.1 The reindexed differential goes from $C_{-q}$ to $C_{-q-1}$, and its square is zero because d squared is zero in C. Thus $C^\vee$ is a cochain complex. [given, construct]

2.1 Its degree-q kernel and incoming image are exactly the degree-(−q) cycles and boundaries of C. Their quotients are therefore identical, giving the claimed canonical isomorphism. [given, step 1.1] ∎

## Cohomology after an even cochain shift

[Open item](item-lem-author-91088613574d-even-shift) · level 0

### Statement
For a cochain complex $A$, integers $i,j$, and the standard shift convention $A[m]^q=A^{q+m}$ with differential multiplied by $(-1)^m$, there is a canonical isomorphism $H^i(A[-2j])\cong H^{i-2j}(A)$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A cochain complex $A$ and integers $i,j$.

**Goal:** Compute the cohomology of its indicated shift.

### Proof
1.1 In degree $i$ the shifted group is $A^{i-2j}$, and both adjacent differentials are the corresponding differentials of $A$ because $(-1)^{-2j}=1$. [given, algebra]

2.1 The kernels and images defining the two displayed cohomology groups are consequently identical, giving the canonical isomorphism. [step 1.1] ∎

## Exact linear hyperdescent and derived-localization input

[Open item](item-thm-author-58e57d689702-linear-hyperdescent-input) · level 0

### Statement
For a small Grothendieck site $\mathcal C$ and a commutative unital ring $\Lambda$, the localization of presheaves of unbounded complexes of $\Lambda$-modules at maps inducing isomorphisms on all associated cohomology sheaves has as its local objects exactly the objects satisfying descent for every hypercover. Its homotopy category is $D(\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C,\Lambda))$. Equivalently its hypercomplete reflector is $L^h=Ri\,a$, represented by evaluating a K-injective sheaf resolution after exact degreewise sheafification. Hypercover descent means that evaluation on an augmented hypercover is the derived product totalization of the cosimplicial evaluation diagram.

Every hypercomplete local object is ordinary local; no equivalence $L^oP\simeq L^hP$ for arbitrary unbounded $P$ is asserted.

## External symmetric P¹ model, orientation criterion and fundamental stabilization

[Open item](item-thm-author-4f94f7982b0d-p1-spectrum-input) · level 0

### Statement
In the source’s non-A¹ theory over a qcqs derived scheme $S$, a symmetric lax P¹-spectrum is a module over the free commutative sphere algebra generated by P¹ in symmetric-sequence degree1 (Definition1.3.4). It is a P¹-spectrum precisely when its adjoint bonding maps are equivalences (Definition1.3.8). The localization is symmetric monoidal. A commutative algebra over that sphere algebra therefore gives a motivic ring spectrum when the Ω-condition holds. Coefficient stabilization has the induced adjunction with lax monoidal right adjoint Ω∞, and the P¹-shift evaluates at the next Ω-spectrum level (Notation2.2.7–8).
A pointed Picard class restricting along $\mathcal O(1)$ to the P¹-suspended unit gives a linear orientation (Lemma3.1.4/Remark3.1.5). An orientable spectrum is fundamental. On fundamental spectra coefficient stabilization is an equivalence (Theorem2.4.5), and modules over an oriented ring spectrum form a stable category (Corollary2.4.8). The PBF is the actual finite sum of powers of that first class; Lemma3.2.3 gives the bundle version. These results are over arbitrary qcqs derived bases and require no A¹-invariance.

### External input
Import exactly these formal constructions and criteria. They permit the concrete model assembled in the local lemmas; they do not assert that any abstract bigraded oriented theory automatically satisfies the source’s stronger hypotheses.

The first comparison is the canonical topology-change map, not a chosen isomorphism of groups; the second is derived Yoneda evaluation. ## Unique divisibility excludes torsion

[Open item](item-lem-author-b87d598e83f3-unique-roots-torsion) · level 0

### Statement
Let $G$ be an abelian group. Suppose that for every integer $n\geq1$, multiplication by $n$ is a bijection on $G$. Then $G$ is torsion-free: if $ng=0$ for some $n\geq1$, then $g=0$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The abelian group and bijectivity hypotheses in the statement.

**Goal:** Prove the stated torsion-freeness.

### Proof
1.1 For any $n\geq1$, the multiplication map $n:G\to G$ is injective by the given bijectivity. It sends $0$ to $0$. [given]

2.1 If $ng=0$, then $ng=n0$; injectivity from step 1.1 gives $g=0$. This holds for every positive $n$, proving the claim. [step 1.1] ∎

## An injection identifies its domain with its image

[Open item](item-lem-author-b87d598e83f3-injective-image-isomorphism) · level 0

### Statement
If $f:G\to H$ is an injective homomorphism of abelian groups, its corestriction $G\to\operatorname{im}f$ is an isomorphism.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The injective group homomorphism in the statement.

**Goal:** Construct the asserted isomorphism.

### Proof
1.1 The corestriction is a homomorphism and is surjective by the definition of image. It remains injective because the original map is injective. [given]

2.1 Its set-theoretic inverse preserves addition: if $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are image elements, their sum is $f(a+b)$. Thus the inverse sends their sum to the sum of their inverse images. The corestriction is consequently an isomorphism. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Unique divisibility is invariant under group isomorphism

[Open item](item-lem-author-b87d598e83f3-isomorphism-transfers-roots) · level 0

### Statement
Let $u:G\to H$ be an isomorphism of abelian groups. If multiplication by every positive integer is bijective on $G$, then the same is true on $H$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The isomorphism and bijectivity hypotheses in the statement.

**Goal:** Transfer bijectivity to $H$.

### Proof
1.1 For each integer $n\geq1$, homomorphism compatibility gives $n_H=u\circ n_G\circ u^{-1}$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Each factor on the right is bijective, so $n_H$ is bijective. This holds for every positive integer, as required. [step 1.1] ∎

$$K^Q(P(A))=\Omega BQ(P(A))\simeq K^W(C(A)).$$

Over $\mathbb Z$, the canonical framed vector-bundle map is an equivalence $\Sigma^\infty_{\rm fr}\mathrm{Vect}\simeq f_0KGL$. Its rank-induced Bott-cofiber map to $\Sigma^\infty_{\rm fr}\mathbb Z$ is an equivalence. The latter object is naturally Spitzweck's absolute integral $HZ$ as an $E_\infty$ ring, by the adjunction construction from constant integers; constant $1$ is the ring unit. The required condition $f_1HZ=0$ holds over the Dedekind base $\mathbb Z$. No characteristic inversion or $1/2$ assumption is imposed on this KGL assertion.

For a prime field $F$, EM supplies natural multiplicative augmented comparison maps from its motivic K-filtration to its cdh KH-filtration, hence natural graded coefficient maps $\eta:\mathbb Z(\star)_{\rm mot}\to\mathbb Z(\star)_{\rm cdh}$. Each $\eta_j(X)$ is an equivalence when $X/F$ is regular Noetherian. On smooth $F$-schemes the composite of the classical-to-EM map with $\eta$ is the canonical classical left-Kan/cdh comparison. EM's actual first-Chern map is obtained from the classical weight-one map on smooth $F$-algebras by left Kan extension and Nisnevich sheafification, as in Lemma 5.1.

BEM supplies natural multiplicative graded maps from cdh coefficients through its base-changed represented coefficients to $\mathbb Z(\star)^{\mathbb A}$ represented by the KGL slices. Their composite is an equivalence on equal-characteristic schemes. Its cdh coefficients restrict along every field extension by the canonical base-independent left-Kan/cdh construction. The represented theory has zero negative weights, the projective bundle formula and the Picard first class induced by $1-[L^\vee]$. On regular Noetherian bases its spectral Picard map is the determinant/unstable-slice-edge map of Construction 4.35; the cdh-local left Kan extension in Theorem 4.39(4), followed by Remark 4.45, supplies the indicated map on all qcqs schemes. For an $\mathbb A^1$-invariant Nisnevich graded ring theory with zero negative weights in every degree and PBF after every smooth base change, the mapping-limit argument in the proof of BEM Lemma 3.27 detects the Picard-space maps in (3.28) by the reduced $\mathbb P^1$ class: the projective-space tower has zero $\lim^1$ obstruction. This is a statement about these Picard-space maps, not arbitrary higher spectral maps.

Over a perfect field, Spitzweck's integral field spectrum identifies with ordinary Voevodsky motivic cohomology and the Bloch cycle model, compatibly with the product and actual $\mathbb G_m$ bonding map. Its canonical orientation classifies its tautological Picard line. Integral positive-characteristic specialization and arbitrary field extension have the hypotheses of Theorem 9.16 and Lemma 9.17. The occurrence of the tautological subline $\mathcal O(-1)$ in its line-projectivization convention does not replace the class of a given line by the class of its dual.

For a closed immersion $Z\hookrightarrow V$ between smooth separated finite-type schemes over a perfect field, smooth homotopy purity gives the coefficient-independent pointed equivalence $V/(V\setminus Z)\simeq\operatorname{Th}(N_{Z/V})$ by the canonical deformation maps. On these regular smooth pairs the refined motivic Gysin map is the Thom isomorphism followed by purity; its forget-support map is the quotient projection. Navarro's supported Chern maps arise from the actual universal pointed K-space map and commute with forgetting support. Only this smooth-pair Gysin construction is used in the field-comparison application.

## Finite projective complements

[Open item](item-lem-finite-projective-complements) · level 1

### Statement
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unit. Every finite projective $A$-module $P$ admits a finite projective $A$-module $Q$ and an integer $N\geq 0$ such that $P\oplus Q\cong A^N$.

Assume additionally the Axiom of Choice and that $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ is locally noetherian. Every class in the vector-bundle Grothendieck group $K^0(X)$ is of the form $[E]-[\mathcal O_X^N]$ for a vector bundle $E$ and an integer $N\geq0$. Its rank at each point $x\in X$ is $\operatorname{rank}_x E-N$; this is a locally constant integer-valued function, hence is constant on each connected component.

A finite projective module is a finitely generated module $P$ such that every homomorphism from $P$ to the target of a surjective module homomorphism lifts through that surjection. A vector bundle is a finite locally free $\mathcal O_X$-module: locally it is isomorphic to a finite direct sum of copies of $\mathcal O_X$. Its rank at a point is the number of copies in a local trivialization containing that point. A locally noetherian scheme is one covered by spectra of noetherian rings. The group $K^0(X)$ is generated by isomorphism classes $[E]$ of vector bundles, with $[E]=[E']+[E'']$ for each short exact sequence $0\to E'\to E\to E''\to0$ of vector bundles.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $A$ with unit and a finite projective $A$-module $P$. For the assertions about $K^0$, also assume the Axiom of Choice and that $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ is locally noetherian.

**Goal:** Construct a finite projective complement to $P$ in a finite free module, then prove the representative and rank assertions.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is used only to invoke the bundle and Grothendieck-group suppliers [F1]–[F2]; steps 1.1–3.1 use finite choices only. [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

[F1] Under the Axiom of Choice, associated sheaf and global sections give an equivalence between finite projective $A$-modules and vector bundles on $X$, preserving finite direct sums and ranks. In particular $\widetilde{A^N}\cong\mathcal O_X^N$. [lem-affine-bundle-module-interface](item-lem-affine-bundle-module-interface)

[F2] For a locally noetherian scheme under the Axiom of Choice, $K^0(X)$ has the generators and exact-sequence relations stated above. [math:def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Split a finite free presentation and use complements to replace negative bundle classes by negative free classes.

1.1 Choose finitely many generators $p_1,\ldots,p_N$ of $P$ and let $q:A^N\to P$ send the standard basis vectors to them. This map is surjective. By the lifting property of $P$, the identity map of $P$ lifts to a homomorphism $s:P\to A^N$ with $q s=\operatorname{id}_P$. This construction uses only the given finite generating family, including the empty family when $P=0$. [given, construct]

2.1 Put $Q=\ker q$. The map $P\oplus Q\to A^N$, $(p,z)\mapsto s(p)+z$, is an isomorphism: its inverse sends $a$ to $(q(a),a-sq(a))$. The projection $e=\operatorname{id}_{A^N}-sq$ has image $Q$, so $Q$ is generated by the finitely many elements $e(e_i)$, where $e_i$ are the standard basis vectors. [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The module $A^N$ has the lifting property: lift the images of its finitely many basis vectors separately through any given surjection. A direct summand of a module with this property also has it: compose a map from the summand with the projection from the ambient module, lift, and restrict the lift to the summand. By step 2.1, $Q$ is such a summand of $A^N$ and is finitely generated. Thus $Q$ is finite projective, proving the first assertion. [step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Now impose the additional hypotheses. Every element of $K^0(X)$ is a finite integer linear combination of bundle classes by [F2]. Collecting positive and negative terms using the relation for the split exact sequence $0\to E'\to E'\oplus E''\to E''\to0$, write it as $[B]-[C]$ for vector bundles $B,C$; the zero bundle handles an empty sum. [F2, assume-hyp, step 3.1]

5.1 By [F1], $C\cong\widetilde P$ for a finite projective module $P$. Apply steps 1.1–3.1 to obtain $P\oplus Q\cong A^N$. With $D=\widetilde Q$, [F1] gives $C\oplus D\cong\mathcal O_X^N$. Therefore the split exact-sequence relation gives $[B]-[C]=[B\oplus D]-[C\oplus D]=[B\oplus D]-[\mathcal O_X^N].$ Taking $E=B\oplus D$ proves the representative assertion. [F1, F2, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 For a point $x$, rank is additive in every short exact sequence of vector bundles: after passing to the stalk and tensoring with the residue field, the sequence becomes a short exact sequence of finite-dimensional vector spaces, since the quotient stalk is free; dimensions are additive. Thus assigning a bundle its pointwise rank respects the relations in [F2] and defines a homomorphism from $K^0(X)$ to integer-valued functions on $X$. Local triviality makes every such rank function locally constant. Consequently the representative in step 5.1 has rank $\operatorname{rank}_x E-N$ at $x$. A locally constant function to the discrete space $\mathbb Z$ is constant on each connected component, since otherwise its distinct nonempty fibers would separate that component. [F2, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 Steps 3.1, 5.1 and 6.1 establish all the assertions under their stated hypotheses. [step 3.1, step 5.1, step 6.1] ∎



## Unimodular elements and trivial summands

[Open item](item-def-unimodular-sections) · level 1

### Definition
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with identity and $P$ a finite projective $A$-module: $P$ is finitely generated, and maps from $P$ lift through surjective module homomorphisms. An element $p\in P$ is **unimodular** if there is an $A$-linear functional $\phi:P\to A$ with $\phi(p)=1$. A functional $\phi:P\to A$ is **unimodular** if it is surjective. A pair $(p,\phi)$ with $\phi(p)=1$ is a **unimodular pair**.

A vector bundle $E$ on a scheme $X$ is a finite locally free $\mathcal O_X$-module: every point has an open neighbourhood on which $E$ is a finite direct sum of copies of $\mathcal O_X$. Its dual is $E^\vee=\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(E,\mathcal O_X)$. A global section $s\in\Gamma(X,E)$ is **nowhere zero** if, at every point $x$, its image in the fiber $E\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}k(x)$ is nonzero, where $k(x)$ is the residue field of the local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$. Equivalently, locally on $X$ the map $\mathcal O_X\to E$, $1\mapsto s$, identifies $\mathcal O_X$ with a direct summand of $E$. A morphism $E\to\mathcal O_X$ is instead a global section of the dual $E^\vee$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the following affine correspondence. On $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$, the bundle associated to a finite projective module $P$ has global sections $P$; under this identification a section is nowhere zero exactly when its element is unimodular. A unimodular pair gives an isomorphism $A\oplus\ker\phi\to P$, $(a,q)\mapsto ap+q$. In particular, a surjective functional on $P$ belongs to such a pair.

### Justification
The fiber condition uses the actual residue class of the section and is independent of a choice of local frame. The equivalences and the displayed direct-sum decomposition are established below. The affine assertion uses the stated Axiom of Choice through the cited affine module–bundle interface.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $A$, a finite projective $A$-module $P$, a scheme $X$ with a vector bundle $E$, and the Axiom of Choice for the affine assertions.

**Goal:** Justify the local description of nowhere-zero sections and the stated affine equivalences and splitting.

[F1] Under the Axiom of Choice, finite projective $A$-modules and vector bundles on $\operatorname{Spec}A$ correspond by associated sheaf and global sections, compatibly with localizations and duals; a finite projective module is a direct summand of a finite free module. [lem-affine-bundle-module-interface](item-lem-affine-bundle-module-interface)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; use local coordinates and the affine module–bundle correspondence.

1.1 On a neighbourhood of a point $x$, choose a frame of $E$ and write $s=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$. Its fiber value at $x$ is nonzero exactly when some $a_i$ has nonzero image in the residue field of $\mathcal O_{X,x}$, equivalently is a unit in that local ring. After shrinking the neighbourhood, that coordinate is invertible. Projection to this coordinate followed by multiplication by $a_i^{-1}$ is then a functional taking $s$ to $1$, so $s$ generates a direct summand. Conversely, if such a local splitting exists, its fiber sends the fiber value of $s$ to $1$, so that value is nonzero. Thus the two local descriptions agree. [given, construct]

1.2 If $\phi(p)=1$, the map $(a,q)\mapsto ap+q$ from $A\oplus\ker\phi$ to $P$ has inverse $v\mapsto(\phi(v),v-\phi(v)p)$. If $\phi$ is surjective, choose $p$ with $\phi(p)=1$. These statements also hold for the zero ring, where $1=0$. [given, algebra, construct]

1.3 For the affine converse, write $P$ as a direct summand of $A^n$ using [F1]. The resulting coordinate functionals $\lambda_i\in P^\vee$ and elements $e_i\in P$ satisfy $v=\sum_i\lambda_i(v)e_i$ for every $v\in P$. Put $I=(\lambda_1(p),\ldots,\lambda_n(p))$. At a prime $\mathfrak p$, the fiber of the associated section is zero exactly when all $\lambda_i(p)$ lie in $\mathfrak p$: one direction follows by applying the functionals and the other from the displayed expansion. If the section is nowhere zero, $I$ is contained in no prime. Under Choice a proper ideal lies in a maximal, hence prime, ideal, so $I=A$. Coefficients expressing $1$ as a linear combination of the $\lambda_i(p)$ yield a functional $\phi$ with $\phi(p)=1$. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 Conversely, if $\phi(p)=1$, its localization and passage to every residue field send the fiber value of $p$ to $1$; hence that value is nonzero. Steps 1.1 through 1.3 and this implication establish all the stated equivalences and the splitting. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

## Determinants and exact sequences

[Open item](item-lem-determinants-of-short-exact-sequences) · level 1

### Statement
Let $X$ be a scheme and let $0\to E'\xrightarrow{i}E\xrightarrow{p}E''\to0$ be a short exact sequence of vector bundles, meaning finite locally free $\mathcal O_X$-modules. There is a canonical isomorphism of line bundles

$$\det E'\otimes\det E''\xrightarrow{\sim}\det E.$$

It is natural for isomorphisms of short exact sequences and compatible with pullback along scheme morphisms. Ranks may be locally constant rather than constant: the determinant is defined on each open rank locus by the corresponding top exterior power.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and suppose $X$ is locally Noetherian. Then determinant induces a group homomorphism $K^0(X)\to\operatorname{Pic}(X)$ from the vector-bundle Grothendieck group to the Picard group, given by $[E]-[F]\mapsto[\det E\otimes(\det F)^{-1}]$. Here $(\det F)^{-1}$ is the tensor-inverse line bundle, and Picard group addition is tensor product. This assertion concerns $K^0$, not the coherent-sheaf group $K_0$.

### Statement references

[def-exterior-determinant-bundles](item-def-exterior-determinant-bundles)

[math:def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme)

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A scheme $X$ and a short exact sequence of vector bundles as in the statement; for the Grothendieck-group assertion, also assume the Axiom of Choice and that $X$ is locally Noetherian.

**Goal:** Construct the canonical determinant isomorphism, prove its functorial properties, and show that determinant respects the defining relations of $K^0(X)$.

[F1] The surjection $E\to E''$ splits locally. On a splitting neighbourhood, $E\cong E'\oplus E''$; ranks add there. [lem-surjection-kernel-bundle](item-lem-surjection-kernel-bundle)

[F2] Exterior powers and determinant of a constant-rank bundle are defined by sheafified exterior algebra. For a free module with an ordered basis, increasing wedges form a basis of each exterior power; in particular the top wedge is a line and wedges above the rank vanish. Exterior powers commute naturally with pullback. The Picard group consists of line-bundle isomorphism classes under tensor product. [def-exterior-determinant-bundles](item-def-exterior-determinant-bundles)

[F3] Under the stated choice and locally Noetherian hypotheses, $K^0(X)$ is generated by isomorphism classes of vector bundles with the relations $[E]=[E']+[E'']$ for short exact sequences. [math:def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; construct the map locally by wedging lifts and use the exact-sequence presentation.

1.1 The rank of a vector bundle is locally constant because it is constant on each local trivialization. Its rank loci are disjoint open subsets covering $X$. Define its determinant separately on these loci by [F2]; the pieces glue uniquely across the disjoint cover. The empty wedge defines the determinant of a rank-zero bundle as $\mathcal O$. [given, F2, construct]

1.2 Work on an open set where the sequence splits and $E',E''$ are free of ranks $a,b$. For local sections $e'_1,\ldots,e'_a$ and $e''_1,\ldots,e''_b$, choose lifts $\widetilde e''_j$ of the latter and send $(e'_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e'_a)\otimes(e''_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e''_b)$ to $i(e'_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge i(e'_a)\wedge\widetilde e''_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\widetilde e''_b$. This formula is multilinear and alternating in each block, so it induces a map from the tensor product of the two top exterior powers. If a lift changes, its difference is a section of $E'$; every new term has $a+1$ factors from $E'$ and vanishes by [F2]. Thus the map is independent of the chosen lifts, including when either rank is zero. [F1, F2, construct]

2.1 With bases of $E'$ and $E''$ and lifts supplied by a splitting, the concatenated vectors form a basis of $E$. The map of step 1.2 sends the generator formed from the two top wedges to the top wedge of that basis, so it is an isomorphism. Its lift-independent formula agrees on overlaps; hence the local maps glue to the asserted global isomorphism. The formula is preserved by isomorphisms of short exact sequences. Pulling it back gives the same wedge formula for the pulled-back sequence, which remains locally split; the exterior-power pullback isomorphisms therefore identify the two determinant maps. [F1, F2, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 Isomorphic bundles have isomorphic determinants by functoriality. Step 2.1 shows that every exact-sequence relation in [F3] maps to the identity relation in $\operatorname{Pic}(X)$. Consequently the assignment $[E]\mapsto[\det E]$ descends from the free abelian group on bundle classes to a homomorphism on $K^0(X)$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Every element of $K^0(X)$ is a difference $[E]-[F]$: collect positive and negative terms into finite direct sums, using the split exact-sequence relations, and use the zero bundle for an empty sum. The homomorphism of step 3.1 therefore has the displayed formula, with inverse in the Picard group represented by the tensor-inverse line bundle. This completes the proof. [F2, F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Normal noetherian schemes reduce to integral components

[Open item](item-lem-normal-scheme-component-reduction) · level 1

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. A noetherian normal scheme $X$ is a finite disjoint union of open-and-closed integral normal subschemes, namely its irreducible components with their restricted structure sheaves. Every affine open $\operatorname{Spec} A\subseteq X$ has $A$ a finite product of noetherian integrally closed domains. Consequently functions, units, line bundles and finite-rank vector bundles are specified componentwise; the rank of a vector bundle is constant on each component.

Here a scheme is noetherian if it has a finite affine open cover by spectra of noetherian rings; it is normal if every local ring is an integrally closed domain. An irreducible space is a nonempty space that is not the union of two proper closed subsets; an irreducible component is a maximal irreducible subset. A scheme is integral if it is irreducible and reduced, where reduced means that its structure sheaf has no nonzero nilpotent local sections. A line bundle is a locally free sheaf of rank one; a finite-rank vector bundle is a locally free sheaf of finite rank, whose rank at a point is the rank on a trivializing neighborhood.

### Statement references

[lem-author-a9a51f3554f8-normal-ring-product](item-lem-author-a9a51f3554f8-normal-ring-product)

[math:def-normal-noetherian-ring](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-normal-noetherian-ring)

### Facts & Assumptions

[F1] Under the Axiom of Choice, a normal noetherian ring is a finite product of noetherian integrally closed domains ([lem-author-a9a51f3554f8-normal-ring-product](item-lem-author-a9a51f3554f8-normal-ring-product)).

[F2] Under the Axiom of Choice, a noetherian topological space is a finite union of its irreducible closed components ([math:lem-noetherian-space-has-finitely-many-irreducible-components](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/lem-noetherian-space-has-finitely-many-irreducible-components)).

[F3] On an affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec} A$, the stalk at a prime $\mathfrak p$ is $A_{\mathfrak p}$ ([math:thm-stalk-structure-sheaf-prime-localization](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-stalk-structure-sheaf-prime-localization)). A noetherian ring is normal when all these localizations are integrally closed domains ([math:def-normal-noetherian-ring](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-normal-noetherian-ring)).

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed; it supplies the choice used by [F1] and [F2] ([math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)).

### Proof

**Given:** A noetherian normal scheme $X$ and the Axiom of Choice.

**Goal:** Prove the finite open-and-closed integral normal decomposition and its stated componentwise consequences.

1.1 Every affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec} A$ has $A$ noetherian: a finite cover of $X$ by noetherian affine opens refines the quasi-compact open $U$ by finitely many principal opens whose coordinate rings are localizations of noetherian rings; the ascending-chain condition on ideals can then be checked after these finitely many localizations, where equality of localized ideals implies equality on $U$. By [F3] and normality of $X$, every prime localization of $A$ is an integrally closed domain. Thus [F1] writes $A$ as a finite product of noetherian integrally closed domains. The corresponding spectra are disjoint open-and-closed subschemes of $U$; each is irreducible and reduced, since it is the spectrum of a domain. In particular, every point of $X$ has an integral affine open neighborhood. [F1, F3, A1, given]

2.1 The underlying topological space of $X$ is noetherian: each member of a finite noetherian affine cover has descending-chain condition on closed sets, and a descending chain of closed subsets of $X$ stabilizes once its restrictions to these finitely many opens stabilize. By [F2], $X$ is the union of finitely many irreducible closed components. If such a component $C$ contains $x$, choose an integral open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ from step 1.1. The nonempty open subset $C\cap U$ is dense in $C$; its closure is contained in the irreducible closure $\overline U$. Maximality of $C$ therefore gives $C=\overline U$. Consequently two components containing $x$ are equal. The finitely many components are thus pairwise disjoint, and each is open as the complement of the union of the others. The empty scheme corresponds to the empty union. [F2, A1, step 1.1]

3.1 Give each open-and-closed component $C$ the restricted structure sheaf. It is irreducible by construction. It is reduced because the integral affine neighborhoods from step 1.1 cover $X$, and nilpotence and vanishing of sections can be checked locally. Its local rings are those of $X$, so they are integrally closed domains; hence $C$ is normal and integral. This proves the decomposition and the affine-ring assertion. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given]

4.1 For a finite disjoint open cover $X=\coprod_i C_i$, restriction and gluing give an equivalence between sheaves on $X$ and tuples of sheaves on the $C_i$: overlaps between different components are empty, so there are no compatibility conditions. Applied to the structure sheaf and its invertible sections, this gives functions and units componentwise; applied to locally free sheaves, it gives line bundles and finite-rank vector bundles componentwise. The rank is locally constant by local freeness; on an irreducible space two disjoint nonempty open rank loci cannot occur, so it is constant on each $C_i$. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Projective bundle pullback detects cohomology classes

[Open item](item-lem-projective-pullback-detection) · level 1

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $H^{*,*}$ be an additively oriented bigraded theory with the projective bundle contract on a category $\mathcal C$ as specified in the contract. For a finite locally free $\mathcal O_X$-module $E$ of constant rank $r>0$, the pullback $\pi^*:H^{*,*}(X)\to H^{*,*}(\mathbb P_X(E))$ along the projective bundle projection is injective. Under the contract's direct-sum isomorphism, $\pi^*$ is the map from the summand indexed by zero. Consequently, pullback along any finite composite of such projective-bundle projections is injective. This conclusion does not assert injectivity for arbitrary pullbacks.

### Statement references
[def-bigraded-oriented-theory](item-def-bigraded-oriented-theory)

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, the category and theory in the statement, an object $X$ of $\mathcal C$, and a finite locally free module $E$ of constant rank $r>0$. A finite locally free module of rank $r$ is locally isomorphic to $\mathcal O_X^r$; $\mathbb P_X(E)$ uses the quotient convention.

**Goal:** Prove the stated injectivity and its preservation under finite iteration.

[F1] The projective bundle contract says that, for each $(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^2$, the map $\Phi_{a,b}:\bigoplus_{m=0}^{r-1}H^{a-2m,b-m}(X)\to H^{a,b}(\mathbb P_X(E))$ sending $(x_m)$ to $\sum_m\pi^*(x_m)\xi^m$ is an isomorphism, where $\xi$ is the first Chern class of the tautological quotient line bundle. Pullbacks preserve bidegrees and are contravariantly functorial; $H^{*,*}$ is the direct sum of its bidegree groups ([def-bigraded-oriented-theory](item-def-bigraded-oriented-theory)).

### Proof
**Proof technique:** Identify pullback with a direct-summand inclusion and compose injective maps.

1.1 Fix $(a,b)$. Since $r>0$, the index zero occurs in the direct sum of [F1]. Let $j_0$ insert $x\in H^{a,b}(X)$ in that summand and put zero in all other summands. The coordinate projection onto that summand is a left inverse to $j_0$, so $j_0$ is injective. By the displayed formula, $\Phi_{a,b}j_0(x)=\pi^*(x)\xi^0=\pi^*(x)$. As $\Phi_{a,b}$ is an isomorphism, $\pi^*:H^{a,b}(X)\to H^{a,b}(\mathbb P_X(E))$ is injective. [F1, construct]

2.1 A class in $H^{*,*}(X)$ has finitely many nonzero bidegree components, and pullback preserves bidegrees. If its pullback vanishes, each component pulls back to zero and is therefore zero by step 1.1. Thus $\pi^*$ is injective on the whole bigraded group. For a finite tower of projections satisfying the same positive-rank hypotheses at each stage, each pullback is injective by the same argument; their composite is injective, and functoriality identifies it with pullback along the composite projection. The empty composite gives the identity. [F1, step 1.1] ∎

## Flag towers with line-bundle quotients

[Open item](item-lem-flag-tower-line-quotients) · level 1

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a scheme and $E$ a vector bundle of constant rank $r\geq 0$. There is a finite tower $q:Y\to X$, obtained by successively projectivizing the current positive-rank kernel in the line-quotient convention, such that $q^*E$ has a filtration
$$0=F_0\subset F_1\subset\cdots\subset F_r=q^*E$$
whose successive quotients $F_i/F_{i-1}$ are line bundles. Each inclusion is locally split. For $r=0$ take $Y=X$ and the zero filtration. No global splitting of the extensions is asserted.

If $X$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, then $Y$ is also quasi-compact and quasi-separated. For finitely many vector bundles, each of constant rank, their towers can be concatenated to obtain one such $Y$ and a filtration for every pulled-back bundle. More generally, over a quasi-compact and quasi-separated $X$, the same simultaneous conclusion holds for finitely many finite locally free bundles of possibly nonconstant rank, with a locally varying length of filtration: construct the tower separately on the finitely many open-and-closed common rank strata and take their finite disjoint union.

A **vector bundle** is a finite locally free $\mathcal O_X$-module; its rank is the number of basis elements on a local free chart. A **line bundle** is a locally free module of rank one. A filtration is **locally split** when each inclusion is locally the inclusion of a direct summand. A scheme is **quasi-compact** if every open cover has a finite subcover, and **quasi-separated** if the intersection of any two quasi-compact open subsets is quasi-compact. A common rank stratum is the subset on which every bundle in the given finite family has its prescribed rank.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, a scheme $X$, and the finite locally free bundles specified in the statement.

**Goal:** Construct the tower and locally split line-quotient filtrations, and prove the stated quasi-compactness and quasi-separatedness properties.

[F1] For a finite locally free bundle $G$ on a scheme $S$, its projective bundle $\pi:\mathbb P_S(G)\to S$ represents invertible quotients and has a tautological surjection $\pi^*G\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal O(1)$ onto a line bundle. Over a trivializing open for $G$ of positive rank $n$, it is $\mathbb P^{n-1}$ over that open. This supplier assumes the Axiom of Choice. [math:thm-projective-bundle-represents-line-quotients](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-projective-bundle-represents-line-quotients)

[F2] The kernel of a surjection of finite locally free modules is finite locally free; the surjection splits locally and the kernel rank is the difference of ranks. [lem-surjection-kernel-bundle](item-lem-surjection-kernel-bundle)

[F3] Over an affine base, projective space has finitely many standard affine charts, and its diagonal over the base is a closed immersion. These constructions restrict over open base subschemes. [math:def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts), [math:lem-projective-space-diagonal-closed](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/lem-projective-space-diagonal-closed)

[F4] The Axiom of Choice supplies the choices inherited from [F1] and the selection of trivializing covers. [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Iterate tautological quotients, pull locally split exact sequences to the final stage, and check the topology on affine charts.

1.1 Set $X_0=X$ and $K_0=E$. For $j=1,\ldots,r$, provided $K_{j-1}$ has rank $r-j+1$, put $X_j=\mathbb P_{X_{j-1}}(K_{j-1})$ with projection $p_j$, and define $K_j$ as the kernel of the tautological surjection $p_j^*K_{j-1}\twoheadrightarrow L_j:=\mathcal O_{X_j}(1)$. By [F1], $L_j$ is a line bundle, and by [F2] $K_j$ is a vector bundle of rank $r-j$ and the resulting short exact sequence is locally split. Induction constructs all $r$ stages. The rank-zero bundle $K_r$ is zero. For $r=0$ no stage is taken. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Put $Y=X_r$ and $q=p_1\circ\cdots\circ p_r$, with the identity map when $r=0$. Pull every sequence of step 1.1 to $Y$ along the composite of the subsequent projections. A locally split exact sequence remains split after pullback on the inverse images of its splitting neighbourhoods; consequently these pullbacks are exact and their kernels embed as locally direct summands. Write $\overline K_j$ for the pullback of $K_j$ to $Y$, and $\overline L_j$ for the pullback of $L_j$. Then $\overline K_0=q^*E$, $\overline K_r=0$, and $0\longrightarrow\overline K_j\longrightarrow\overline K_{j-1}\longrightarrow\overline L_j\longrightarrow0$ is locally split, with $\overline L_j$ a line bundle. Set $F_i=\overline K_{r-i}$. This gives the required filtration, with $F_i/F_{i-1}\cong\overline L_{r-i+1}$. Pullback preserves local freeness because it takes a local free basis to a local free basis. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 We prove the topological assertion for one projective-bundle stage $\pi:P=\mathbb P_S(G)\to S$ with $S$ quasi-compact and quasi-separated and $G$ of positive constant rank. Choose a finite affine cover $U_1,\ldots,U_m$ of $S$ on which $G$ is free: refine a trivializing cover by affine opens and use quasi-compactness. By [F1] and [F3], each $\pi^{-1}(U_i)$ is covered by finitely many standard affine charts, so $P$ is quasi-compact. [F1, F3, F4, construct, step 2.1]

4.1 Let $A$ and $B$ be two of those affine charts, lying over $U_i$ and $U_j$. The intersection $U_i\cap U_j$ is quasi-compact because $S$ is quasi-separated; cover it by finitely many affine opens $W_\nu$. The inverse images of $W_\nu$ in $A$ and $B$ are affine: each chart is affine over its base open, and the inverse image of an affine open under an affine morphism is affine. They are affine opens of $P_{W_\nu}\cong\mathbb P^{n-1}_{W_\nu}$. Their intersection is affine, since the diagonal of this projective space over the affine scheme $W_\nu$ is closed by [F3]: the intersection is its inverse image in the affine fibre product of the two affine opens, hence is a closed subscheme of an affine scheme. These finitely many intersections cover $A\cap B$, so $A\cap B$ is quasi-compact. A scheme with a finite affine open cover whose pairwise intersections are quasi-compact is quasi-separated: any quasi-compact open is covered by finitely many principal affine opens inside the cover, and intersections of such opens are quasi-compact as principal opens in the quasi-compact pairwise chart intersections. Thus $P$ is quasi-separated. [F1, F3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Applying steps 3.1–4.1 successively to the finitely many stages in step 1.1 shows that $Y$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated whenever $X$ is. The rank-zero case is immediate because $Y=X$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 For a finite family of constant-rank bundles, first construct the tower for the first bundle, then pull the second bundle back to its top and construct its tower, and continue. Pullback of each previously constructed locally split filtration remains a locally split filtration with line-bundle quotients, by the argument of step 2.1. The concatenation is finite, and step 5.1 applies at every stage when the initial scheme is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. [step 2.1, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 For a finite family with locally varying ranks on a quasi-compact quasi-separated $X$, each rank function is locally constant: a local free chart has a fixed number of basis elements. Hence every common rank stratum is open, its complement is the union of the other open strata, and it is therefore also closed. The common strata form an open cover of $X$; quasi-compactness makes the set of nonempty strata finite. Each is quasi-compact as a closed subset of $X$ and quasi-separated as an open subscheme: intersections of its quasi-compact opens are intersections in $X$. Apply step 6.1 on each stratum and take the finite disjoint union of the resulting towers and maps. The filtrations have constant length on each stratum, and their pullbacks give the claimed locally varying filtrations. The finite disjoint union is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, since intersections between distinct components are empty and the same properties hold within each component. [step 6.1, construct]

8.1 Steps 1.1–2.1 construct the flag tower and its line quotients; steps 5.1 and 6.1–7.1 prove the remaining claims. Only local splittings have been used, so no global direct-sum decomposition is claimed. [step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1] ∎



## Chern coefficients of the projective relation

[Open item](item-lem-chern-relation-uniqueness) · level 1

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the data and axioms of [def-bigraded-oriented-theory](item-def-bigraded-oriented-theory). Let $E$ be a finite locally free module of constant rank $r>0$ on an object $X$ of the specified category. Write $\pi:\mathbb P_X(E)\to X$ for the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients and $\xi=c_1(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P_X(E)}(1))\in H^{2,1}(\mathbb P_X(E))$ for the first Chern class of its tautological quotient line bundle.

There are unique classes $c_i(E)\in H^{2i,i}(X)$ for $1\leq i\leq r$ such that
$$\xi^r+\sum_{i=1}^r(-1)^i\pi^*c_i(E)\xi^{r-i}=0.$$
They are natural under every morphism $f:Y\to X$ in the specified category: $f^*c_i(E)=c_i(f^*E)$. For the rank-zero bundle, set its total Chern series $c_t(0)=1$ separately; equivalently, $c_0(0)=1$ and $c_i(0)=0$ for $i>0$. No coefficient is recovered from its empty projective bundle.

### Facts & Assumptions

[F1] By [def-bigraded-oriented-theory](item-def-bigraded-oriented-theory), pullbacks are functorial degree-preserving ring homomorphisms, first Chern classes of line bundles are natural, and the projective bundle map $\bigoplus_{m=0}^{r-1}H^{a-2m,b-m}(X)\to H^{a,b}(\mathbb P_X(E))$, $(x_m)\mapsto\sum_m\pi^*x_m\xi^m$, is an isomorphism. The contract includes the quotient projective bundle and its base change, and assumes the Axiom of Choice.

### Proof

**Given:** The theory and bundle in the statement, and a morphism $f:Y\to X$ in the specified category.

**Goal:** Establish existence, uniqueness, bidegrees and base-change naturality of the coefficients, with the separate rank-zero convention.

1.1 Apply the isomorphism in [F1] in bidegree $(2r,r)$ to $-\xi^r$. It gives a unique tuple $a_m\in H^{2(r-m),r-m}(X)$, $0\leq m<r$, with $-\xi^r=\sum_{m=0}^{r-1}\pi^*a_m\xi^m$. Set $c_i(E)=(-1)^i a_{r-i}$. Then $c_i(E)$ has bidegree $(2i,i)$ and the displayed relation holds. Conversely, any tuple satisfying that relation gives the same expansion of $-\xi^r$, so the isomorphism makes every coefficient unique. [F1, given]

2.1 Let $g:\mathbb P_Y(f^*E)\to\mathbb P_X(E)$ be the base-change morphism and $\pi_Y$ the projection. The quotient construction identifies $g^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P_X(E)}(1)$ with $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P_Y(f^*E)}(1)$; hence naturality of $c_1$ gives $g^*\xi=\xi_Y$. Pulling back the relation in step 1.1 and using $\pi\circ g=f\circ\pi_Y$ gives the same relation for $f^*E$ with coefficients $f^*c_i(E)$. Their degrees are preserved, so uniqueness in step 1.1 applied over $Y$ yields $f^*c_i(E)=c_i(f^*E)$. For rank zero, the separately prescribed series $1$ has the stated coefficients and is preserved by unital pullback; no projective-bundle isomorphism for rank zero is invoked. This proves the statement. [F1, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Extending a Whitney class to K zero

[Open item](item-lem-virtual-chern-extension-interface) · level 1

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be an additively oriented bigraded theory with the projective bundle contract on a category $\mathcal C$ of schemes. For each $X$ in $\mathcal C$, suppose that every finite locally free $\mathcal O_X$-module $E$ is assigned a series
$$c_t(E)=1+\sum_{i\geq 1}c_i(E)t^i,\qquad c_i(E)\in H^{2i,i}(X),$$
depending only on its isomorphism class. Assume that these series are natural under morphisms in $\mathcal C$ and satisfy the Whitney identity $c_t(E)=c_t(E')c_t(E'')$ for every short exact sequence $0\to E'\to E\to E''\to0$ of finite locally free modules.

Write $K^0_{\mathrm{vb}}(X)$ for the abelian group generated by the isomorphism classes $[E]$ of finite locally free modules, with the relations $[E]=[E']+[E'']$ for all such exact sequences. Then there is a unique group homomorphism
$$c_t:K^0_{\mathrm{vb}}(X)\longrightarrow \left\{1+\sum_{i\geq1}a_i t^i:a_i\in H^{2i,i}(X)\right\},$$
where the target group uses multiplication of formal series, taking $[E]$ to $c_t(E)$. Every element can be written $[E]-[F]$, and its image is $c_t(E)c_t(F)^{-1}$. The construction is natural in $X$. When $X$ is locally Noetherian, $K^0_{\mathrm{vb}}(X)$ is the vector-bundle Grothendieck group $K^0(X)$ of the cited library definition. The extension is conditional on the stated exact-sequence Whitney identity; the individual coefficients are not asserted to be additive. In particular, the second coefficient obeys the cross-term formula $c_2(x+y)=c_2(x)+c_1(x)c_1(y)+c_2(y)$.

A finite locally free module is an $\mathcal O_X$-module locally isomorphic to a finite direct sum of copies of $\mathcal O_X$. Naturality of the given series means $f^*c_i(E)=c_i(f^*E)$ for every morphism $f:Y\to X$ in $\mathcal C$. A short exact sequence here is an exact sequence of sheaves whose three terms are finite locally free. Formal-series multiplication uses the finite coefficient sums $(ab)_n=\sum_{j=0}^n a_jb_{n-j}$.

### Statement references
[def-bigraded-oriented-theory](item-def-bigraded-oriented-theory)

[math:def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme)

[math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The category, theory, natural bundle series and exact-sequence Whitney identity in the statement, together with the Axiom of Choice.

**Goal:** Construct the unique natural extension, establish the difference formula and the stated coefficient identity, and identify the locally Noetherian case.

[F1] The theory has associative unital bigraded rings, multiplication of bidegree $(0,0)$, graded commutativity in the first degree, and degree-preserving contravariant unital ring pullbacks. These are part of the given theory's contract ([def-bigraded-oriented-theory](item-def-bigraded-oriented-theory)).

[F2] Under Choice, the published vector-bundle Grothendieck group for a locally Noetherian scheme has exactly the generator-and-exact-sequence presentation stated above ([math:def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme), [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)).

[A1] The assigned bundle series are invariant under isomorphism, natural, and multiplicative in every short exact sequence, as stated in the hypotheses.

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Construct the target group coefficient by coefficient and descend a map through the presentation.

1.1 Put $R_X=\bigoplus_{i\geq0}H^{2i,i}(X)$. By [F1], this is a commutative graded ring: the first degree of each homogeneous summand is even. The displayed target consists of series with constant coefficient $1$ and coefficient of $t^i$ in $H^{2i,i}(X)$. Finite coefficient sums show that it is closed under associative, commutative multiplication and contains $1$. For $a(t)=1+\sum_{i\geq1}a_i t^i$, define $b_0=1$ and recursively $b_n=-\sum_{j=1}^n a_jb_{n-j}$. Each $b_n$ has bidegree $(2n,n)$, and the coefficient of $t^n$ in $a(t)b(t)$ is zero for $n>0$. Thus $b(t)$ is an inverse in the displayed set, which is therefore an abelian group. [F1, construct]

1.2 The isomorphism classes of finite locally free modules form a set: choose local trivializations on open subsets, and encode a bundle by a set-indexed open cover, finite ranks, and invertible transition matrices satisfying the overlap identities. The opens, covers and matrices form sets, and the usual gluing construction produces the represented sheaves. Take the free abelian group on these classes, realized as the finitely supported integer-valued functions on that set, and quotient by the subgroup generated by the exact-sequence relations. This gives the group in the statement. The split exact sequence $0\to E\to E\oplus F\to F\to0$ gives $[E\oplus F]=[E]+[F]$, and the zero exact sequence gives $[0]=0$. Consequently, collecting positive and negative terms in any finite expression writes every element as $[E]-[F]$, using the zero bundle for an empty sum. [construct, algebra]

2.1 By [A1] and step 1.1, sending the generator $[E]$ to $c_t(E)$ defines a homomorphism from the free abelian group to the target. For every defining exact-sequence relation its image is $c_t(E)c_t(E')^{-1}c_t(E'')^{-1}=1$ by the Whitney identity. It therefore descends to the quotient. Its value on $[E]-[F]$ is $c_t(E)c_t(F)^{-1}$. Since the classes $[E]$ generate the quotient, these prescribed values also make the extension unique. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 For $f:Y\to X$, pullback sends finite locally free modules to finite locally free modules and preserves the exact sequences used in the presentation: locally the quotient term is free, so the sequence splits, and a split exact sequence remains exact after pullback. Thus $[E]\mapsto[f^*E]$ defines a homomorphism on the presented groups. Degree-preserving ring pullback acts coefficientwise on the target series and respects multiplication and inverses. The assumed naturality gives $f^*c_t(E)=c_t(f^*E)$ on generators, hence on every virtual class by step 2.1. For locally Noetherian $X$, [F2] identifies this same presentation with the published $K^0(X)$; no locally Noetherian hypothesis is used in the preceding construction. [F1, F2, A1, step 2.1]

4.1 Comparing the coefficient of $t^2$ in $c_t(x+y)=c_t(x)c_t(y)$ gives $c_2(x+y)=c_2(x)+c_1(x)c_1(y)+c_2(y)$. Thus coefficientwise additivity does not follow from the group homomorphism: for example, in the formal series group over $\mathbb Z[u]$, the homomorphism $n\mapsto(1+ut)^n$ has second coefficient zero at $1$ and $u^2$ at $2$. This formal example illustrates the cross term; it makes no additional assertion about a particular cohomology theory. The construction and all claimed properties follow. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎


## Dual conventions for the exterior Euler class

[Open item](item-lem-exterior-euler-duality) · level 1

### Statement

Let $X$ be a scheme and $E$ a locally free $\mathcal O_X$-module of constant finite rank $r\geq 0$. Write $E^\vee=\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(E,\mathcal O_X)$ and $\det E=\Lambda^r E$. For every $0\leq i\leq r$ there is a canonical isomorphism
$$\Lambda^{r-i}E\cong\det E\otimes\Lambda^iE^\vee.$$

Let $K^0_{\mathrm{vb}}(X)$ be the vector-bundle Grothendieck ring: its additive group is generated by isomorphism classes $[F]$ of finite locally free $\mathcal O_X$-modules, subject to $[F]=[F']+[F'']$ for every short exact sequence $0\to F'\to F\to F''\to0$ of such modules; multiplication is induced by tensor product and its identity is $[\mathcal O_X]$. Define the exterior Euler class of a rank-$r$ bundle by
$$\lambda_{-1}(E)=\sum_{i=0}^{r}(-1)^i[\Lambda^i E].$$
Then
$$\lambda_{-1}(E)=(-1)^r[\det E]\,\lambda_{-1}(E^\vee).$$
The class $[\det E]$ is a unit, so $\lambda_{-1}(E)=0$ if and only if $\lambda_{-1}(E^\vee)=0$.

The exterior powers, their local increasing-wedge bases, and the determinant line are as in [def-exterior-determinant-bundles](item-def-exterior-determinant-bundles). A line bundle is a locally free module of rank one; a unit in a ring is an element with a multiplicative inverse.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A scheme $X$ and a locally free $\mathcal O_X$-module $E$ of constant finite rank $r\geq0$.

**Goal:** Construct the stated canonical exterior-power isomorphisms and prove the Euler-class identity and simultaneous vanishing.

[F1] On a trivializing open set for $E$ with ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_r$, the increasing wedges of these basis vectors form bases for the exterior powers; $\det E=\Lambda^rE$ is a line bundle. These constructions are functorial in $E$. [def-exterior-determinant-bundles](item-def-exterior-determinant-bundles)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Use the perfect exterior-product pairing and then reindex the finite alternating sum.

1.1 The presentation of $K^0_{\mathrm{vb}}(X)$ is well defined: isomorphism classes of finite locally free modules form a set, since bundles can be encoded by open covers, finite ranks and transition matrices satisfying the overlap identities. Form the free abelian group on those classes and quotient by the subgroup generated by the stated exact-sequence relations. Tensoring an exact sequence of finite locally free modules with another such module preserves exactness, since locally all terms are free and the sequence splits. Consequently tensor product respects the relations in each variable and gives the stated ring multiplication; associativity, commutativity and the identity follow from the corresponding canonical tensor-product isomorphisms. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For each $i$, exterior multiplication gives a canonical pairing $\Lambda^{r-i}E\otimes\Lambda^iE\longrightarrow\det E.$ It induces a map $\Lambda^{r-i}E\to\mathcal Hom(\Lambda^iE,\det E)$. On a trivializing open set, the increasing wedge indexed by a subset $J$ of size $r-i$ pairs to zero with every increasing $i$-wedge except the one indexed by the complementary subset, with which it pairs to $\pm e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_r$. Thus its matrix is a signed permutation matrix, including in characteristic two, and the induced map is an isomorphism. Because the pairing is defined by exterior multiplication, these local isomorphisms agree on overlaps. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Locally, $E^\vee$ has the dual basis $e_1^\vee,\ldots,e_r^\vee$. The canonical map $\Lambda^i E^\vee\to(\Lambda^i E)^\vee$ sends $\phi_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\phi_i$ to the functional $v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_i\mapsto\det(\phi_a(v_b))$. It sends each increasing dual wedge to the dual of the corresponding increasing wedge basis vector, hence is an isomorphism. Likewise the evaluation map $\det E\otimes(\Lambda^i E)^\vee\to\mathcal Hom(\Lambda^iE,\det E)$ is locally an isomorphism. These maps are canonical and therefore glue. Combining their inverses with step 1.2 gives the asserted canonical isomorphism. The same argument covers $i=0$, $i=r$, and $r=0$, using the empty wedge. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Taking classes in the ring and substituting $j=r-i$ gives $\begin{aligned} \lambda_{-1}(E)&=\sum_{i=0}^r(-1)^i[\Lambda^iE] =\sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^{r-j}[\det E][\Lambda^jE^\vee]\\ &=(-1)^r[\det E]\lambda_{-1}(E^\vee). \end{aligned}$ The dual line $(\det E)^\vee$ has the property that the evaluation map $\det E\otimes(\det E)^\vee\to\mathcal O_X$ is an isomorphism locally and hence globally. Thus $[(\det E)^\vee]$ is the inverse of $[\det E]$. Multiplication by the unit $(-1)^r[\det E]$ is bijective, proving simultaneous vanishing. This establishes all claims. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Local ranks in the affine bundle correspondence

[Open item](item-lem-author-3af31ead36fb-local-rank) · level 1

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $E$ is a rank-$r$ vector bundle on $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and $P=\Gamma(X,E)$, then $P$ is finite projective and $P_{\mathfrak p}$ is free of rank $r$ over $A_{\mathfrak p}$ for every prime $\mathfrak p$. A vector bundle is a finite locally free sheaf, and rank $r$ means that its local free rank is $r$ at every point.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative unital ring $A$, a rank-$r$ vector bundle $E$ on $\operatorname{Spec}A$, and the Axiom of Choice.

**Goal:** Identify the projectivity and local ranks of $P=\Gamma(X,E)$.

[F1] The affine bundle–module equivalence preserves rank and identifies the stalk of the associated sheaf at $\mathfrak p$ with the localization of the module. [lem-affine-bundle-module-interface](item-lem-affine-bundle-module-interface)

### Proof

1.1 By the affine equivalence, $P$ is finite projective and its associated sheaf is isomorphic to $E$. [F1, given]

2.1 At each prime, the stalk of $E$ is free of rank $r$ over the local ring $A_{\mathfrak p}$ by the definition of rank. The stalk identification in [F1] therefore gives $P_{\mathfrak p}\cong A_{\mathfrak p}^r$. [F1, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Projectivity and rank of a free-summand complement

[Open item](item-lem-author-3af31ead36fb-split-complement) · level 1

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P$ be a finite projective module of constant rank $r\geq1$ over a nonzero commutative ring $A$. If $P\cong A\oplus Q$, then $Q$ is finite projective of constant rank $r-1$, and the associated bundles satisfy $\widetilde P\cong\mathcal O_{\operatorname{Spec}A}\oplus\widetilde Q$. Constant rank means that every prime localization is free of the specified rank.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $A$, $P$, $Q$, $r$, the decomposition, and the Axiom of Choice as in the statement.

**Goal:** Establish finite projectivity, rank, and the associated bundle decomposition.

[F1] Under Choice, the affine bundle–module correspondence preserves direct sums and rank, and finite projective modules correspond to vector bundles. [lem-affine-bundle-module-interface](item-lem-affine-bundle-module-interface)

### Proof

1.1 The projection of a finite generating set of $P$ generates $Q$. A direct summand of a projective module is projective: to lift a map from $Q$ through a surjection, precompose it with the projection $P\to Q$, lift from $P$, and restrict to $Q$. Hence $Q$ is finite projective. [given, construct]

2.1 By [F1], $\widetilde P\cong\mathcal O_X\oplus\widetilde Q$, where $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$, and $\widetilde Q$ is a vector bundle. At any prime, taking residue-field fibers of this decomposition gives $r=1+\dim_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}(Q\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p))$. The rank correspondence in [F1] gives rank $r-1$ at every prime. [F1, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Affine bundle classes are actual projective-module classes

[Open item](item-lem-author-f08c343a07fc-cancel-module-classes) · level 1

### Statement
Assume AC. For a commutative unital ring $A$, the maps $E\mapsto\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}A,E)$ and $P\mapsto\widetilde P$ induce inverse bijections between rank-$r$ bundle isomorphism classes and constant-rank-$r$ finite projective module isomorphism classes. In particular two bundles are isomorphic if and only if their modules of sections are isomorphic.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data and hypotheses in the statement.

**Goal:** Establish the stated conclusion.

[F1] The affine equivalence preserves rank and is quasi-inverse. [lem-affine-bundle-module-interface](item-lem-affine-bundle-module-interface)

### Proof

1.1 The equivalence sends rank-$r$ objects into rank-$r$ objects. A functor sends an invertible morphism to an invertible morphism, so both assignments descend to isomorphism classes. [F1]

2.1 The unit and counit are isomorphisms. Thus the composites induce the identity on classes, and a module isomorphism sheafifies to a bundle isomorphism and conversely. [F1, step 1.1] ∎

## Normal affine threefolds have controlled nonsmooth strata

[Open item](item-lem-author-fc2380accb47-normal-smooth-strata) · level 1

### Statement
Let $k$ be algebraically closed and let $X$ be a normal affine finite-type $k$-scheme of dimension at most three. It has finitely many open-and-closed integral normal components. Let $X_3$ be the union of its three-dimensional components, $W=(X_3)_{\mathrm{sm}/k}$, and $D=X\setminus W$ with reduced structure. Then $W$ is smooth of pure dimension three and $D$ is closed with $\dim D\leq2$. On $X_3$ its nonsmooth locus has dimension at most one. If $X$ is pure three-dimensional, $D$ is exactly its singular locus and has dimension at most one. This formulation also handles a definition of threefold meaning merely dimension three.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The field and scheme above; the empty stratum is allowed.

**Goal:** Isolate a smooth three-dimensional locus and a closed avoidance locus of dimension less than the rank three.

[F1] [thm-author-fc2380accb47-normal-geometric-input](item-thm-author-fc2380accb47-normal-geometric-input) supplies finite clopen normal components, normality implying regularity in codimension one, and equality of smooth and regular loci for reduced finite-type schemes over a perfect field.

[F2] [thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input](item-thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input) supplies finite-type dimension and codimension formulas.

### Proof
1.1 The scheme is Noetherian. By [F1] its irreducible components are disjoint open-and-closed integral normal schemes, and there are finitely many because $X$ is quasi-compact. Their union $X_3$ is therefore clopen. The other components have dimension at most two. [F1, given]

2.1 An algebraically closed field is perfect. On each three-dimensional component, [F1] identifies smoothness over $k$ with regularity and makes the smooth locus open. The nonsmooth locus has no points of codimension zero or one, since normality gives $(R_1)$. By [F2] every irreducible closed subset of that nonsmooth locus has dimension at most $3-2=1$. Hence it is closed of dimension at most one. Combining it with the other clopen components proves that $D$ is closed of dimension at most two. Removing it leaves the smooth pure-dimensional locus $W$. In the pure-dimensional case there are no other components, giving the sharper bound. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎


## Coordinate multiples of dual generators span all first jets

[Open item](item-lem-author-fc2380accb47-coordinate-first-jets) · level 1

### Statement
Assume AC. Let $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ be finite type over an algebraically closed field, let $E$ be a rank-three bundle, and let $W\hookrightarrow X$ be a locally closed smooth $k$-subscheme of pure dimension three. Choose $k$-algebra generators $f_1,\ldots,f_d$ of $A$ and generators $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m$ of the coherent bundle $E$. The finite indexed family
$$\phi_i,\ f_l\phi_i\quad(1\leq i\leq m,\ 1\leq l\leq d)$$
defines a parameter space $T=\mathbb A_k^N$, where $N=m(d+1)$; linear relations among the listed sections are permitted. The evaluation $\mathcal O_X^N\twoheadrightarrow E$ is surjective. On $W$ its first-jet map $j:\mathcal O_W^N\twoheadrightarrow J^1(E|_W)$ is also surjective, and $J^1(E|_W)$ has rank twelve.

Here the first-jet bundle is defined by local pairs $(v,\omega)$ in $E\oplus(\Omega^1_{W/k}\otimes E)$. Under a change of frame $G$ the pair transforms by $(v,\omega)\mapsto(Gv,G\omega+(dG)v)$. The product rule verifies the cocycle law and invertibility, so these charts define a vector bundle with exact sequence $0\to\Omega^1_{W/k}\otimes E\to J^1E\to E\to0$. The jet of a section with coefficient column $a$ is $(a,da)$. Thus at a closed point $x\in W$ the jet fiber is $(E|_W)_x/\mathfrak m_{W,x}^2(E|_W)_x$ over $k$, where both the stalk and maximal ideal are on $W$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The stated affine scheme and bundles. Generators exist by [lem-affine-coherent-global-generation](item-lem-affine-coherent-global-generation) applied to $E$, with AC.

**Goal:** Obtain actual first-order separation, beyond fiberwise generation.

[F1] The completed affine-generation and kernel lemmas give the finite generators and local splittings of surjections between bundles. [lem-affine-coherent-global-generation](item-lem-affine-coherent-global-generation), [lem-surjection-kernel-bundle](item-lem-surjection-kernel-bundle), [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

[F2] Finite-type $k$-schemes are Jacobson and their closed points are $k$-rational. A coherent sheaf with no closed points in its support is zero. [thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input](item-thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input)

### Proof
1.1 Evaluation is surjective because the listed sections already include the generators $\phi_i$. The transition formula in the Statement follows by differentiating $Ga$; the product rule also shows that its composition for two frame changes equals the formula for their product. It therefore constructs $J^1E$ and the global $\mathcal O_W$-linear jet evaluation map from the indexed list. Since $W$ is smooth three-dimensional, $\Omega^1_{W/k}$ has rank three; the exact sequence gives rank $3+9=12$. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 Fix a closed $x\in W$. The elements $f_l-f_l(x)$ generate the maximal ideal of $x$ in $A$, because $A$ is generated by the $f_l$ and its residue map is evaluation at their $k$-values. The immersion induces a surjection $\mathfrak m_{X,x}/\mathfrak m_{X,x}^2\twoheadrightarrow\mathfrak m_{W,x}/\mathfrak m_{W,x}^2$: locally a locally closed immersion is a quotient of the ambient local ring. Consequently the restrictions of those differences span the latter cotangent space. The values of the $\phi_i$ span the three-dimensional bundle fiber. Constants times $\phi_i$ can consequently realize an arbitrary prescribed value at $x$. Each section $(f_l-f_l(x))\phi_i$ is in the $k$-linear span of our indexed family, vanishes at $x$, and has first-order class $d f_l\otimes\phi_i(x)$. These classes span the entire kernel $(\mathfrak m_{W,x}/\mathfrak m_{W,x}^2)\otimes_k E(x)$ of the jet-to-value map. Adjusting the initial chosen section by their linear combinations therefore realizes any prescribed first jet. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The jet-evaluation cokernel is coherent. Step 2.1 makes its fiber zero at every closed point, and Nakayama's lemma makes its stalk zero there. Its support is closed and cannot be nonempty by the Jacobson property in [F2]. It is zero, so $j$ is a bundle surjection everywhere, not just on the closed points. It splits locally by [F1]. All constructions use ordinary products and derivatives, with no division by a positive integer. [F1, F2, step 2.1] ∎
