## Integer multiplication on rational complexes

[Open item](item-lem-author-4b6f215bcf3b-rational-complex-multiplication) · level 1

### Statement
Let C be a cochain complex of Q-vector spaces, with Q-linear differentials, and n a positive integer. Multiplication by n is an isomorphism of C as a complex of abelian groups and hence in the derived category D(Z). Here D(Z) is the category of cochain complexes of abelian groups with quasi-isomorphisms inverted; a quasi-isomorphism induces isomorphisms on all cohomology groups.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** C and n as in the statement.

**Goal:** Prove that multiplication by n on C is an isomorphism in D(Z).

[F1] Multiplication by n on each Q-vector space is invertible, with inverse multiplication by 1/n. [lem-author-4b6f215bcf3b-rational-module-multiplication](item-lem-author-4b6f215bcf3b-rational-module-multiplication)

### Proof

1.1 By [F1], multiplication by 1/n is the inverse of multiplication by n in every degree. Q-linearity of the differentials makes multiplication by 1/n commute with them, so these inverses form a chain map. [F1, given]

2.1 The two chain maps are mutually inverse, and their images remain inverse in D(Z). [step 1.1] ∎

## Derived finite coefficients preserve mapping cones

[Open item](item-lem-author-4b6f215bcf3b-quotient-cofiber) · level 1


### Statement
For a morphism $f:A\to B$ in $D(\mathbb Z)$ and a positive integer $n$, there is an isomorphism
$$\operatorname{cofib}(f\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n)\cong\operatorname{cofib}(f)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n.$$
Here cofibers in the triangulated category $D(\mathbb Z)$ are considered up to isomorphism. More precisely, fix the complex $P=[\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb Z]$ in degrees $-1$ and $0$. For every cochain map $g:A'\to B'$ representing a derived morphism, there is a chain isomorphism
$$\operatorname{Cone}(g)\otimes P\cong\operatorname{Cone}(g\otimes 1_P),$$
natural for strictly commutative squares of cochain maps. Naturality refers to this chain-level construction with fixed $n$ and $P$.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A morphism $f$ in $D(\mathbb Z)$ and $n>0$.

**Goal:** Identify the two indicated cofibers.

[F1] The two-term complex $P=[\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb Z]$ in degrees $-1$ and $0$ is K-flat and resolves $\mathbb Z/n$. Thus tensoring with $P$ computes derived finite coefficients. [lem-derived-coefficient-exact-sequence](item-lem-derived-coefficient-exact-sequence)

### Proof

1.1 Represent $f$ by a cochain map $g:A'\to B'$ after quasi-isomorphic replacements if necessary. Use the convention $\operatorname{Cone}(g)^k=B'^k\oplus A'^{k+1}$, with differential $(b,a)\mapsto(d_{B'}b+g(a),-d_{A'}a)$. Since $P$ has only two nonzero terms, each degree of the tensor total complex is a finite direct sum. Splitting its summands gives a degreewise isomorphism $\operatorname{Cone}(g)\otimes P\to\operatorname{Cone}(g\otimes 1_P)$, sending $b\otimes p$ to the target summand and $a\otimes p$ to the shifted source summand without changing either tensor. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 For homogeneous $a\in A'^{i+1}$ and $p\in P^j$, the differential on the shifted source tensor has components $g(a)\otimes p$, $-d_{A'}a\otimes p$ and $(-1)^i a\otimes d_Pp$ on both sides. On $b\otimes p$, both differentials are the ordinary tensor differential. Thus the degreewise identification is a chain isomorphism. For any strictly commutative square from $g$ to another cochain map, the induced cone maps act separately on the source and target summands; hence they commute with this identification. This proves the claimed chain-level naturality. By K-flatness of $P$, tensoring with $P$ computes derived finite coefficients and preserves the quasi-isomorphisms used for the representatives. The two chain complexes therefore give the asserted isomorphism of derived objects, with cofibers considered up to isomorphism. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## External non-A¹ projective-relation filtered and Whitney theorem

[Open item](item-thm-author-4f94f7982b0d-non-a1-whitney-input) · level 1


### Statement
Let $\mathcal E$ be a homotopy-commutative linearly oriented motivic ring spectrum over a qcqs derived scheme $S$, satisfying its actual class-power PBF. For a bundle $V$ of positive constant rank $r$ on $Y\in\mathrm{Sm}_S$, define $\widetilde c_i(V)$ by the quotient-projective relation
$$\sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^j\xi^j p^*\widetilde c_{r-j}(V)=0,\qquad\widetilde c_0=1.$$
Then a subbundle filtration with line quotients $L_s$ satisfies $\widetilde c_t(V)=\prod_s(1+c_1(L_s)t)$, and every fiber sequence of vector bundles $V'\to V\to V''$ satisfies $\widetilde c_t(V)=\widetilde c_t(V')\widetilde c_t(V'')$.

For the zero bundle adopt $\widetilde c_t(0)=1$, and read coefficients above the degree of any Chern polynomial as zero. These are explicit local coefficient conventions extending the positive-rank definition. With them both identities also hold when a bundle has rank zero: a zero end term in a fiber sequence makes the other map an isomorphism, and the rank-zero filtered formula is the empty product $1$.

The rank-zero extension and the polynomial coefficient convention are local, rather than assertions that Definition 4.4.1 defines a zero-bundle class. For a zero end term, the isomorphism just noted preserves the positive-rank coefficients because their projective relation and orientation are preserved; if the middle bundle is zero, all three bundles are zero.

The local chain verifies the model, orientation, product and PBF hypotheses and applies the input with base $S=X$, evaluated at the smooth identity $X\to X$. Thus smooth-relative scope imposes no smoothness of $X/k$. The substantial geometric splitting and vanishing argument is imported through the stated source result; its proof and upstream machinery are not reconstructed here.

## Stable triviality as the kernel of a right-invertible matrix

[Open item](item-lem-author-b02e51f9da03-matrix-kernel) · level 1

### Statement
Assume AC. Let $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$, and let $E$ be a bundle of constant rank $r$. Then $E$ is stably trivial if and only if, for some $N\geq0$, it is the bundle associated to $\ker q$ for an $A$-linear map $q:A^{r+N}\to A^N$ admitting a right inverse $j:A^N\to A^{r+N}$, $qj=\operatorname{id}$. Such a map is a **right-invertible matrix** after the standard free bases are fixed. Its kernel $P$ is finite projective of rank $r$, with actual splitting $P\oplus A^N\xrightarrow{\sim}A^{r+N}$ given by $(v,w)\mapsto v+j(w)$.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data and hypotheses in the statement, AC and the article's fixed universe bounds where its K-theory is used.

**Goal:** Establish the stated conclusion.

[F1] Stable triviality means an actual isomorphism $E\oplus\mathcal O_X^N\cong\mathcal O_X^{r+N}$ for some N. [def-stably-free-bundles](item-def-stably-free-bundles)

[F2] The affine equivalence preserves rank, direct sums and actual bundle/module isomorphisms. [lem-affine-bundle-module-interface](item-lem-affine-bundle-module-interface)

### Proof

1.1 If $E$ is stably trivial, use [F2] to obtain an isomorphism $\alpha:P\oplus A^N\to A^{r+N}$, where $P=\Gamma(X,E)$. Transport projection onto $A^N$ and its standard section through $\alpha$; they give $q=\operatorname{pr}_2\alpha^{-1}$ and $j(w)=\alpha(0,w)$. Then $qj=\operatorname{id}$ and $\alpha(P\oplus0)=\ker q$. [F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Conversely, if $qj=\operatorname{id}$, the displayed splitting has inverse $z\mapsto(z-jq(z),q(z))$. The first coordinate is in $\ker q$. Hence this kernel is a direct summand of a finite free module, thus finite projective. Localize the decomposition at each prime; its local free rank is $(r+N)-N=r$. By [F2] its associated bundle, stabilized by the indicated trivial bundle, is trivial. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

### Statement
Fix a perfect field $k$. Write $H_{\rm Spi}$ for Spitzweck's integral field spectrum, $H_{\mathbb A}=s^0KGL_k$, and $U=s^0\mathbf1_k$. There is a specified zigzag of unital motivic ring equivalences
$$H_{\rm Spi}\xleftarrow{u_{\rm Spi}}U\xrightarrow{u_K}H_{\mathbb A}.$$
Both arrows are induced by units and the zeroth-slice functor. Their integral equivalence, including in characteristic $p$, is justified below using the canonical rank construction over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ and base change, rather than inferring it from a product-compatible field coefficient model. The shifted graded coefficient maps preserve products, units and the unit-adjoint reduced $\mathbb P^1$ class, with the same Tate-coordinate convention on both sides.

$$(\Sigma^\infty_{\rm fr}\mathrm{Vect})/\beta\longrightarrow\Sigma^\infty_{\rm fr}\mathbb Z\simeq H_{\rm Spi}.$$
Here $f_1H_{\rm Spi}=0$ holds over the Dedekind base $\mathbb Z$ as explicitly stated with Theorem1.1; the 1/2 assumption belongs only to the separate KO assertion. Bott periodicity identifies the displayed cofiber with $s^0KGL_{\mathbb Z}$.

[F3] Hoyois, The localization theorem for framed motivic spaces, Theorem21 and proof, identify $\Sigma^\infty_{\rm fr}\mathbb Z$ with Spitzweck HZ by a natural E∞ equivalence, adjoint to the actual ring isomorphism on constant integers. It sends the rank-one constant to the ring unit, and is stable under arbitrary base change. Spitzweck Remark11.2 supplies the canonical unit-induced E∞ map $u_{\rm Spi}:s^0\mathbf1\to s^0H_{\rm Spi}\simeq H_{\rm Spi}$ over fields. Consequently the composite of the sphere unit through $f_0KGL$, its Bott cofiber, and $a$ is the actual unit of $H_{\rm Spi}$, by the adjunction construction in [F3]. Thus the triangle in step 1.1 identifies $b$ with $a\circ u_{K,\mathbb Z}$. Both factors are integral equivalences by [F1]–[F2], so $b$ is an equivalence. Its E∞ structure is the one supplied by multiplicative slices and the actual unit; no multiplicative structure on an arbitrary chosen Bott quotient is required for this inference. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Pull this unit triangle back along $g$. Spitzweck HZ is absolute, and BEM Corollary9.7 identifies $g^*s^0\mathbf1_{\mathbb Z}$ with $s^0\mathbf1_k$. Naturality of units and slice comparison identifies the resulting map with the canonical $u_{{\rm Spi},k}$ in [F3]: both factor the same unit into the field zero-slice target. ## Equality in affine K zero and stable isomorphism

[Open item](item-lem-k-zero-stable-equivalence) · level 2


### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X=\operatorname{Spec} A$ be a noetherian affine scheme, where $A$ is a commutative ring with unit, and let $E$ and $F$ be vector bundles on $X$. Their classes in the vector-bundle Grothendieck group $K^0(X)$ are equal if and only if there is an integer $N\geq 0$ and an isomorphism $E\oplus\mathcal O_X^N\cong F\oplus\mathcal O_X^N$.

A **vector bundle** is a finite locally free $\mathcal O_X$-module: each point has a neighbourhood on which the module is isomorphic to a finite direct sum of copies of $\mathcal O_X$. The displayed isomorphism is called a **stable isomorphism**. The group $K^0(X)$ is the abelian group generated by isomorphism classes $[V]$ of vector bundles, with the relation $[V]=[V']+[V'']$ for every short exact sequence $0\to V'\to V\to V''\to0$ of vector bundles. In particular, it is the vector-bundle group, not the Grothendieck group of coherent sheaves.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, a noetherian affine scheme $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$, and vector bundles $E,F$ on $X$.

**Goal:** Prove that $[E]=[F]$ in $K^0(X)$ exactly when $E$ and $F$ are stably isomorphic as stated.

[A1] The assumed Axiom of Choice is used through the affine bundle–module equivalence and splitting in [F1] and the Grothendieck-group convention in [F3]. The complement construction in [F2] itself uses only finite choices. [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

[F1] Under the Axiom of Choice, every short exact sequence of vector bundles on an affine scheme splits. Associated sheaf and global sections give an equivalence between vector bundles on $X$ and finite projective $A$-modules, preserving finite direct sums; the sheaf associated to $A^N$ is $\mathcal O_X^N$. A finite projective module is a finitely generated module with the lifting property for maps through surjective module homomorphisms. [lem-affine-bundle-module-interface](item-lem-affine-bundle-module-interface)

[F2] Every finite projective $A$-module $P$ has a finite projective complement $Q$ with $P\oplus Q\cong A^N$ for some $N\geq0$. [lem-finite-projective-complements](item-lem-finite-projective-complements)

[F3] Since $X$ is locally noetherian, the vector-bundle group has the generators and exact-sequence relations in the statement. Its bundle isomorphism classes form a set. [math:def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Construct the group completion of the direct-sum monoid and then replace a common bundle summand by a free one.

1.1 Let $M$ be the set of isomorphism classes of vector bundles, with addition induced by direct sum and zero the class of the zero bundle. Direct sum is associative and commutative up to isomorphism, so $M$ is a commutative monoid. On $M\times M$ define $(a,b)\sim(c,d)$ when there is $t\in M$ such that $a+d+t=b+c+t$. This is an equivalence relation: reflexivity and symmetry are immediate; for transitivity, if $a+d+t=b+c+t$ and $c+f+u=d+e+u$, adding $f+u$ to the first equality and $b+t$ to the second yields $a+f+(d+t+u)=b+e+(d+t+u)$. Componentwise addition respects the relation. Thus the quotient is an abelian group, with zero represented by $(0,0)$ and inverse of $(a,b)$ represented by $(b,a)$; indeed $(a+b,a+b)\sim(0,0)$. [F3, construct]

2.1 The assignment sending a bundle class $a$ to the class of $(a,0)$ is additive. By [F1], each short exact sequence in the presentation of $K^0(X)$ splits, so its middle bundle is isomorphic to the direct sum of its ends. Consequently this assignment respects every relation in [F3] and induces a homomorphism from $K^0(X)$ to the group constructed in step 1.1. If $[E]=[F]$ in $K^0(X)$, their images are equal, so by the definition of $\sim$ there is a vector bundle $H$ with $E\oplus H\cong F\oplus H$. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F1], $H$ corresponds to a finite projective $A$-module $P$. Choose $Q$ and $N$ as in [F2], and let $H'$ be the vector bundle associated to $Q$. The direct-sum compatibility in [F1] gives $H\oplus H'\cong\mathcal O_X^N$. Adding $H'$ to both sides of the isomorphism in step 2.1 and using associativity therefore gives $E\oplus\mathcal O_X^N\cong F\oplus\mathcal O_X^N$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Conversely, if such an isomorphism holds, the split exact-sequence relations in [F3] give $[E]+[\mathcal O_X^N]=[F]+[\mathcal O_X^N]$ in the abelian group $K^0(X)$. Adding the inverse of $[\mathcal O_X^N]$ proves $[E]=[F]$. Together with step 3.1 this establishes the equivalence. [F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎


## Functions extend across codimension two

[Open item](item-lem-codimension-two-extension) · level 2

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a noetherian normal scheme and let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be an open immersion whose image contains every point of codimension at most one in its irreducible component. Then restriction is an isomorphism of sheaves of rings $\mathcal O_X\cong j_*\mathcal O_U$. Consequently restriction gives isomorphisms on global functions and on groups of global units.

Here a noetherian normal scheme is a scheme with a finite cover by spectra of noetherian rings and with all local rings integrally closed domains. The codimension of a point in its irreducible component is the supremum of the lengths of chains of strict specializations from that component's generic point to the given point. A global unit is a global function admitting a multiplicative inverse.

### Facts & Assumptions

[F1] Under the Axiom of Choice, every affine open of a noetherian normal scheme is the spectrum of a finite product of noetherian integrally closed domains; the corresponding factor spectra are open and closed integral subschemes ([lem-normal-scheme-component-reduction](item-lem-normal-scheme-component-reduction)).

[F2] Under the Axiom of Choice, a noetherian integrally closed domain $A$ with fraction field $K$ equals the intersection of its height-one localizations inside $K$ ([math:lem-normal-noetherian-domain-intersection-of-height-one-localizations](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/lem-normal-noetherian-domain-intersection-of-height-one-localizations)). If there are no height-one primes, the intersection is understood to be $K$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed for [F1] and [F2] ([math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)).

### Proof

**Given:** A noetherian normal scheme $X$, an open immersion $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ containing all points of component codimension at most one, and the Axiom of Choice.

**Goal:** Show that $\mathcal O_X\to j_*\mathcal O_U$ is an isomorphism and obtain the asserted global isomorphisms.

1.1 It suffices to prove that restriction $\mathcal O_X(V)\to\mathcal O_U(U\cap V)$ is an isomorphism on a basis of affine opens $V$: the kernel and cokernel sheaves then have zero stalks. By [F1], each such $V$ is a finite disjoint union of affine spectra of noetherian integrally closed domains. These factor spectra form a basis as $V$ varies, and restriction to a factor preserves its structure sheaf. Thus it is enough to consider $V=\operatorname{Spec} A$ for such a domain $A$. Its generic point and each point corresponding to a height-one prime of $A$ belong to $U$: codimension is unchanged when passing to an open neighborhood, since chains of generalizations of a point in an open set remain in that open set. [F1, A1, given]

2.1 Put $W=U\cap V$ and let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. Since $W$ contains the generic point, it is dense in the integral scheme $V$. A section $s$ on $W$ determines an element $z\in K$ by its generic stalk. For every height-one prime $\mathfrak p$, the point $\mathfrak p$ lies in $W$, so the germ of $s$ there belongs to $A_{\mathfrak p}$ and maps to $z$ in $K$. Hence $z$ lies in every height-one localization, and [F2] gives $z\in A$. The section defined by $z$ agrees with $s$ on $W$: on any principal open $D(f)\subseteq W$, both are elements of the domain $A_f$ and have the same image in $K$, so they are equal; such opens cover $W$. Thus restriction from $A$ to $\mathcal O_U(W)$ is surjective. It is injective because $W$ contains the generic point and $A\hookrightarrow K$ is injective. This also covers the case that $A$ is a field. [F2, A1, step 1.1, given]

3.1 Steps 1.1 and 2.1 show that the restriction morphism is an isomorphism on a basis and therefore an isomorphism of sheaves of rings. Taking sections over $X$ gives $\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)\cong\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$. A ring isomorphism carries precisely the invertible elements to invertible elements, with inverses preserved, so it also gives an isomorphism of global unit groups. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Smooth density and normal codimension over a perfect field

[Open item](item-lem-perfect-base-smooth-density) · level 2

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a reduced finite-type scheme over a perfect field $k$. Its smooth locus is open and meets every irreducible component in a dense open subset. If $X$ is normal, its nonsmooth locus has codimension at least two in every irreducible component.

A field is perfect if all its algebraic extensions are separable. Finite type means that $X$ has a finite affine cover by spectra of finitely generated $k$-algebras. Reduced means that every local ring has no nonzero nilpotents; normal means that every local ring is an integrally closed domain. The smooth locus is the set of points where $X\to\operatorname{Spec} k$ is smooth. For an integral component $C$, the codimension of a point is the supremum of lengths of strict chains of irreducible closed subsets from $C$ to the closure of the point; the codimension of a subset is the infimum over its points, with the empty subset having codimension $+\infty$.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a perfect field $k$, and a reduced finite-type $k$-scheme $X$.

**Goal:** Prove openness and componentwise density of the smooth locus and, when $X$ is normal, the codimension bound on its complement.

[F1] A finite-variable polynomial algebra over a field is noetherian ([math:lem-finite-variable-polynomial-algebras-over-fields-are-noetherian-direct](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/lem-finite-variable-polynomial-algebras-over-fields-are-noetherian-direct)). Its quotients are noetherian, because the preimage of every ideal is finitely generated.

[F2] Under AC, the smooth locus of a locally finitely presented morphism is open ([math:thm-smooth-locus-open](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-smooth-locus-open)). AC means that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)).

[F3] For a reduced scheme locally of finite type over a perfect field, smoothness at a point is equivalent to regularity of its local ring; this is an external input ([lem-author-2389e5bafea8-perfect-pointwise-smoothness](item-lem-author-2389e5bafea8-perfect-pointwise-smoothness)).

[F4] Under the assumed AC, a generic local ring of a reduced scheme is a field, and every field is regular local ([lem-author-2389e5bafea8-generic-reduced-local-ring](item-lem-author-2389e5bafea8-generic-reduced-local-ring), [lem-author-2389e5bafea8-field-regular-local](item-lem-author-2389e5bafea8-field-regular-local)). An open subset containing the generic point of a component meets it densely ([lem-author-2389e5bafea8-open-generic-density](item-lem-author-2389e5bafea8-open-generic-density)).

[F5] Under AC, a noetherian normal scheme is a finite disjoint union of open-and-closed integral normal components, and each affine coordinate ring is a finite product of noetherian integrally closed domains ([lem-normal-scheme-component-reduction](item-lem-normal-scheme-component-reduction)). For a noetherian integrally closed domain, localization at a height-one prime is a discrete valuation ring ([math:thm-height-one-localisation-of-normal-noetherian-domain-is-dvr](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-height-one-localisation-of-normal-noetherian-domain-is-dvr)), and such a ring is regular local ([lem-author-2389e5bafea8-dvr-regular-local](item-lem-author-2389e5bafea8-dvr-regular-local)). Affine stalks are prime localizations ([math:thm-stalk-structure-sheaf-prime-localization](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-stalk-structure-sheaf-prime-localization)).

[F6] A subset of an integral scheme with no points of codimension zero or one has codimension at least two ([lem-author-2389e5bafea8-codimension-exclusion](item-lem-author-2389e5bafea8-codimension-exclusion)).

### Proof

1.1 On each finite-type affine chart $\operatorname{Spec} A$, write $A=k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/I$. By [F1], the polynomial ring is noetherian, so $I$ is finitely generated and $A$ is both noetherian and finitely presented over $k$. Thus $X$ is noetherian and its structure morphism is locally finitely presented. By [F2] its smooth locus $U$ is open. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 Each irreducible component of a scheme has a generic point $\eta$. By reducedness and [F4], $\mathcal O_{X,\eta}$ is a field and hence regular local. The pointwise input [F3] therefore gives $\eta\in U$. By [F4], $U\cap C$ is dense open in each component $C$. This also covers the empty scheme vacuously. [F3, F4, step 1.1, given]

2.2 Now suppose $X$ normal. By step 1.1 and [F5], its components are open-and-closed integral normal schemes. Fix one component $C$ and a point $x$ of codimension one in it. Choose an affine neighborhood $\operatorname{Spec} A\subset C$ of $x$. The component reduction [F5] makes $A$ a finite product of noetherian integrally closed domains; since its spectrum is a nonempty open subset of the irreducible space $C$, it is irreducible, so there is only one nonzero factor. Thus $A$ is a noetherian integrally closed domain. The prime $\mathfrak p$ corresponding to $x$ has height one: chains of primes below $\mathfrak p$ correspond to chains of irreducible closed subsets of $C$ ending at $\overline{\{x\}}$, because intersecting with this open neighborhood and taking closures are inverse on such chains. By [F5], $\mathcal O_{X,x}\cong A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a discrete valuation ring and hence regular local. [F5, step 1.1, given]

3.1 The generic point of $C$ is smooth by step 2.1, and every codimension-one point is smooth by step 2.2 and [F3]. Hence $C\setminus U$ contains no point of codimension zero or one. Applying [F6] proves its codimension is at least two. AC is used through the explicitly AC-dependent suppliers [F2], [F4] and [F5]. [F2, F3, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Seminormality and seminormalization

[Open item](item-def-seminormal-scheme-interface) · level 2

### Definition
A commutative ring $A$ is **seminormal** if, whenever $x^3=y^2$ in $A$, there is a unique $a\in A$ with $a^2=x$ and $a^3=y$. A scheme is seminormal if every point has an affine open neighbourhood whose coordinate ring is seminormal. In particular it is reduced: its affine coordinate rings have no nonzero nilpotents.

A morphism $f:Y\to X$ is **subintegral** if it is integral, is bijective on underlying points, and induces an isomorphism $\kappa(x)\to\kappa(y)$ at every point $y$ over $x$. Integral means affine and given on affine inverse images by integral ring maps; an element is integral when it satisfies a monic polynomial over the base ring. A universal homeomorphism is a morphism whose pullback along every scheme morphism is a homeomorphism on underlying spaces. Integral, bijective morphisms inducing residue-field isomorphisms are universal homeomorphisms, and conversely a universal homeomorphism with residue-field isomorphisms is integral and bijective.

For a scheme $X$, its **seminormalization** $X^{\mathrm{sn}}\to X$ is the initial object in the category of subintegral morphisms to $X$: it has a unique $X$-morphism to every object of that category. Its source is seminormal. The construction is functorial: every morphism $h:Y\to X$ induces a unique compatible $h^{\mathrm{sn}}:Y^{\mathrm{sn}}\to X^{\mathrm{sn}}$. The map factors through the reduction $X_{\mathrm{red}}$, the scheme obtained by quotienting the structure sheaf by its nilradical. When $X$ is locally of finite type over a field, the resulting map $X^{\mathrm{sn}}\to X_{\mathrm{red}}$ is finite. In this scope a normal scheme is seminormal, and a reduced scheme is seminormal exactly when every finite subintegral morphism to it from a reduced scheme is an isomorphism.

### Justification
The initial object and functoriality are the established input [thm-author-30ec96de6e59-seminormalization-input](item-thm-author-30ec96de6e59-seminormalization-input); [lem-author-30ec96de6e59-initial-object-uniqueness](item-lem-author-30ec96de6e59-initial-object-uniqueness) proves uniqueness up to unique isomorphism. The standard characterization of universal homeomorphisms as integral, surjective and universally injective identifies the two formulations: residue-field isomorphisms make the fibers universally injective. A map from a reduced scheme factors uniquely through the reduction, because its structure sheaf has no nonzero nilpotents.

The square-cube condition implies reducedness by [lem-author-30ec96de6e59-seminormal-ring-reduced](item-lem-author-30ec96de6e59-seminormal-ring-reduced), while [lem-author-30ec96de6e59-square-cube-uniqueness](item-lem-author-30ec96de6e59-square-cube-uniqueness) explains uniqueness in any reduced ring. As a local illustration, every integrally closed domain satisfies the condition by [lem-author-30ec96de6e59-normal-domain-square-cube](item-lem-author-30ec96de6e59-normal-domain-square-cube). The scheme-level normality implication is supplied by the cited input. Its finite-type construction uses an intermediate ring in a finite normalization; [lem-author-30ec96de6e59-finite-intermediate-module](item-lem-author-30ec96de6e59-finite-intermediate-module) supplies the noetherian finiteness step. If a reduced finite-type scheme passes the finite-morphism test, apply that test to its finite seminormalization; the resulting isomorphism makes it seminormal. Conversely, the input proves the stronger test for all subintegral morphisms with reduced source.

## Picard group of an affine curve through its boundary

[Open item](item-lem-affine-curve-picard-boundary) · level 2

### Statement
Let $k$ be algebraically closed and let $C$ be a smooth connected affine curve over $k$. Then a smooth projective completion $j:C\hookrightarrow\overline C$ exists and its boundary $B=\overline C\setminus C$ is a nonempty finite set of closed points. For any such completion, the sequence $\bigoplus_{b\in B}\mathbb Z[b]\to\operatorname{Pic}(\overline C)\to\operatorname{Pic}(C)\to0$ is exact, the first map sending $[b]$ to $[\mathcal O_{\overline C}(b)]$ and the second being restriction. Each $b$ has degree one. Consequently the degree-zero Picard group $\operatorname{Pic}^0(\overline C)(k)$ surjects onto $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$.

Here a curve means a nonempty finite-type scheme of pure dimension one; smoothness is over $k$. A completion means a dense open immersion into a smooth projective integral curve. A line bundle is a sheaf locally isomorphic to the structure sheaf; its isomorphism classes form the Picard group under tensor product. The degree of a closed point is the dimension of its residue field over $k$. The degree-zero Picard group is the kernel of the degree homomorphism on line-bundle classes, identified with the $k$-points of the degree-zero Picard variety by the cited geometric input.

### Facts & Assumptions

[F1] A regular integral separated finite-type curve over a perfect field has a smooth projective completion with finite closed-point boundary; if affine, the boundary is nonempty. For smooth integral curves, divisor classes identify naturally with Picard classes and restriction deletes coefficients outside the open. On a smooth projective curve, degree is additive, a point class has its residue-field degree, and the degree-zero kernel is the group of $k$-points of the degree-zero Picard variety ([lem-author-4057f3195e4f-curve-geometric-input](item-lem-author-4057f3195e4f-curve-geometric-input)).

[F2] If $d:K\to\mathbb Z^{(S)}$ is a homomorphism and $B\subseteq S$, restriction induces an exact sequence $\mathbb Z^{(B)}\to\operatorname{coker}(d)\to\operatorname{coker}(r d)\to0$ ([lem-author-4057f3195e4f-divisor-class-localization](item-lem-author-4057f3195e4f-divisor-class-localization)). Exactness transports across compatible isomorphisms ([lem-author-4057f3195e4f-transfer-exactness](item-lem-author-4057f3195e4f-transfer-exactness)).

[F3] If a surjective homomorphism $q:A\to D$ kills an element of degree one for a homomorphism $\deg:A\to\mathbb Z$, then $q(\ker\deg)=D$ ([lem-author-4057f3195e4f-degree-adjustment](item-lem-author-4057f3195e4f-degree-adjustment)).

[F4] Closed points of a finite-type scheme over an algebraically closed field have residue field $k$, by the weak Nullstellensatz on affine charts ([math:cor-weak-nullstellensatz-algebraically-closed-coordinate-form](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/cor-weak-nullstellensatz-algebraically-closed-coordinate-form)). Picard groups and restriction use line bundles and tensor product ([math:def-picard-group-scheme](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-picard-group-scheme)).

**Given:** $k$ and $C$ as stated.

**Goal:** Prove existence and nonemptiness of the boundary, exactness, and the degree-zero surjection.

### Proof

1.1 An algebraically closed field is perfect. Smoothness makes $C$ regular. Its regular local rings are domains, so distinct irreducible components cannot meet; finite type gives finitely many components, hence connectedness makes $C$ integral. Since $C$ is affine over $k$, it is separated over $k$. Apply [F1] to obtain a smooth projective integral completion with finite boundary. It is nonempty because an affine positive-dimensional curve is not proper. The same argument proves nonemptiness for any completion in the statement. [F1, given]

2.1 Let $S$ be the closed points of $\overline C$ and $K=k(\overline C)^\times$, the multiplicative group of nonzero rational functions. The principal-divisor homomorphism $d:K\to\mathbb Z^{(S)}$ assigns each function its finite sum of orders at closed points. The open curve has the same function field, and its principal-divisor homomorphism is restriction of $d$ to $S\setminus B$. Apply [F2], then use the compatible divisor-class and Picard isomorphisms of [F1]. The boundary basis element $[b]$ maps to $[\mathcal O_{\overline C}(b)]$, giving the exact sequence in the statement. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F4], every $b\in B$ has residue field $k$, hence degree one; [F1] gives $\deg[\mathcal O_{\overline C}(b)]=1$. Exactness in step 2.1 shows that this class lies in the kernel of restriction. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Restriction is surjective by step 2.1. Applying [F3] with the boundary class from step 3.1 shows that its restriction from the degree-zero kernel is still surjective. The identification in [F1] gives the stated map from $\operatorname{Pic}^0(\overline C)(k)$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Formal Chern arithmetic through degree three

[Open item](item-lem-third-order-chern-inversion) · level 2

### Statement
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit. A formal series $C(t)=1+\sum_{i\geq1}a_i t^i$ has a multiplicative inverse, and, modulo terms of degree at least four,
$$C(t)^{-1}=1-a_1t+(a_1^2-a_2)t^2+(-a_1^3+2a_1a_2-a_3)t^3.$$
For $D(t)=1+\sum_{i\geq1}b_i t^i$, the coefficients in degrees one, two and three of $C(t)D(t)$ are respectively $a_1+b_1$, $a_2+a_1b_1+b_2$, and $a_3+a_2b_1+a_1b_2+b_3$.

More generally, let $G$ be an abelian group and let $c_t:G\to 1+tR[\![t]\!]$ be a group homomorphism, where the target uses series multiplication. Write $c_t(x)=1+\sum_{i\geq1}c_i(x)t^i$. If $r\geq1$ and $H$ is a subgroup of $G$ on which $c_i$ vanishes for every $1\leq i<r$, then $c_r:H\to(R,+)$ is a group homomorphism. In particular, under the hypotheses of the virtual Chern extension, these formulas apply to its total Chern series, with $R=\bigoplus_{i\geq0}H^{2i,i}(X)$. If $c_1(x)=c_1(y)$, then $c_2(x-y)=c_2(x)-c_2(y)$.

Here $R[\![t]\!]$ denotes the ring of formal sequences of coefficients, with multiplication defined by the finite convolution formula $[t^n](AB)=\sum_{i=0}^n[t^i]A\,[t^{n-i}]B$. The notation $1+tR[\![t]\!]$ means the series with constant coefficient one, and $[t^n]A$ denotes the coefficient of $t^n$. Equality modulo terms of degree at least four means equality of coefficients in degrees zero through three. A virtual Chern class is an element of the bundle Grothendieck group equipped with the extended series described by the cited interface.

### Statement references
[lem-virtual-chern-extension-interface](item-lem-virtual-chern-extension-interface)

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative unital ring $R$, the series $C$ and $D$, and, for the additivity assertion, the group homomorphism $c_t$, integer $r$ and subgroup $H$ specified in the statement.

**Goal:** Establish the inverse and product formulas, the subgroup additivity assertion and the stated conditional virtual Chern consequences.

[F1] Under its stated hypotheses, including the Axiom of Choice and the exact-sequence Whitney identity, the virtual Chern extension supplies a homomorphism from the bundle Grothendieck group to the multiplicative group of total series. Its coefficients lie in $H^{2i,i}(X)$, and $\bigoplus_{i\geq0}H^{2i,i}(X)$ is commutative because the first grading of each summand is even. [lem-virtual-chern-extension-interface](item-lem-virtual-chern-extension-interface)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Compare coefficients of formal series.

1.1 Set $q_0=1$ and recursively $q_n=-\sum_{i=1}^n a_iq_{n-i}$ for $n\geq1$. Every sum is finite, so $Q(t)=\sum_{n\geq0}q_nt^n$ is a formal series. The coefficient of $t^n$ in $C Q$ is zero for $n>0$ and one for $n=0$; commutativity gives $Q C=1$ as well. The recursion yields $q_1=-a_1$, $q_2=a_1^2-a_2$, and $q_3=-a_1^3+2a_1a_2-a_3$, proving the inverse formula. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 The convolution formula gives $[t^n](CD)=a_n+b_n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}a_i b_{n-i}$ for $n\geq1$, taking the constant coefficients to be one. Substituting $n=1,2,3$ gives the three displayed product coefficients. [given, algebra]

2.1 For $x,y\in H$, the homomorphism property gives $c_t(x+y)=c_t(x)c_t(y)$. Comparing degree $r$ as in step 1.2 gives $c_r(x+y)=c_r(x)+c_r(y)+\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}c_i(x)c_{r-i}(y)$. Each summand vanishes by the hypothesis on $H$, including the empty-sum case $r=1$. The identity element maps to the series $1$, so $c_r(0)=0$; the addition formula also gives $c_r(-x)=-c_r(x)$. Thus $c_r$ is a group homomorphism. [given, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Under the hypotheses in [F1], the total series satisfy the hypotheses just used, so all preceding formulas apply to virtual classes. For $x,y$ with common first coefficient $u$, steps 1.1 and 1.2 give $c_2(x-y)=c_2(x)+(u^2-c_2(y))-u^2=c_2(x)-c_2(y)$. This proves the stated virtual consequences and completes the proof. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎


## Exterior-square line factors on a flag space

[Open item](item-lem-exterior-square-root-formula) · level 2


### Statement
Let $S$ be a scheme and $E$ a rank-three vector bundle with a filtration $0=F_0\subset F_1\subset F_2\subset F_3=E$ whose successive quotients $L_i=F_i/F_{i-1}$ are line bundles and whose inclusions are locally split. Then $\Lambda^2E$ has a locally split filtration with successive line-bundle quotients $L_1\otimes L_2$, $L_1\otimes L_3$, and $L_2\otimes L_3$, in that order. There is an isomorphism $\det E\cong L_1\otimes L_2\otimes L_3$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and that $S$ is locally noetherian. In the vector-bundle Grothendieck ring $K^0(S)$, write $[L_i]$ for the class of $L_i$. Then $[\Lambda^2E]=[L_1][L_2]+[L_1][L_3]+[L_2][L_3]$ and $[\det E]=[L_1][L_2][L_3]$. If $c_1$ is any homomorphism from the Picard group of $S$ to an abelian group, and $\ell_i=c_1(L_i)$, the first Chern classes of the three exterior-square line factors are respectively $\ell_1+\ell_2$, $\ell_1+\ell_3$, and $\ell_2+\ell_3$.

A vector bundle is a finite locally free $\mathcal O_S$-module, and a line bundle has rank one. Locally split means that every inclusion in the filtration is locally the inclusion of a direct summand. The Picard group consists of line-bundle isomorphism classes under tensor product. The stated homomorphism condition means $c_1(L\otimes M)=c_1(L)+c_1(M)$; these line-factor classes are the exterior-square roots relative to the chosen flag. In particular, under the Axiom of Choice, the flag-tower supplier provides such a filtration after pulling a rank-three bundle back to its flag tower.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A scheme $S$, a rank-three bundle $E$, and the locally split line-quotient filtration in the statement. For the $K^0$ assertions, also assume the Axiom of Choice and that $S$ is locally noetherian. For the root assertion, also assume the stated additive map $c_1$.

**Goal:** Construct the exterior-square filtration and determinant isomorphism and derive the displayed class formulas.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is used only through the flag-tower supplier [F2] and the Grothendieck-ring supplier [F3]; the filtration and determinant constructions for a given flag require no additional Choice assumption. [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

[F1] Exterior powers and determinant are functorial for bundle maps; the exterior power of a free module has the basis of increasing wedges. In particular the determinant of a rank-three bundle is its third exterior power. [def-exterior-determinant-bundles](item-def-exterior-determinant-bundles) [math:lem-exterior-algebra-basis-monomials](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/lem-exterior-algebra-basis-monomials)

[F2] Under the Axiom of Choice, the flag tower of a rank-three bundle carries a locally split filtration with line-bundle quotients. [lem-flag-tower-line-quotients](item-lem-flag-tower-line-quotients)

[F3] Under the Axiom of Choice, for a locally noetherian scheme $S$, $K^0(S)$ is generated by vector-bundle classes with the relations $[B]=[A]+[C]$ for short exact sequences $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ of vector bundles; multiplication is induced by tensor product. [math:def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Construct the filtration by wedge images and identify its quotients on bases adapted to the flag.

1.1 Let $G_1$ be the image of the wedge map $F_1\otimes F_2\to\Lambda^2E$, and let $G_2$ be the image of $F_1\otimes E\to\Lambda^2E$. These are subsheaves with $G_1\subseteq G_2\subseteq\Lambda^2E$. Locally the two short exact sequences defining the flag split, and the three line quotients are trivial. Thus there is a local basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $E$ with $F_1$ generated by $e_1$ and $F_2$ by $e_1,e_2$. By [F1], $G_1$ is generated by $e_1\wedge e_2$, $G_2$ by $e_1\wedge e_2,e_1\wedge e_3$, and $\Lambda^2E$ by these two wedges and $e_2\wedge e_3$. Consequently these subsheaves are locally direct summands and the successive quotients are line bundles. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Wedge multiplication induces maps $L_1\otimes L_2\to G_1$, $L_1\otimes L_3\to G_2/G_1$, and $L_2\otimes L_3\to\Lambda^2E/G_2$. They are well defined: changing a lift by a vector in the preceding flag term changes its wedge by zero or by a section of the indicated preceding $G$ term. On an adapted basis as in step 1.1, the maps send the tensor products of the quotient basis vectors to the corresponding wedge generators. They are therefore local isomorphisms, hence global isomorphisms. This proves the claimed filtration without choosing a global splitting. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 The map $L_1\otimes L_2\otimes L_3\to\Lambda^3E$ sending local quotient sections, with arbitrary lifts to their flag terms, to the wedge of those lifts is well defined: changing a lift adds a wedge containing two vectors from $F_1$ or three from $F_2$, which vanishes locally on an adapted basis. On that basis it sends the tensor product of quotient generators to $e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3$, a generator by [F1]. It is thus an isomorphism to $\det E=\Lambda^3E$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Under the additional $K^0$ hypotheses, apply [F3] to the short exact sequences $0\to G_1\to G_2\to G_2/G_1\to0$ and $0\to G_2\to\Lambda^2E\to\Lambda^2E/G_2\to0$. Using step 2.1 and the tensor-product multiplication gives the displayed formula for $[\Lambda^2E]$. Step 2.2 and the same multiplication give the determinant formula. [A1, F3, step 2.1, step 2.2, assume-hyp]

4.1 Apply the assumed homomorphism $c_1$ to the three tensor-product line bundles identified in step 2.1. Additivity gives the three pairwise sums. Finally, [F2] supplies the required flag after pullback to the flag tower when the Axiom of Choice is assumed. All stated conclusions follow. [A1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, assume-hyp] ∎


## Finite-dimensional families of generated bundle functionals

[Open item](item-lem-regular-section-parameter-family) · level 2

### Statement
Let $k$ be a field, $U$ a $k$-scheme, and $E$ a vector bundle of constant rank $r$ on $U$. Write $E^\vee=\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_U}(E,\mathcal O_U)$, and suppose that global sections $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m$ generate $E^\vee$, meaning that the morphism $q:\mathcal O_U^m\to E^\vee$ sending the standard basis to these sections is surjective. Here $m$ and $r$ may be zero.

The affine parameter space $\mathbb A_k^m=\operatorname{Spec}k[T_1,\ldots,T_m]$ carries a universal functional $\Phi=\sum_i T_i\phi_i$ on the pullback of $E$ to $U\times_k\mathbb A_k^m$. Its zero-incidence subscheme $I$ is the closed subscheme defined locally by the coefficients of $\Phi$ in a frame of $E^\vee$. For every point $u\in U$, evaluation gives a surjective linear map $\kappa(u)^m\to E^\vee\otimes_{\mathcal O_U}\kappa(u)$, and this remains surjective after any field extension of $\kappa(u)$.

For every closed subscheme $Z\hookrightarrow U$, the incidence subscheme constructed from the restricted sections on $Z$ is canonically $I\times_U Z$, viewed as a closed subscheme of $Z\times_k\mathbb A_k^m$. More generally, for any $k$-scheme $T$ and any $T$-valued parameter $(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, the pullback of $I$ to $U\times_k T$ is the zero subscheme of the functional $\sum_i a_i\phi_i$.

### Statement references
[lem-surjection-kernel-bundle](item-lem-surjection-kernel-bundle)

[def-unimodular-sections](item-def-unimodular-sections)

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The field $k$, the $k$-scheme $U$, the rank-$r$ vector bundle $E$, and the surjective generating map $q$ in the statement.

**Goal:** Construct the universal zero-incidence subscheme, prove fiberwise surjectivity of evaluation, and identify its base changes.

[F1] A vector bundle is a finite locally free module; its dual is the sheaf of homomorphisms to the structure sheaf, and a functional is a section of that dual. [def-unimodular-sections](item-def-unimodular-sections)

[F2] A surjective morphism between finite locally free sheaves splits locally. [lem-surjection-kernel-bundle](item-lem-surjection-kernel-bundle)

### Proof
**Proof technique:** Use local frames and the locally split generating map.

1.1 Let $p:U\times_k\mathbb A_k^m\to U$ be the projection. The coordinate functions $T_i$ and the pullbacks $p^*\phi_i$ define a section $\Phi=\sum_i T_i p^*\phi_i$ of $p^*E^\vee$, hence a functional $p^*E\to\mathcal O_{U\times_k\mathbb A_k^m}$. On a trivializing open for $E$, write its coefficients as $f_1,\ldots,f_r$. Define $I$ there by the ideal $(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$. On overlapping trivializations the coefficient columns differ by an invertible matrix, so they generate the same ideal. These ideals glue to a closed subscheme $I$; equivalently, its ideal is the image of the functional $\Phi$. This also covers rank zero, where the ideal is zero. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 By [F2], $q$ has a right inverse locally on $U$. Pulling this local splitting back to the residue field $\kappa(u)$ of any point $u$ gives a right inverse to the evaluation map $\kappa(u)^m\to E^\vee\otimes\kappa(u)$, so that map is surjective. Tensoring the same right inverse with any field extension of $\kappa(u)$ proves the asserted surjectivity over the extension. [F2, given, step 1.1]

2.2 A morphism $T\to\mathbb A_k^m$ is specified by the images $a_i$ of the coordinate functions. Pulling back the local coefficients $f_j$ along $U\times_k T\to U\times_k\mathbb A_k^m$ substitutes $a_i$ for $T_i$; their generated ideal is therefore the image ideal of $\sum_i a_i\phi_i$. The scheme-theoretic inverse image of a closed subscheme is defined by the extended ideal, so this pullback is exactly the stated zero subscheme. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 For a closed subscheme $Z\hookrightarrow U$, pulling the same coefficient ideals back to $Z\times_k\mathbb A_k^m$ gives the coefficients of the restricted sections of $E^\vee|_Z\cong(E|_Z)^\vee$ in the restricted frames. Thus their incidence subscheme is canonically $I\times_U Z$. Together with steps 1.1 through 2.2 this proves all the assertions. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

### Remarks
This construction alone does not assert smoothness, irreducibility, codimension, or avoidance for any parameter. Generation of $E$ does not by itself supply the assumed generation of $E^\vee$.

## A rank-two bundle with a trivial quotient and determinant

[Open item](item-lem-trivial-determinant-rank-two-kernel) · level 2

### Statement
Let $V$ be a scheme and $Q$ a rank-two vector bundle on $V$ with $\det Q\cong\mathcal O_V$. If $Q\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal O_V$ is a surjective morphism, its kernel is isomorphic to $\mathcal O_V$, so there is a short exact sequence $0\to\mathcal O_V\to Q\to\mathcal O_V\to0$.

Assume also the Axiom of Choice and that $V$ is locally Noetherian. Then $[Q]=2[\mathcal O_V]$ in the vector-bundle Grothendieck group $K^0(V)$, whether or not the sequence splits globally. If in addition $P$ is a vector bundle in a short exact sequence $0\to Q\to P\to\mathcal O_V\to0$, then $[P]=3[\mathcal O_V]$ in $K^0(V)$.

Here a vector bundle of rank $r$ is an $\mathcal O_V$-module locally isomorphic to $\mathcal O_V^r$; a line bundle is a rank-one vector bundle. The determinant of a rank-$r$ bundle is its top exterior power $\Lambda^r E$, and a trivial determinant means an isomorphism with $\mathcal O_V$. A short exact sequence is exact at each term, equivalently on stalks. Under the stated Choice and locally Noetherian hypotheses, $K^0(V)$ is the abelian group generated by isomorphism classes $[E]$ of vector bundles, with $[E]=[E']+[E'']$ for every short exact sequence $0\to E'\to E\to E''\to0$.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A scheme $V$, a rank-two vector bundle $Q$, an isomorphism $\det Q\cong\mathcal O_V$, and a surjection $Q\to\mathcal O_V$. For the group assertions, also the Axiom of Choice and locally Noetherianity of $V$; for the final assertion, the displayed short exact sequence involving $P$.

**Goal:** Identify the kernel with $\mathcal O_V$ and prove the stated group identities under their additional hypotheses.

[F1] The kernel of a surjection of finite locally free sheaves is finite locally free, with rank equal to the difference of ranks; the surjection splits locally. [lem-surjection-kernel-bundle](item-lem-surjection-kernel-bundle)

[F2] A short exact sequence $0\to E'\to E\to E''\to0$ of vector bundles has a canonical isomorphism $\det E'\otimes\det E''\cong\det E$. [lem-determinants-of-short-exact-sequences](item-lem-determinants-of-short-exact-sequences)

[F3] The determinant of a rank-one bundle $L$ is $\Lambda^1L$, canonically $L$; in particular $\det\mathcal O_V\cong\mathcal O_V$. Tensoring an $\mathcal O_V$-module with $\mathcal O_V$ gives that module canonically. [def-exterior-determinant-bundles](item-def-exterior-determinant-bundles)

[F4] Under Choice and locally Noetherianity, isomorphic vector bundles have the same generator in $K^0(V)$, and every short exact sequence of vector bundles gives the additive relation in the statement. [math:def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme) [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** direct application of the determinant and exact-sequence relations.

1.1 Let $L$ be the kernel of the given surjection. By [F1], $L$ is a vector bundle of rank $2-1=1$, and $0\to L\to Q\to\mathcal O_V\to0$ is short exact. [given, F1]

2.1 By [F2] applied to that sequence, $\det L\otimes\det\mathcal O_V\cong\det Q$. By [F3] and the given trivialization of $\det Q$, this yields an isomorphism $L\cong\mathcal O_V$. Substitution in the sequence of step 1.1 gives the asserted short exact sequence. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Under the additional Choice and locally Noetherian hypotheses, [F4] applied to that sequence gives $[Q]=[L]+[\mathcal O_V]=2[\mathcal O_V]$. This uses the exact-sequence relation and does not require a global splitting. [given, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 If the additional sequence $0\to Q\to P\to\mathcal O_V\to0$ is given, [F4] gives $[P]=[Q]+[\mathcal O_V]=3[\mathcal O_V]$. Thus all conclusions hold under their stated hypotheses. [given, F4, step 3.1] ∎

## Iterating a conditional free-summand criterion

[Open item](item-lem-author-3af31ead36fb-iteration) · level 2

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring and let $d$ be a nonnegative integer. Suppose every finite projective $A$-module of constant rank greater than $d$ has a free rank-one direct summand. Then every finite projective $A$-module $P$ of constant rank $r>d$ is isomorphic to $A^{r-d}\oplus Q$ for a finite projective module $Q$ of constant rank $d$. The criterion is an explicit hypothesis of this lemma.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $A$, $d$, $P$, $r$, Choice, and the conditional free-summand criterion in the statement.

**Goal:** Obtain the displayed decomposition and rank.

[A1] Choice is assumed to invoke the supplied split-complement result, including its associated-bundle clause; the finite iteration introduces no further choice use. [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

[F1] The complement of a free rank-one summand of a finite projective constant-rank module is finite projective and has rank one less. [lem-author-3af31ead36fb-split-complement](item-lem-author-3af31ead36fb-split-complement)

### Proof

1.1 Apply the assumed criterion to $P$ to split off $A$. By [F1], its complement is finite projective of rank $r-1$. If this rank is still greater than $d$, the same criterion applies again. [F1, given]

2.1 Repeat the preceding finite operation exactly $r-d$ times. At the $j$th application, the current rank is $r-j+1>d$; [F1] supplies a finite projective complement of rank $r-j$. Associativity of finite direct sums gives $P\cong A^{r-d}\oplus Q$ with $Q$ of rank $d$. [F1, given, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Free stabilization passes through global sections

[Open item](item-lem-author-f08c343a07fc-cancel-module-stabilization) · level 2

### Statement
Assume AC and put $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$. For bundles $E,F$ and an integer $N\geq0$, $E\oplus\mathcal O_X^N\cong F\oplus\mathcal O_X^N$ if and only if $\Gamma(X,E)\oplus A^N\cong\Gamma(X,F)\oplus A^N$. All modules here are finite projective.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data and hypotheses in the statement.

**Goal:** Establish the stated conclusion.

[F1] The affine equivalence preserves finite direct sums and sends $A^N$ to $\mathcal O_X^N$. [lem-affine-bundle-module-interface](item-lem-affine-bundle-module-interface)

[F2] It reflects and preserves isomorphism classes. [lem-author-f08c343a07fc-cancel-module-classes](item-lem-author-f08c343a07fc-cancel-module-classes)

### Proof

1.1 Apply global sections to a stabilized bundle isomorphism. Its inverse remains an inverse; direct-sum compatibility identifies its source and target with the displayed modules. [F1, F2]

2.1 Conversely sheafify a module isomorphism and use the counit to identify its ends with the displayed bundles. The equivalence also supplies finite projectivity. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎


## Common projective complements and cancellation by free modules

[Open item](item-lem-author-f08c343a07fc-cancel-cancellative-free-summands) · level 2

### Statement
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unit. Call a finite projective $A$-module $P$ cancellative if, for every finite projective $Q$ and every integer $N\geq0$, $P\oplus A^N\cong Q\oplus A^N$ implies $P\cong Q$. This is equivalent to cancellation of an arbitrary common finite projective summand: $P\oplus T\cong Q\oplus T$ implies $P\cong Q$.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data and hypotheses in the statement.

**Goal:** Establish the stated conclusion.

[F1] The choice-free module clause states that every finite projective $T$ has a finite projective complement $T\prime$ with $T\oplus T\prime\cong A^N$. [lem-finite-projective-complements](item-lem-finite-projective-complements)

### Proof

1.1 If $P$ is cancellative in the free-summand sense and $P\oplus T\cong Q\oplus T$, add the complement $T\prime$ to both sides. Associativity converts this into $P\oplus A^N\cong Q\oplus A^N$, so $P\cong Q$. [F1, given]

2.1 Conversely $A^N$ is finite projective and can itself be used as the common summand $T$. Thus cancellation of arbitrary common summands implies the free-summand definition. This also proves the definition has the claimed precise meaning. [given, step 1.1] ∎

[Open item](item-lem-author-7dc5154c7a6f-cancellative-free-summands) · level 2

### Statement
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unit. Call a finite projective $A$-module $P$ cancellative if, for every finite projective $Q$ and every integer $N\geq0$, $P\oplus A^N\cong Q\oplus A^N$ implies $P\cong Q$. ## Finite derived quotients of rational complexes vanish

[Open item](item-lem-author-4b6f215bcf3b-rational-derived-quotient) · level 2

### Statement
Let $C$ be an object of $D(\mathbb Z)$ isomorphic to the underlying complex of a complex of $\mathbb Q$-vector spaces, and let $n>0$ be an integer. Then $C\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n$ is zero in $D(\mathbb Z)$. The derived tensor product is the total tensor product computed with a K-flat replacement; zero in $D(\mathbb Z)$ means an acyclic complex.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** $C$ and $n$ as stated.

**Goal:** Show $C\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n\simeq0$.

[F1] Multiplication by $n$ is an isomorphism on the underlying complex of a complex of $\mathbb Q$-vector spaces. [lem-author-4b6f215bcf3b-rational-complex-multiplication](item-lem-author-4b6f215bcf3b-rational-complex-multiplication)

[F2] The derived tensor product with $\mathbb Z/n$ is represented by the mapping cone of multiplication by $n$. Its cohomology lies in the natural exact sequence of [lem-derived-coefficient-exact-sequence](item-lem-derived-coefficient-exact-sequence).

### Proof
1.1 Transporting [F1] across the given isomorphism shows that multiplication by $n$ induces an automorphism of every $H^i(C)$. [F1, given]

2.1 In [F2], both $H^i(C)/nH^i(C)$ and $H^{i+1}(C)[n]$ therefore vanish. The exact sequence gives $H^i(C\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n)=0$ for every $i$. Hence the derived quotient is zero. [F2, step 1.1] ∎


## Matrix completion detects the actual nontrivial bundle

[Open item](item-lem-author-b02e51f9da03-matrix-completion) · level 2

### Statement
Assume AC. For $q:A^{r+N}\to A^N$ with right inverse as above, say that $q$ is **completable** if it is the last $N$ rows of an invertible $(r+N)\times(r+N)$ matrix $B$, equivalently $q=\operatorname{pr}_2 B$ under $A^{r+N}=A^r\oplus A^N$. The associated rank-$r$ kernel bundle is trivial if and only if $q$ is completable. Thus failure of completion is a precise obstruction to trivializing this bundle, even though its displayed free stabilization is trivial.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data and hypotheses in the statement, AC and the article's fixed universe bounds where its K-theory is used.

**Goal:** Establish the stated conclusion.

[F1] The kernel is finite projective and the actual free stabilization is explicit. [lem-author-b02e51f9da03-matrix-kernel](item-lem-author-b02e51f9da03-matrix-kernel)

[F2] The affine equivalence detects isomorphisms with finite free modules. [lem-affine-bundle-module-interface](item-lem-affine-bundle-module-interface)

### Proof

1.1 If $q=\operatorname{pr}_2 B$ and $B$ is invertible, restriction of $B$ identifies $\ker q$ with $\ker\operatorname{pr}_2=A^r\oplus0$. Thus the kernel is free and its associated bundle is trivial by [F2]. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 Conversely suppose $\ker q$ is free, and choose an isomorphism $u:A^r\to\ker q$. The map $T:A^r\oplus A^N\to A^{r+N}$, $T(v,w)=u(v)+j(w)$, is an isomorphism by [F1] and satisfies $qT=\operatorname{pr}_2$. Hence $B=T^{-1}$ is invertible and $q=\operatorname{pr}_2B$. This supplies the completion and proves the equivalence with actual triviality. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct] ∎


## Divisibility of an image with torsion kernel

[Open item](item-lem-author-b87d598e83f3-cycle-image-roots) · level 2

### Statement
Let $f:G\to H$ be a homomorphism of abelian groups. If multiplication by every positive integer is bijective on $G$ and every element of $\ker f$ is torsion, then multiplication by every positive integer is bijective on the subgroup $\operatorname{im}f\subseteq H$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The map and hypotheses in the statement.

**Goal:** Prove unique divisibility of its image.

[F1] [lem-author-b87d598e83f3-torsion-kernel-injective](item-lem-author-b87d598e83f3-torsion-kernel-injective) makes $f$ injective.

[F2] [lem-author-b87d598e83f3-injective-image-isomorphism](item-lem-author-b87d598e83f3-injective-image-isomorphism) identifies an injective map's domain with its image.

[F3] [lem-author-b87d598e83f3-isomorphism-transfers-roots](item-lem-author-b87d598e83f3-isomorphism-transfers-roots) transfers unique divisibility across an isomorphism.

### Proof
1.1 By [F1], the kernel hypothesis and unique divisibility make $f$ injective. Its corestriction to its image is therefore an isomorphism by [F2]. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 Apply [F3] to that isomorphism and the given multiplication maps on $G$. Every positive multiplication map on $\operatorname{im}f$ is bijective. [F3, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Line bundles are detected off codimension two

[Open item](item-lem-codimension-two-picard-restriction) · level 3

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a noetherian normal scheme and let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be an open immersion whose image contains every point of codimension at most one in its irreducible component. Then restriction $\operatorname{Pic}(X)\to\operatorname{Pic}(U)$ is injective. More precisely, a trivialization $\mathcal O_U\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal L|_U$ of a line bundle $\mathcal L$ determines a section of $\mathcal L|_U$ and an inverse section of its dual; both extend uniquely to $X$, and their evaluation product is $1$.

A noetherian normal scheme is a scheme with a finite cover by spectra of noetherian rings and with all local rings integrally closed domains. The codimension of a point in its irreducible component is the supremum of the lengths of chains of strict specializations from the component's generic point to that point. A line bundle is an $\mathcal O_X$-module locally isomorphic to $\mathcal O_X$; its dual is $\mathcal L^\vee=\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal L,\mathcal O_X)$. The Picard group consists of isomorphism classes of line bundles, with tensor product as its operation and $[\mathcal O_X]$ as identity. Restriction sends a class to the class of its restriction.

### Statement references

[lem-codimension-two-extension](item-lem-codimension-two-extension)

[math:def-picard-group-scheme](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-picard-group-scheme)

### Facts & Assumptions

[F1] Under the stated hypotheses and the Axiom of Choice, restriction is an isomorphism of sheaves of rings $\mathcal O_X\xrightarrow{\sim}j_*\mathcal O_U$ ([lem-codimension-two-extension](item-lem-codimension-two-extension)).

[F2] The Picard group has the stated tensor-product law, identity and dual inverses ([math:def-picard-group-scheme](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-picard-group-scheme)).

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed as required by [F1] ([math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)).

### Proof

**Given:** $X$, $U$ and $j$ as in the statement, the Axiom of Choice, and a line bundle $\mathcal L$ on $X$.

**Goal:** Extend a trivialization on $U$ as stated and prove injectivity of restriction on Picard groups.

1.1 For any line bundle $\mathcal M$ on $X$, the natural restriction morphism $\mathcal M\to j_*(\mathcal M|_U)$ is an isomorphism. Indeed, on every open set $V$ where $\mathcal M\cong\mathcal O_V$, it identifies with the restriction of the isomorphism in [F1] to $V$. Such opens cover $X$, and a morphism of sheaves that is an isomorphism locally is an isomorphism: its local inverses agree on overlaps and glue. In particular, sections of $\mathcal M|_U$ extend uniquely to sections of $\mathcal M$ on $X$. The dual $\mathcal L^\vee$ is also a line bundle, since the dual of a local copy of $\mathcal O_X$ is a local copy of $\mathcal O_X$. [F1, A1, given]

2.1 Suppose $\phi:\mathcal O_U\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal L|_U$ is a trivialization. Set $s_U=\phi(1)$ and let $t_U$ be the section of $\mathcal L^\vee|_U$ corresponding to $\phi^{-1}$; thus $t_U(s_U)=1$. By step 1.1, these sections extend uniquely to $s\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal L)$ and $t\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal L^\vee)$. The evaluation $t(s)$ restricts to $1$ on $U$, so [F1] implies $t(s)=1$ on $X$. Locally write $s=a e$ and $t=b e^\vee$ in a basis $e$ and its dual. Then $ba=1$, so the maps $\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal L$, $1\mapsto s$, and $\mathcal L\to\mathcal O_X$ defined by $t$ are inverse isomorphisms locally, hence globally. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Restriction respects tensor products and the identity by their local constructions, so it is a homomorphism of the Picard groups in [F2]. If a class restricts to the identity, its representative admits a trivialization on $U$; step 2.1 makes that representative trivial on $X$. Thus the kernel is trivial, and the restriction homomorphism is injective. [F2, step 2.1] ∎

## Bloch cycle complexes and higher Chow groups

[Open item](item-def-bloch-higher-cycle-complex) · level 3


### Definition
Let $k$ be a field, $X$ smooth of finite type over $k$, and $r\geq0$. For $n\geq0$ put $\Delta^n=\operatorname{Spec}k[t_0,\ldots,t_n]/(\sum_a t_a-1)$. A nonempty coordinate face is obtained by setting a proper subset of the coordinates to zero. An integral closed subscheme $W\subset X\times\Delta^n$ of codimension $r$ is **admissible** if every component of its intersection with every such face has codimension $r$ in that face; empty intersections are allowed. Codimension is measured on the ambient irreducible component containing the generic point. Define $z^r(X,n)$ as the free abelian group on the admissible subschemes.

For $n\geq1$, identify $\{t_i=0\}$ with $\Delta^{n-1}$ by retaining the remaining coordinates in increasing order and set
$$d_i^n[W]=\sum_T\ell_{\mathcal O_{W,\eta_T}}(\mathcal O_{W,\eta_T}/(t_i))[T],$$
where $T$ ranges over the components of $W\cap\{t_i=0\}$ and $\eta_T$ is its generic point. The empty sum is zero. Extend by integral linearity and set $\partial_n=\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^i d_i^n$. Put $z^r(X,n)=0$ for $n<0$ and $\partial_n=0:z^r(X,n)\to z^r(X,n-1)$ for every $n\leq0$. The resulting homological complex is **Bloch's cycle complex** $z^r(X,\bullet)$, and its **higher Chow groups** are
$$\mathrm{CH}^r(X,n)=H_n(z^r(X,\bullet))=\ker\partial_n/\operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1}.$$
In particular they vanish for $n<0$. This is the unnormalized complex; no quotient by degenerate simplices is taken.

[lem-author-89250b1d710c-admissible-face-identities](item-lem-author-89250b1d710c-admissible-face-identities)

[lem-author-89250b1d710c-alternating-face-boundary](item-lem-author-89250b1d710c-alternating-face-boundary)

[math:def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex)

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $k,X,r$ as above.

**Goal:** Justify the coefficients, differential and homology quotient.

[F1] The admissible face lemma supplies finite coefficients, admissible face images and the identities $d_i d_j=d_{j-1}d_i$ for $i<j$. [lem-author-89250b1d710c-admissible-face-identities](item-lem-author-89250b1d710c-admissible-face-identities)

[F2] Alternating face sums form a chain complex, whose homology is the displayed quotient and vanishes in negative degrees. [lem-author-89250b1d710c-alternating-face-boundary](item-lem-author-89250b1d710c-alternating-face-boundary), [math:def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex)

### Justification
The local rings in the coefficient formula need not be discrete valuation rings and the cycles need not be smooth. The proper single-face calculation in [F1] supplies exactly the finite lengths shown. The cycle-level compatibility in [F1] uses the explicitly imported simplicial-cycle input locally on integral smooth affine opens; no quotient by rational equivalence is used. Thus all face maps are defined, and [F2] gives $\partial^2=0$ and makes the homology quotient well-defined. This definition does not assert the separate comparison with motivic cohomology or the identification of degree zero with the classical Chow group.


## Stable spectra and exact triangles

[Open item](item-def-stable-spectra-interface) · level 3

### Definition
Use the symmetric monoidal stable infinity-category $\mathrm{Sp}=\operatorname{Exc}_*(S_*^{\mathrm{fin}},S)$ supplied by the stable enhancement input. Here $S$ is the infinity-category of spaces, $S_*^{\mathrm{fin}}$ is the infinity-category of finite pointed spaces, and $\operatorname{Exc}_*$ consists of functors taking the point to a contractible space and pushouts to pullbacks. An infinity-category retains mapping spaces and coherent higher compositions. Diagrams are coherent functors, and limits and colimits are their homotopy limits and colimits; these exist for small diagrams.

Write $0$ for the zero spectrum. For $f:A\to B$, define $\operatorname{fib}(f)=A\times_B0$ and $\operatorname{cofib}(f)=B\sqcup_A0$. A fiber or cofiber sequence includes its nullhomotopy and defining pullback or pushout square. Define suspension $E[1]=0\sqcup_E0$ and desuspension $E[-1]=0\times_E0$. A fiber sequence $F\to A\to B$ extends to the cofiber triangle $F\to A\to B\to F[1]$, and $\operatorname{cofib}(f)\simeq\operatorname{fib}(f)[1]$. Let $\mathbb S=\Sigma^\infty S^0$ be the sphere spectrum and define $\pi_i(E)=\pi_0\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Sp}}(\mathbb S[i],E)$. These are abelian groups for every $i\in\mathbb Z$, and $\pi_i(E[1])\cong\pi_{i-1}(E)$.

Products are coherent homotopy products. The smash product $E\wedge F$ is the separately colimit-preserving symmetric monoidal product with unit $\mathbb S$; its associativity, symmetry and unit include higher coherences. A ring spectrum means an associative or commutative algebra object for smash, with the intended type specified. Smash is separately exact: it preserves finite limits and finite colimits in each variable.

To connect this interface with the published sequential-prespectrum definition, let $E$ be a sequential prespectrum of well-pointed based compactly generated weak Hausdorff spaces, with $\sigma_n:S^1\wedge E_n\to E_{n+1}$ and the sphere coordinate first. Form $X=\operatorname{Sing} E$ with the structure maps of the singular sequential comparison, then form $QX$ as in the Omega replacement comparison. Regard its coherent Omega tower as an object $\mathcal RE$ of $\mathrm{Sp}$ using the imported tower equivalence. For every $i\in\mathbb Z$ there is a natural isomorphism

$$\pi_i^{\mathrm{seq}}(E)=\operatorname*{colim}_{n\gg0}\pi_{n+i}(E_n)\xrightarrow{\sim}\pi_i(\mathcal RE).$$

The left bonding map is suspension with $S^1$ first followed by $\sigma_n$, with the published sphere-coordinate identification. If $E$ is already an Omega-prespectrum, its adjoint structure maps are weak equivalences and the comparison agrees with evaluation at each sufficiently late level. The tower $(QX)_{n+1}$ represents $(\mathcal RE)[1]$, so $\pi_i((\mathcal RE)[1])\cong\pi_{i-1}^{\mathrm{seq}}(E)$. In particular, a map inducing isomorphisms on all published stable groups is sent to an equivalence in $\mathrm{Sp}$.

If $E$ is already an Omega-prespectrum, its adjoint weak equivalences make each sufficiently late bonding map an isomorphism, so the colimit agrees with evaluation there. [F2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 For a map inducing isomorphisms on all published stable groups, step 1.2 gives isomorphisms on all enhanced groups. At every level of an Omega tower, these detect all homotopy groups, including components by shifting to a double loop space.
