## Serre splitting above the dimension

[Open item](item-thm-serre-affine-splitting) · level 3


### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a nonempty noetherian affine scheme of finite dimension $d\geq0$, and let $E$ be a vector bundle of constant rank $r>d$. Then $E\cong\mathcal O_X\oplus E_1$ for a vector bundle $E_1$ of rank $r-1$. More precisely, iteration gives $E\cong\mathcal O_X^{\oplus(r-d)}\oplus F$ for a vector bundle $F$ of rank $d$, hence at most $d$. On the empty affine scheme the corresponding splitting assertion is immediate because all sheaves of modules are zero.

A vector bundle means a finite locally free sheaf, and constant rank $r$ means that its local free rank is $r$ at every point. The dimension of $X$ is the supremum of the lengths of strict chains of irreducible closed subsets.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $X$, $d$, $E$, $r$, and the Axiom of Choice as in the statement.

**Goal:** Split off a trivial line and iterate down to rank $d$.

[A1] The assumed Axiom of Choice is used through the affine bundle–module equivalence in [F1] and its finite-projective and rank suppliers [F2]–[F4]. The iteration in [F6] is finite. [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

[F1] The affine bundle–module equivalence preserves direct sums and rank. [lem-affine-bundle-module-interface](item-lem-affine-bundle-module-interface)

[F2] A finite projective module is finitely presented. [lem-author-3af31ead36fb-finite-projective-presentation](item-lem-author-3af31ead36fb-finite-projective-presentation)

[F3] For a nonzero noetherian ring of finite dimension $d$, the maximal spectrum is noetherian and has dimension at most $d$. [lem-author-3af31ead36fb-max-spectrum-dimension](item-lem-author-3af31ead36fb-max-spectrum-dimension)

[F4] The global sections of a rank-$r$ affine bundle form a finite projective module whose localizations at primes are free of rank $r$. [lem-author-3af31ead36fb-local-rank](item-lem-author-3af31ead36fb-local-rank)

[F5] A free rank-one complement of a finite projective constant-rank module is finite projective of rank one less. [lem-author-3af31ead36fb-split-complement](item-lem-author-3af31ead36fb-split-complement)

[F6] A criterion splitting a free line from every finite projective module of rank greater than $d$ iterates down to rank $d$. [lem-author-3af31ead36fb-iteration](item-lem-author-3af31ead36fb-iteration)

[F7] The imported Serre module theorem applies to a finitely presented module when the maximal spectrum is noetherian of finite dimension $e$ and every maximal localization has a free direct summand of rank greater than $e$. [thm-author-3af31ead36fb-serre-module-input](item-thm-author-3af31ead36fb-serre-module-input)

### Proof

1.1 Write $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$. Since $X$ is nonempty, $A$ is nonzero. The ring $A$ is noetherian and its Krull dimension is $d$: irreducible closed subsets of an affine spectrum are the sets $V(\mathfrak p)$ for prime ideals, with inclusion reversed. By [F3], its maximal spectrum is noetherian of some finite dimension $e\leq d$. [F3, given]

2.1 Let $P$ be any finite projective $A$-module of constant rank $s>d$. It is finitely presented by [F2]. At each maximal ideal its localization is free of rank $s$, so it has a free direct summand of rank $s>e$. The imported theorem [F7] therefore gives $P\cong A\oplus P'$. Thus the hypothesis of [F6] holds for this ring and $d$. [F2, F7, given, step 1.1]

3.1 The module $P=\Gamma(X,E)$ is finite projective of constant rank $r$ by [F4]. Applying step 2.1 gives a decomposition $P\cong A\oplus P'$; [F5] makes $P'$ finite projective of rank $r-1$. The equivalence [F1] turns this into $E\cong\mathcal O_X\oplus E_1$ with $E_1$ a rank-$(r-1)$ bundle. [A1, F1, F4, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 By [F6] and step 2.1, $P\cong A^{r-d}\oplus Q$ with $Q$ finite projective of rank $d$. Applying [F1] yields the asserted bundle decomposition. On the empty scheme every sheaf of modules is the zero sheaf, so the stated empty-case splitting is immediate. [F1, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎


## Divisibility of the Picard group of an affine curve

[Open item](item-prop-affine-curve-picard-divisible) · level 3


### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. The Picard group of a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field is divisible.

A curve is a finite-type scheme of pure dimension one. A line bundle is a locally free module of rank one, and the Picard group consists of its isomorphism classes under tensor product. Divisible means that for each nonzero integer $n$ and each Picard class $L$ there is a class $M$ with $nM = L$; in multiplicative notation this means that the $n$-fold tensor power of $M$ is $L$ for positive $n$.

### Facts & Assumptions

[F1] A smooth connected affine curve $C$ over an algebraically closed field has a smooth projective integral completion $X$, and restriction maps the degree-zero Picard group $\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)$ surjectively onto $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$ ([lem-affine-curve-picard-boundary](item-lem-affine-curve-picard-boundary)).

[F2] For such $X$, $\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)$ is isomorphic to $J(k)$ for an abelian variety $J$ over $k$; multiplication by every positive integer is surjective on $J(k)$, without a characteristic restriction ([thm-author-9ab3274efad8-jacobian-input](item-thm-author-9ab3274efad8-jacobian-input), [thm-author-9ab3274efad8-abelian-variety-divisibility-input](item-thm-author-9ab3274efad8-abelian-variety-divisibility-input)).

[F3] Roots descend along surjective homomorphisms, and finite products retain surjectivity of a fixed positive multiplication map ([lem-author-9ab3274efad8-surjective-image-roots](item-lem-author-9ab3274efad8-surjective-image-roots), [lem-author-9ab3274efad8-finite-product-roots](item-lem-author-9ab3274efad8-finite-product-roots)).

[F4] Under the Axiom of Choice, a smooth affine curve is a finite disjoint union of open and closed connected smooth affine curves, and its Picard group is the product of their Picard groups ([lem-author-9ab3274efad8-smooth-affine-components](item-lem-author-9ab3274efad8-smooth-affine-components), [lem-author-9ab3274efad8-picard-disjoint-union](item-lem-author-9ab3274efad8-picard-disjoint-union)).

[F5] Surjectivity of multiplication by every positive integer is equivalent to divisibility of an abelian group ([lem-author-9ab3274efad8-positive-roots](item-lem-author-9ab3274efad8-positive-roots)).

[A1] Assume the Axiom of Choice, used in the component suppliers ([math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)).

**Given:** A smooth affine curve $C$ over an algebraically closed field $k$, and the Axiom of Choice.

**Goal:** Prove $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$ divisible.

### Proof

1.1 First suppose $C$ is connected and fix a positive integer $n$. Choose $X$ and the surjective restriction map $\operatorname{Pic}^0(X) \to \operatorname{Pic}(C)$ from [F1]. By [F2], transport multiplication by $n$ across the group isomorphism $\operatorname{Pic}^0(X) \cong J(k)$; it is surjective on $\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)$, including if the characteristic divides $n$. [F1, F2, A1, given, choose]

2.1 Apply the surjective-image result in [F3] to restriction. Multiplication by $n$ is therefore surjective on $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$. Since $n$ was arbitrary, this holds for every positive integer. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 In general, decompose $C$ into finitely many connected smooth affine components as in [F4]. Step 2.1 applies to each component. By [F3], multiplication by each positive $n$ is surjective on the finite product of their Picard groups, and [F4] transports that conclusion to $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$. The empty product case is included. [F3, F4, A1, step 2.1]

4.1 By [F5], $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$ is divisible, as required. [F5, step 3.1] ∎


## Cohomology descends to the derived category

[Open item](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-cohomology) · level 3

### Statement
For each integer $i$, cohomology defines a functor $H^i:D(\mathbb Z)\to\operatorname{Ab}$. Here $D(\mathbb Z)$ is the derived category of cochain complexes of abelian groups, obtained by inverting quasi-isomorphisms; a quasi-isomorphism is a cochain map inducing an isomorphism on every cohomology group.

### Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The derived category is the localization of the homotopy category of complexes at quasi-isomorphisms and has the corresponding universal property ([math:def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category)).

[F2] Cochain maps induce functorial cohomology maps, and homotopic maps induce equal maps ([lem-author-b747b28c359f-cochain-maps](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-cochain-maps), [lem-author-b747b28c359f-homotopy-cohomology](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-homotopy-cohomology)).

### Proof

**Given:** An integer $i$ and the derived category described in the statement.

**Goal:** Construct the stated functor.

1.1 By [F2], taking $i$th cohomology is a functor on the homotopy category. Every quasi-isomorphism becomes an isomorphism under this functor by the definition of quasi-isomorphism. [F2, given]

2.1 The localization universal property in [F1] therefore gives a functor on $D(\mathbb Z)$ whose composite with localization is the functor of step 1.1. Thus cohomology and its maps depend only on the derived-category object and morphism. [F1, step 1.1] ∎

## The scheme of nontransverse zero jets has small dimension

[Open item](item-lem-author-fc2380accb47-nontransverse-incidence) · level 3


### Statement
Use the family and $T=\mathbb A^N$ above. Let $I_W\subset W\times T$ be the universal zero-incidence scheme. On it, differentiation in the $W$ direction defines the intrinsic linear map $d_W\Phi:T_{W/k}\to E$ (pulled back to $I_W$). Let $B\subset I_W$ be its determinant-zero closed subscheme. Then $\dim B\leq N-1$. A point of a specialized zero scheme is outside $B$ exactly when this derivative is an isomorphism. These are equations for the scheme and its derivative, rather than only a count of set-theoretic fibers.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The smooth three-dimensional $W$, the rank-three $E$, and the surjective first-jet map of the preceding lemma, retaining that lemma's Axiom of Choice assumption.

**Goal:** Bound the complete incidence of nontransverse zeros in every characteristic.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the first-jet family supplier in [F1], where it supplies affine global generation. The subsequent local determinant and dimension calculations introduce no additional choice. [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

[F1] [lem-author-fc2380accb47-coordinate-first-jets](item-lem-author-fc2380accb47-coordinate-first-jets) constructs the rank-twelve jet bundle and its locally split surjection from $\mathcal O_W^N$ under [A1].

[F2] [lem-regular-section-parameter-family](item-lem-regular-section-parameter-family) constructs the actual universal zero ideal and its parameter fibers. Apply its functional-family construction to $E^\vee$; local dual bases identify $E^{\vee\vee}$ with $E$, so the resulting functional has the same coefficients and zero ideal as the present section of $E$. [lem-surjection-kernel-bundle](item-lem-surjection-kernel-bundle) supplies local splitting.

[F3] Dimension adds for products of finite-type schemes over a field and does not exceed the source dimension on taking image closure. [thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input](item-thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input)

### Proof
1.1 On a frame chart the universal section has three coefficients. At a zero, differentiating a change of frame adds $(dG)\Phi=0$, so the derivative transforms by invertible matrices. Hence its determinant-zero condition glues to the stated closed subscheme $B$. In jet space it is the condition that the value part is zero and the derivative, a $3\times3$ matrix, is singular. These equations are pulled back by the actual jet-evaluation morphism of [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, given]

1.2 Singular $3\times3$ matrices form a variety of dimension eight over any field. On a chart where a chosen $2\times2$ minor is invertible, a block matrix has rank at most two precisely when its last entry is the forced Schur complement; the other eight entries are free with that minor inverted. These charts cover rank two. For rank at most one, choosing a nonzero entry as pivot expresses the remaining entries from its row and column, leaving five free parameters; the zero matrix is a further point. Thus the dimension is eight, without a characteristic restriction. The bad jets in each twelve-dimensional jet fiber have zero value and this eight-dimensional derivative locus. [algebra]

2.1 Locally split the surjection of [F1] and trivialize $E$ and $\Omega^1$. The inverse image of that bad-jet locus is locally its product with affine space of dimension $N-12$. Its dimension is therefore at most $\dim W+8+N-12=N-1$ by [F3]. A finite such open cover suffices because $W$ is Noetherian and quasi-compact. This proves the bound globally, and the determinant definition proves the specialized derivative assertion. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎


## Rational cofiber implies finite-coefficient equivalence

[Open item](item-lem-author-4b6f215bcf3b-rational-cofiber-comparison) · level 3

### Statement
Let $f:A\to B$ be a morphism in $D(\mathbb Z)$ whose cofiber is isomorphic in $D(\mathbb Z)$ to the underlying complex of a complex of $\mathbb Q$-vector spaces. For every positive integer $n$, $f\otimes_{\mathbb Z}^{\mathbf L}\mathbb Z/n$ is an isomorphism in $D(\mathbb Z)$, and consequently induces an isomorphism on $H^i$ for every integer $i$.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $f$ and $n$ as stated.

**Goal:** Prove the finite-coefficient equivalence and its cohomological consequence.

[F1] A rational complex has zero derived quotient by $n$. [lem-author-4b6f215bcf3b-rational-derived-quotient](item-lem-author-4b6f215bcf3b-rational-derived-quotient)

[F2] Taking the derived quotient by $n$ commutes with mapping cones. [lem-author-4b6f215bcf3b-quotient-cofiber](item-lem-author-4b6f215bcf3b-quotient-cofiber)

### Proof

1.1 By [F1] and [F2], the mapping cone of $f\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathbb Z/n$ is zero in $D(\mathbb Z)$, equivalently it is acyclic. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 The long exact cohomology sequence of the mapping cone, obtained from the degreewise split sequence $B\to\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to A[1]$, shows that a chain map with acyclic cone induces an isomorphism on every cohomology group. Thus the finite-coefficient map is a quasi-isomorphism and hence an isomorphism in $D(\mathbb Z)$. Applying $H^i$ gives the stated group isomorphism. [step 1.1] ∎

## Mohan Kumar existence of a nontrivial stably trivial bundle on a complex affine fourfold

[Open item](item-thm-author-b02e51f9da03-mohan-kumar-existence-input) · level 3

### Statement
There exist a nonempty smooth affine complex algebraic variety $X$ of dimension four and a rank-two vector bundle $E$ with $E\not\cong\mathcal O_X^2$ but $E\oplus\mathcal O_X^N\cong\mathcal O_X^{2+N}$ for some integer $N\geq1$. The variety can be taken to be the complement of a union of three hypersurfaces in $\mathbb P^3_{\mathbb C}\times\mathbb A^1_{\mathbb C}$, as in Mohan Kumar\'s construction. No particular defining equations are selected in this input. On writing $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$, there is therefore a right-invertible matrix $q:A^{2+N}\to A^N$ whose associated kernel bundle is $E$ and which cannot be completed to an invertible $(2+N)\times(2+N)$ matrix.

### External input
The deep construction and the assertion of algebraic nontriviality are explicitly imported from the precise authoritative subsequent statement. The local numbered steps expand the definition and translate nontriviality into a matrix-completion obstruction. No equations for the hypersurfaces or entries of a matrix are invented, and no original Kumar proof or independent Hermitian-K-theory invariant computation is claimed. The five preceding fully authored prerequisites give the construction/application interface and the actual Chern-class consequences.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data and hypotheses in the statement, AC and the article's fixed universe bounds where its K-theory is used.

**Goal:** Establish the stated conclusion.

[F1] The exact established existence statement and the geometric description are imported from Brazelton–Opie–Syed Example 6.6, which attributes them to N. Mohan Kumar MK84/MK85.

[F2] Stable triviality means an actual finite free stabilization. [def-stably-free-bundles](item-def-stably-free-bundles)

[F3] The local matrix-kernel construction and completion criterion are [lem-author-b02e51f9da03-matrix-kernel](item-lem-author-b02e51f9da03-matrix-kernel) and [lem-author-b02e51f9da03-matrix-completion](item-lem-author-b02e51f9da03-matrix-completion).

### Proof

1.1 Apply the imported existence statement over the explicit base field $\mathbb C$. It supplies the smooth affine fourfold X and the rank-two nontrivial stably trivial bundle E, with the stated geometric description. Expanding stable triviality via [F2] supplies a finite N and an actual isomorphism. Since E is nontrivial, N cannot be zero. [F1, F2]

2.1 Choose one such stable isomorphism. By [F3] it yields a right-invertible matrix q whose kernel sheaf is E. If q were completable, the completion criterion in [F3] would make E trivial, contradicting [F1]. Thus q is not completable. This matrix consequence is local algebra deduced from the imported bundle existence; it is not a claim that the source gives this matrix explicitly. [F1, F3, step 1.1] ∎


## Homotopy exactness of a spectral fiber sequence

[Open item](item-lem-fiber-sequence-homotopy-exactness) · level 4

### Statement
For a fiber sequence $A\to B\to C$ of spectra there is a natural exact sequence of abelian groups

$$\cdots\to\pi_{i+1}C\to\pi_iA\to\pi_iB\to\pi_iC\to\pi_{i-1}A\to\cdots.$$

If $\pi_iC=0$, then $\pi_iA\to\pi_iB$ is surjective; if also $\pi_{i+1}C=0$, it is an isomorphism. Exactness is asserted for these homotopy groups themselves, before taking images in another spectrum.

A fiber sequence here consists of maps $A\to B\to C$, a specified nullhomotopy of their composite, and an identification of $A$ with the homotopy pullback $B\times_C0$. For a spectrum $E$ and an integer $i$, $\pi_iE$ is the group of components of the mapping space from the $i$-fold suspension of the sphere spectrum to $E$. Exactness means that the image of each displayed homomorphism equals the kernel of the next.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A fiber sequence $A\to B\to C$ of spectra and an integer $i$.

**Goal:** Construct the natural long exact sequence and prove the stated consequences.

[F1] In the stable spectra interface, mapping spaces represent coherent maps and carry limits in the target to homotopy limits of spaces. Fiber sequences extend to cofiber triangles; pushout and pullback squares agree, and suspension is an equivalence with inverse desuspension. The groups are $\pi_iE=\pi_0\operatorname{Map}(\mathbb S[i],E)$, are abelian, and satisfy $\pi_i(E[1])\cong\pi_{i-1}E$ naturally. [def-stable-spectra-interface](item-def-stable-spectra-interface)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Apply mapping spaces to rotated fiber squares and examine components of their homotopy fibers.

1.1 For any spectrum $T$, apply $\operatorname{Map}(T,-)$ to the defining pullback square for $A$. By its universal property, $\operatorname{Map}(T,A)$ is the homotopy fiber of $\operatorname{Map}(T,B)\to\operatorname{Map}(T,C)$ over the zero map. A point in this fiber is a map $T\to B$ together with a path from its composite with $B\to C$ to zero. Thus a component of $\operatorname{Map}(T,B)$ has zero image in $\pi_0\operatorname{Map}(T,C)$ exactly when it has a representative admitting such a path, equivalently when it lies in the image of $\pi_0\operatorname{Map}(T,A)$. This proves exactness at $\pi_0\operatorname{Map}(T,B)$. [F1, given]

2.1 The defining pullback square is also a pushout, so its cofiber triangle is $A\to B\to C\to A[1]$. The square exhibiting $C$ as the cofiber of $A\to B$ is also a pullback; hence $B\to C\to A[1]$ is a fiber sequence with the induced nullhomotopy. Repeating this rotation and applying inverse suspension produces a bi-infinite sequence of fiber sequences. Applying step 1.1 to each one gives exactness at every term of the resulting sequence of mapping-space component groups. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 Take $T=\mathbb S[i]$. The first rotated terms are $\pi_iA\to\pi_iB\to\pi_iC\to\pi_i(A[1])$, and the natural suspension identification identifies the last group with $\pi_{i-1}A$. Applying the same identification to the other rotations gives the displayed long sequence. The connecting maps are induced by the cofiber-triangle maps, with these suspension identifications. The construction is natural for maps of fiber sequences, including their specified coherences, because it uses the universal properties of the fiber and cofiber squares. The displayed maps are homomorphisms under the abelian group structures of [F1]. [F1, step 2.1]

4.1 Exactness at $\pi_iB$ makes $\pi_iA\to\pi_iB$ surjective when $\pi_iC=0$. Exactness at $\pi_iA$ makes its kernel the image of $\pi_{i+1}C$, so it is also injective when that group vanishes. Hence it is an isomorphism in the latter case. These deductions concern the groups in the fiber sequence; no preservation of exactness after taking images in a further group is asserted. [step 3.1] ∎

## Perfect complexes on schemes and their support

[Open item](item-def-scheme-perfect-complexes) · level 4

### Definition
Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix suitable universes. Let $X$ be any scheme. Let $\mathcal D(X)$ be the stable derived infinity-category obtained from cochain complexes of Zariski $\mathcal O_X$-modules by inverting quasi-isomorphisms. A quasi-isomorphism induces an isomorphism on every cohomology sheaf. Its homotopy category is the ordinary unbounded derived category $D(\mathcal O_X)$.

An object $E$ is **perfect** if every point has an open neighbourhood on which $E$ is equivalent to a bounded complex of finite locally free modules. Bounded means nonzero in only finitely many degrees; finite locally free means locally a finite direct sum of copies of the structure sheaf. Bounds may vary between neighbourhoods. Write $\operatorname{Perf}(X)$ for the full enhanced subcategory on these objects, retaining all ambient mapping spaces and their composition coherences.

The **support** of $E$ is $\operatorname{Supp}(E)=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb Z}\{x\in X:H^n(E)_x\ne0\}$. For any subset $T\subseteq X$, define $\operatorname{Perf}_T(X)$ as the full subcategory of perfect objects with support contained in $T$. If $T$ is closed and $j:X\setminus T\hookrightarrow X$ is the open immersion, this is equivalently the full subcategory on objects with $j^*E\simeq0$; thus these complexes are acyclic on the open complement. For arbitrary $T$, the condition is interpreted stalkwise.

These full subcategories are stable and idempotent complete. Their finite limits and colimits are inherited from $\mathcal D(X)$; their exact triangles are the images in the homotopy category of ambient cofiber sequences $E\to F\to G\to E[1]$. For cochains, $E[1]^n=E^{n+1}$ with differential $-d$.

For a commutative unital ring $A$, degreewise associated sheaf gives an exact equivalence $\operatorname{Perf}(A)\simeq\operatorname{Perf}(\operatorname{Spec}A)$, where $\operatorname{Perf}(A)$ is the full subcategory of $\mathcal D(A)$ on objects represented by bounded complexes of finitely generated projective $A$-modules.

### Justification
[lem-author-4f716d60801a-local-perfect-qc](item-lem-author-4f716d60801a-local-perfect-qc) proves that the local condition is independent of representatives and gives quasi-coherent cohomology. [lem-author-4f716d60801a-restriction-support](item-lem-author-4f716d60801a-restriction-support) proves invariance of support and the open-complement equivalence. [lem-author-4f716d60801a-supported-stability](item-lem-author-4f716d60801a-supported-stability) proves the stable and idempotent-complete subcategory assertions. [lem-author-4f716d60801a-lifted-affine-equivalence](item-lem-author-4f716d60801a-lifted-affine-equivalence) proves the enhanced affine comparison for the actual associated-sheaf functor, and [math:def-perfect-complex-over-a-ring](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-perfect-complex-over-a-ring) supplies the ring convention. No global bound or global vector-bundle resolution is imposed.

## Decreasing spectral filtrations and associated graded

[Open item](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum) · level 4

### Definition
Let $E$ be a spectrum. A **decreasing filtration on $E$** consists of spectra $F^jE$, indexed by $j\in\mathbb Z$, and a coherent diagram whose transition maps $F^jE\to F^kE$ are defined whenever $j\geq k$, together with a coherent compatible family of maps $F^jE\to E$. Thus the composite $F^{j+1}E\to F^jE\to E$ is identified with the given map $F^{j+1}E\to E$. Coherent means that the maps, their composition identifications, and all higher compatibility data form a diagram and a cone in the infinity-category of spectra.

The **associated graded spectrum in degree $j$** is $\operatorname{gr}^jE=\operatorname{cofib}(F^{j+1}E\to F^jE)$. For $i\in\mathbb Z$, its **image filtration** on the homotopy group $\pi_iE$ is the family of subgroups

$$F^j\pi_iE=\operatorname{im}(\pi_iF^jE\longrightarrow\pi_iE).$$

The filtration is **exhaustive** if the canonical map $\operatorname*{colim}_{j\to-\infty}F^jE\to E$ is an equivalence. Here the colimit is over the maps from larger indices to smaller indices. It is **complete**, in the tower-vanishing convention used here, if $\operatorname*{lim}_{j\to+\infty}F^jE$ is equivalent to the zero spectrum; the limit is taken over the same transition maps. It is **nonnegative** if every structure map $F^jE\to E$ is an equivalence for $j\leq0$. Completeness imposes no injectivity condition on the maps $\pi_iF^jE\to\pi_iE$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A spectrum $E$ and a coherent augmented tower as in the definition.

**Goal:** Justify the graded spectra, image filtration, and the stated conditions.

[F1] [def-stable-spectra-interface](item-def-stable-spectra-interface) supplies the stable infinity-category of spectra, its small limits and colimits, cofibers, zero spectrum, and functorial abelian homotopy groups.

### Justification
1.1 The index category has one object for each integer and one arrow $j\to k$ when $j\geq k$. It is small, so the tower has a limit and a colimit. The compatible maps to $E$ form a cone and induce the displayed canonical colimit map. Each transition map has a cofiber, so every $\operatorname{gr}^jE$ is defined. These constructions are invariant under equivalence of the coherent input diagrams. [F1, given]

2.1 Applying $\pi_i$ gives group homomorphisms. The image of each structure map is therefore a subgroup of $\pi_iE$, and compatibility with $F^{j+1}E\to F^jE$ gives $F^{j+1}\pi_iE\subseteq F^j\pi_iE$. Equivalence to $E$ or to the zero spectrum is a well-defined condition on the specified maps or limit. None of the three conditions includes injectivity of the homomorphisms defining the image filtration; in particular, completeness is the stated condition on the tower limit. [F1, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Smooth-locus restriction properties

[Open item](item-lem-normal-smooth-locus-restriction) · level 4

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and $X$ a finite-type $k$-scheme. If $X$ is reduced, its smooth locus $U$ is open and meets every irreducible component densely. In particular, this applies to the reduced seminormal schemes in the proof of Lemma 5.1 of the article. If $X$ is normal, then $U$ is dense, $X\setminus U$ has codimension at least two in every irreducible component, and restriction induces isomorphisms $\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)\cong\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$ and $\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)^\times\cong\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)^\times$, as well as an injection $\operatorname{Pic}(X)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(U)$.

Here algebraically closed means that every nonconstant polynomial over $k$ has a root in $k$. Finite type means that $X$ has a finite affine cover by spectra of finitely generated $k$-algebras. Reduced means that its local rings have no nonzero nilpotents; normal means that its local rings are integrally closed domains. The smooth locus is the set of points at which the structure morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth. Codimension of a point in an irreducible component is the supremum of the lengths of strict chains of irreducible closed subsets from that component to the closure of the point; the codimension of a subset is the infimum of the codimensions of its points, with the empty subset assigned $+\infty$. A global unit is a global function with a multiplicative inverse. The Picard group is the group of isomorphism classes of line bundles, meaning locally free $\mathcal O_X$-modules of rank one, under tensor product. Restriction is induced by pulling back functions or line bundles along $U\hookrightarrow X$.

### Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The article conventions specify the algebraically closed base field and scheme language ([def-article-conventions](item-def-article-conventions)).

[F2] Under the Axiom of Choice, the smooth locus of a reduced finite-type scheme over a perfect field is open and meets every irreducible component densely; for a normal such scheme its complement has codimension at least two in every component ([lem-perfect-base-smooth-density](item-lem-perfect-base-smooth-density)). A field is perfect when all its algebraic extensions are separable.

[F3] Under the Axiom of Choice, if $X$ is a noetherian normal scheme and an open immersion $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ contains all points of component codimension at most one, then $\mathcal O_X\to j_*\mathcal O_U$ is an isomorphism. Consequently global functions and global units restrict isomorphically ([lem-codimension-two-extension](item-lem-codimension-two-extension)).

[F4] Under the same hypotheses as [F3], restriction $\operatorname{Pic}(X)\to\operatorname{Pic}(U)$ is injective ([lem-codimension-two-picard-restriction](item-lem-codimension-two-picard-restriction)).

[F5] Every polynomial algebra in finitely many variables over a field is noetherian ([math:lem-finite-variable-polynomial-algebras-over-fields-are-noetherian-direct](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/lem-finite-variable-polynomial-algebras-over-fields-are-noetherian-direct)).

[A1] The Axiom of Choice, asserting that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function, is assumed for [F2], [F3], and [F4] ([math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)).

### Proof

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, an algebraically closed field $k$, and a finite-type $k$-scheme $X$.

**Goal:** Prove the smooth-density assertion for reduced $X$ and the codimension, function, unit, and Picard assertions for normal $X$.

1.1 The field $k$ is perfect: if $L/k$ is algebraic and $a\in L$, its minimal polynomial over $k$ is irreducible and has a root in $k$ by algebraic closedness. It is therefore linear, so $a\in k$ and is separable over $k$. Thus every algebraic extension is separable. If $X$ is reduced, [F2] now shows that its smooth locus is open and meets every irreducible component densely. This applies in particular whenever a scheme in the article's seminormal setting is reduced; no further property of seminormality is used here. [F1, F2, A1, given]

2.1 Suppose $X$ is normal. Every integrally closed domain is reduced, so $X$ is reduced. Each coordinate ring in a finite affine cover of $X$ is a quotient of a finite-variable polynomial ring over $k$. By [F5] and the correspondence between ideals of a quotient and ideals containing its kernel, each such coordinate ring is noetherian. Hence $X$ is a noetherian normal scheme in the sense required by [F3] and [F4]. By [F2] and step 1.1, $U$ is open and dense and its complement has codimension at least two in every irreducible component. Consequently $U$ contains every point of component codimension zero or one. [F2, F5, A1, step 1.1, given]

3.1 Apply [F3] to $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ using step 2.1. It gives $\mathcal O_X\cong j_*\mathcal O_U$, and therefore the stated isomorphisms on global functions and global units. Applying [F4] to the same open immersion gives injectivity on Picard groups. Together with steps 1.1 and 2.1, these are all the asserted conclusions. [F3, F4, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Functorial finite coefficients for derived complexes

[Open item](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-finite-coefficients) · level 4

### Statement
For $C\in D(\mathbb Z)$ and a positive integer $n$, put $C/n=C\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n$. This construction and its cohomology groups are functorial in $C$. For every integer $i$ there is a natural short exact sequence
$$0\to H^i(C)/nH^i(C)\to H^i(C/n)\to H^{i+1}(C)[n]\to0,$$
where $H^{i+1}(C)[n]$ is the subgroup annihilated by $n$.

### Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [lem-derived-coefficient-exact-sequence](item-lem-derived-coefficient-exact-sequence) identifies derived tensoring with $\mathbb Z/n$ with the cone of multiplication by $n$ and supplies the displayed natural exact sequence for complexes.

[F2] Cohomology is a functor on $D(\mathbb Z)$ ([lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-cohomology](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-cohomology)).

### Proof

**Given:** $C\in D(\mathbb Z)$ and a positive integer $n$.

**Goal:** Establish functoriality and the exact sequence.

1.1 Choose a complex representing $C$. By [F1], its multiplication-by-$n$ cone represents $C\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathbb Z/n$. Derived tensor product is a functor on the derived category; applying [F2] gives functorial cohomology groups, independent of the representative. [F1, F2]

2.1 Apply the natural exact sequence of [F1] to the representative. Step 1.1 identifies its terms with the displayed derived-category terms and transports naturality to maps in $D(\mathbb Z)$. This proves the assertion. [F1, step 1.1] ∎

## Gluing upper bounds through an actual fiber sequence

[Open item](item-lem-author-0bac6b264f4a-motivic-dim-cohomological-glueing) · level 4


### Statement
Let $A\to B\to C$ be a fiber sequence in $D(\mathbb Z)$, and let $N\in\mathbb Z$. If $A$ is supported in cohomological degrees $\leq N$, then $H^N(B)\to H^N(C)$ is surjective and $H^i(B)\to H^i(C)$ is an isomorphism for every $i>N$. If in addition $C$ is supported in degrees $\leq N$, then so is $B$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The specified fiber sequence and integer $N$.

**Goal:** Transfer the two outer bounds to the middle term with the exact degree endpoints.

[F1] [lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-cohomology](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-cohomology) supplies functorial cohomology on $D(\mathbb Z)$.

[F2] In the standard derived triangulated structure, distinguished triangles are the triangles isomorphic to localized mapping-cone triangles, and each gives the long exact cohomology sequence. Use the usual fixed-universe size convention for complexes of abelian groups. [math:thm-the-derived-category-inherits-a-triangulated-structure](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-the-derived-category-inherits-a-triangulated-structure)

### Proof
1.1 The given fiber sequence extends to its distinguished triangle $A\to B\to C\to A[1]$ in the standard derived structure. Applying [F2] and the cohomology functors [F1], its long exact sequence contains $H^i(A)\to H^i(B)\to H^i(C)\to H^{i+1}(A)$. At $i=N$ the last group is zero, which gives the stated surjectivity. At $i>N$ both outer groups are zero, so the middle arrow is an isomorphism. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 If $H^i(C)=0$ for $i>N$, the isomorphism in step 1.1 gives $H^i(B)=0$ for those same degrees. This proves the middle upper bound without any splitting or identification of unrelated groups. [F1, step 1.1] ∎


## External dimension criterion for a cdh-acyclic Nisnevich sheaf

[Open item](item-thm-author-0bac6b264f4a-motivic-dim-dimension-criterion-input) · level 4


### Statement
Let $R$ be a base ring and $W:(\mathrm{Sch}^{\mathrm{qcqs}}_R)^{op}\to D(\mathbb Z)$ a finitary Nisnevich sheaf. Assume:

1. $L_{\mathrm{cdh}}W\simeq0$.
2. $W$ satisfies pro-cdh descent on Noetherian $R$-schemes.
3. For every Noetherian local henselian $R$-algebra $A$ and every nilpotent ideal $I$, $\operatorname{fib}(W(A)\to W(A/I))\in D(\mathbb Z)^{\leq0}$.

Then $W(X)\in D(\mathbb Z)^{\leq\dim X}$ for every Noetherian $R$-scheme $X$ of finite dimension.

### Source contract
**Given:** All three assumptions and the stated sheaf, continuity and scheme hypotheses.

**Goal:** Import the established geometric dimension criterion, including its exact input class.

[F1] EM Proposition8.10 is this statement with arbitrary base ring.

### External input
Import [F1] with the recorded reading limits. Finitary means that inverse limits of qcqs schemes with affine transition maps are sent to the corresponding filtered colimits of complexes. Nisnevich descent means derived descent for the étale completely decomposed covering families. The cdh topology is generated by Nisnevich covers and abstract blowup covers. An abstract blowup square consists of a proper finitely presented map $X'\to X$, a finitely presented closed immersion $Y\to X$, its pullback $Y'$, and an isomorphism $X'\setminus Y'\simeq X\setminus Y$. Pro-cdh descent here has exactly the degreewise convention of EM Theorem 8.2, footnote 14: for each abstract blowup square and its powers-of-ideal thickenings, every cohomology group of the levelwise total fiber is zero as a pro abelian group. No equivalence with a cartesian square in the unbounded category $\operatorname{Pro}(D(\mathbb Z))$ is used. In the modification step of Proposition 8.10, this degreewise hypothesis suffices: for fixed $n>\dim X$, the induction makes the two lower-dimensional relative cohomology systems vanish in the relevant degrees, and the pro long exact sequence gives the required isomorphism on degree $n$ for the two constant top terms. A nilpotent ideal satisfies $I^n=0$ for some $n$; a henselian local algebra has the usual unique lifting of simple roots from its residue field. These are hypotheses of the imported theorem, not new claims that a general sheaf has them.

### Statement
An isomorphism $A\cong B$ in the derived category of complexes of abelian groups induces an isomorphism $H^i(A)\cong H^i(B)$ for each integer $i$. The derived category is the category in which quasi-isomorphisms, meaning cochain maps inducing isomorphisms on all cohomology groups, have been inverted.

**Goal:** Obtain the induced cohomology isomorphism.

2.1 Functoriality sends the two inverse composites to identity maps, so the resulting maps on cohomology are inverse isomorphisms. [F1, step 1.1] ∎

## Cycle-complex degree translation

[Open item](item-lem-author-91088613574d-cycle-reindex) · level 4


### Statement
Let $k$ be a field, $X$ a smooth finite-type $k$-scheme, and $j\geq0$. Regard Bloch's homological cycle complex $z^j(X,\bullet)$ as a cochain complex by placing its degree-$n$ group in cochain degree $-n$. Then
$$H^i(z^j(X,\bullet)[-2j])\cong\mathrm{CH}^j(X,2j-i)$$
for every integer $i$, where the right side is higher Chow homology and is zero in negative homological degrees.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** $k,X,j,i$ as stated.

**Goal:** Translate the shift into higher Chow indexing.

[F1] Bloch's complex and higher Chow groups are the specified chain complex and its homology; the complex is zero in negative degrees. [def-bloch-higher-cycle-complex](item-def-bloch-higher-cycle-complex)

[F2] Chain-to-cochain reindexing identifies degree-$q$ cohomology with degree-$(-q)$ homology. [lem-author-91088613574d-chain-cochain](item-lem-author-91088613574d-chain-cochain)

[F3] The even shift changes cohomological degree $i$ to $i-2j$. [lem-author-91088613574d-even-shift](item-lem-author-91088613574d-even-shift)

### Proof
1.1 By [F3], degree-$i$ cohomology of the shifted complex is degree-$(i-2j)$ cohomology of the reindexed cycle complex. [F3, given]

2.1 By [F2] this is homology in degree $2j-i$, which is the higher Chow group by [F1]. If that degree is negative it is zero by the same definition. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎


## One nonempty parameter open gives smooth-locus avoidance and transversality

[Open item](item-lem-author-fc2380accb47-simultaneous-good-parameters) · level 4


### Statement
In the preceding setting with $X$ normal of dimension at most three, there is a nonempty Zariski open $T^\circ\subset T$ such that the zero scheme of every parameter over any field extension whose point factors through $T^\circ$ avoids $D=X\setminus W$ and has invertible derivative at every zero in $W$. In particular $T^\circ$ has a $k$-rational parameter. On a pure threefold the forbidden incidence over the singular locus has dimension at most $N-2$; with lower-dimensional components permitted it has dimension at most $N-1$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The actual universal family on $X$, with $W,D$ as defined above, retaining the Axiom of Choice assumed by its first-jet construction.

**Goal:** Choose a parameter meeting both requirements simultaneously, without characteristic-zero generic smoothness or an assumed dominant projection.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the first-jet family in [F2] and the nontransverse-incidence supplier in [F3]. It is used there for affine global generation; the subsequent dimension and open-complement argument makes no additional arbitrary choice. [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

[F1] [lem-author-fc2380accb47-normal-smooth-strata](item-lem-author-fc2380accb47-normal-smooth-strata) gives $\dim D\leq2$, or $\leq1$ in pure dimension three.

[F2] [lem-author-fc2380accb47-coordinate-first-jets](item-lem-author-fc2380accb47-coordinate-first-jets) gives value generation on $X$. [lem-regular-section-parameter-family](item-lem-regular-section-parameter-family) identifies incidence and all its base changes; [lem-surjection-kernel-bundle](item-lem-surjection-kernel-bundle) makes the value kernel a rank-$(N-3)$ bundle, also after restriction to $D$.

[F3] [lem-author-fc2380accb47-nontransverse-incidence](item-lem-author-fc2380accb47-nontransverse-incidence) bounds $B$ by $N-1$. Image closures, product dimensions and rational closed points use [thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input](item-thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input).

### Proof
1.1 Under [A1], use the given family of [F2]. The zero-incidence scheme $I_D$ over $D$ is the total space of the kernel of the surjection $\mathcal O_D^N\to E|_D$. Indeed local splitting identifies its equations with three independent parameter coordinates set to zero. Its dimension is at most $\dim D+N-3\leq N-1$, and in pure dimension three it is at most $N-2$. This is a scheme dimension bound even when $D$ is singular. [A1, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 By [F3], the closures of the images of $I_D$ and $B$ in $T$ have dimension at most $N-1$. Their union is a proper closed subset of the irreducible $N$-dimensional affine space $T$. Let $T^\circ$ be its complement. It is nonempty and has a closed $k$-rational point by the Jacobson/residue-field assertion in [F3]. Thus the parameter exists over the original field, not merely over an unspecified extension. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 By definition of those image closures, their open complement has empty inverse image in $I_D$ and $B$. This remains true after any field extension. Therefore every corresponding zero lies in $W$ with nonzero derivative determinant. This controls actual incidence schemes and all geometric zeros. No generic-smoothness assertion from the total dimension of $I_W$ is used, and no dominance of $I_W\to T$ is required for this conclusion. The next lemma identifies its actual fibers over $T^\circ$, including its generic fiber. [F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎


## Smooth affine components and gluing a trivial line

[Open item](item-lem-author-394a5b71198d-components) · level 4

### Statement
Assume AC. A nonempty smooth affine finite-type scheme $X$ over an algebraically closed field has a finite disjoint decomposition $X=\coprod_jX_j$ into integral open and closed smooth affine schemes. Put $d=\dim X$ and $d_j=\dim X_j\leq d$. Bundles, bundle isomorphisms and finite direct sums are given componentwise. Define $\mathrm{CH}^i(X)=\bigoplus_j\mathrm{CH}^i(X_j)$ in the codimension convention; this agrees with the usual Chow ring for pure-dimensional $X$. Chern classes are given componentwise. If a rank-$d$ bundle restricts to a bundle with a trivial line summand on every $X_j$, these decompositions glue to a trivial line summand on $X$. For $d_j<d$, its restriction always splits off a line.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and data in the statement, with AC and the article's fixed universes wherever perfect K-theory is used.

**Goal:** Establish the asserted conclusion.

[F1] Smooth finite-type schemes over a perfect field are regular; regular local rings are domains. [math:thm-regular-equals-smooth-over-perfect-field](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-regular-equals-smooth-over-perfect-field), [math:thm-regular-local-rings-are-domains-and-cohen-macaulay](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-regular-local-rings-are-domains-and-cohen-macaulay)

[F2] A noetherian space has finitely many irreducible components. [math:lem-noetherian-space-has-finitely-many-irreducible-components](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/lem-noetherian-space-has-finitely-many-irreducible-components)

[F3] Chow groups are cycles modulo divisors of rational functions on integral closed subschemes. [math:def-chow-group-of-cycles-mod-rational-equivalence](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-chow-group-of-cycles-mod-rational-equivalence)

[F4] A bundle of rank greater than the dimension on a noetherian affine scheme splits off a trivial line. [thm-serre-affine-splitting](item-thm-serre-affine-splitting)

### Proof

1.1 A finite-type scheme over a field is noetherian. Distinct irreducible components cannot meet: at an intersection the local ring would have distinct minimal primes, contrary to being a domain by [F1]. Finiteness by [F2] makes each component both closed and open. Such a component is affine: glue the functions 1 and 0 on it and its complement to obtain a global idempotent, whose corresponding ring factor has that spectrum. Regularity makes each component reduced, hence integral. [F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Sheaves on a finite disjoint open cover are precisely the tuples of their restrictions: there are no nonempty overlaps imposing further gluing conditions. Thus bundle maps and isomorphisms, and decompositions $E_j\cong\mathcal O_{X_j}\oplus F_j$, glue. An integral closed subscheme and each rational-function relation lie in a single component, so the cycle and relation groups split componentwise. This justifies the stated Chow convention and componentwise Chern operations. [F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 If $d_j<d$, the restricted rank-$d$ bundle satisfies the strict rank inequality in [F4] and therefore splits off a line. This also handles all components below maximal dimension without a critical-rank theorem. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎


## Cofiber bounds imply low-degree cohomology isomorphisms

[Open item](item-lem-author-13e6fe931c45-cone-low-degrees) · level 4


### Statement
Let $f:A\to B$ be a morphism in $D(\mathbb Z)$ and let $C$ be its cofiber, represented by a mapping cone. If $H^j(C)=0$ for every $j\leq n$, then $H^i(f)$ is an isomorphism for every $i\leq n$ and is injective for $i=n+1$. If, in addition, $H^{n+1}(C)=0$, it is an isomorphism also for $i=n+1$.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A derived-category morphism and a cone with the stated vanishing.

**Goal:** Establish the stated low-degree consequences.

[F1] Cohomology is a functor on $D(\mathbb Z)$ ([lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-cohomology](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-cohomology)).

### Proof

1.1 Represent the derived morphism by a chain map after replacing its source by a quasi-isomorphic complex. Its mapping cone fits in a degreewise split short exact sequence of complexes $0\to B\to\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to A[1]\to0$. Taking cycles and boundaries gives the long exact sequence $H^{i-1}(C)\to H^i(A)\to H^i(B)\to H^i(C)$. The result is independent of representatives by [F1]. [F1, construct]

2.1 For $i\leq n$, both adjacent cone groups in step 1.1 vanish, giving an isomorphism. For $i=n+1$, the left group $H^n(C)$ vanishes, giving injectivity; if also $H^{n+1}(C)=0$, the right group vanishes and the map is surjective as well. This proves every claimed range without a condition on $H^{n+2}(C)$. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎


## Scheme sites and sheafification

[Open item](item-def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification) · level 5

### Definition
Fix Grothendieck universes U in V. A scheme site here is a U-small category C whose objects are schemes and whose morphisms are scheme morphisms, equipped with a Grothendieck topology J. A sieve on X is a set of arrows into X closed under precomposition; a topology selects covering sieves, including the maximal sieve, stable under pullback and satisfying transitivity. A presheaf of sets is a contravariant functor C → Set_V. It is a sheaf when, for every covering sieve, every compatible family of sections indexed by its arrows has a unique amalgamation on the target.

The sheafification of a presheaf F is the sheaf aF = (F+)+, equipped with the composite F → F+ → (F+)+. Here F+(X) consists of matching families on covering sieves of X, with two families identified when they agree on a common covering subsieve; restriction uses pullback of sieves. Equivalently, a is left adjoint to the inclusion of sheaves into presheaves, with the displayed composite as unit.

A big site over a base S has a specified category of S-schemes as its objects; an S-scheme is a scheme equipped with a morphism to S, and its morphisms commute with those structure maps. A small site of a fixed S-scheme X instead uses a specified category of schemes over X, such as a suitable category of étale X-schemes. The chosen categories and covering topologies must be stated separately: the words small and big alone do not determine them. A complex of abelian sheaves, or a derived presheaf, requires its own abelian or derived-category conventions; set-valued sheafification alone does not assert a complex-valued descent or localization theorem.

### Definition references
[math:def-scheme-over-base](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-scheme-over-base)

[def-author-cf6ede58b450-site-plus-data](item-def-author-cf6ede58b450-site-plus-data)

### Justification
The size hypotheses make the sets of sieves, matching families and equivalence classes legitimate V-small sets. The plus construction is a presheaf and its unit is natural by [lem-author-cf6ede58b450-plus-presheaf](item-lem-author-cf6ede58b450-plus-presheaf). It is separated by [lem-author-cf6ede58b450-plus-separated](item-lem-author-cf6ede58b450-plus-separated), so its second application is a sheaf by [lem-author-cf6ede58b450-separated-plus-sheaf](item-lem-author-cf6ede58b450-separated-plus-sheaf). For every sheaf G, applying [lem-author-cf6ede58b450-plus-universal](item-lem-author-cf6ede58b450-plus-universal) successively to F and F+ gives natural bijections Hom((F+)+,G) ≅ Hom(F+,G) ≅ Hom(F,G). This proves the stated adjunction and identifies its unit. The definitions of the scheme categories require the separately specified topology and size bound; they do not claim that every possible category of schemes is U-small.

## Stage projections, kernels and image groups

[Open item](item-lem-filtered-stage-exact-sequence) · level 5

### Statement
Let $E$ be a spectrum with a decreasing filtration and let $i,j\in\mathbb Z$. There is a natural exact sequence of abelian groups

$$\pi_{i+1}\operatorname{gr}^jE\longrightarrow\pi_iF^{j+1}E\longrightarrow\pi_iF^jE\xrightarrow{p}\pi_i\operatorname{gr}^jE\longrightarrow\pi_{i-1}F^{j+1}E.$$

Write $q:\pi_iF^jE\to\pi_iE$ for the structure homomorphism and $F^j\pi_iE=\operatorname{im}q$. The stage projection $p$ induces a homomorphism $\bar p:F^j\pi_iE\to\pi_i\operatorname{gr}^jE$ satisfying $\bar p(q(x))=p(x)$ precisely when $\ker q\subseteq\ker p$. When it exists, its kernel is $F^{j+1}\pi_iE$. In particular, injectivity of $q$ is sufficient, and then $q$ identifies $\ker p$ with $F^{j+1}\pi_iE$.

A decreasing filtration consists of spectra $F^jE$ with compatible maps $F^{j+1}E\to F^jE\to E$. Its graded spectrum is the cofiber $\operatorname{gr}^jE=\operatorname{cofib}(F^{j+1}E\to F^jE)$. The image filtration is $F^j\pi_iE=\operatorname{im}(\pi_iF^jE\to\pi_iE)$. Exactness means that the image of each map equals the kernel of the next; $\pi_i$ denotes the $i$th homotopy group of a spectrum.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A spectrum $E$ with a decreasing filtration and integers $i,j$.

**Goal:** Prove the stage exact sequence and determine when its graded projection descends to the image filtration, together with its kernel.

[F1] The filtration supplies the compatible maps $F^{j+1}E\to F^jE\to E$, and $\operatorname{gr}^jE$ is the cofiber of the first map. Its image filtration is defined by the images of the structure maps. [def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum)

[F2] In spectra, a cofiber sequence is also a fiber sequence, with its coherent nullhomotopy. Homotopy groups are functorial abelian groups. [def-stable-spectra-interface](item-def-stable-spectra-interface)

[F3] A fiber sequence $A\to B\to C$ gives a natural long exact sequence $\cdots\to\pi_{i+1}C\to\pi_iA\to\pi_iB\to\pi_iC\to\pi_{i-1}A\to\cdots$. [lem-fiber-sequence-homotopy-exactness](item-lem-fiber-sequence-homotopy-exactness)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Apply homotopy exactness to the cofiber sequence, then use the elementary criterion for a homomorphism to factor through an image.

1.1 By [F1] and [F2], $F^{j+1}E\to F^jE\to\operatorname{gr}^jE$ is a fiber sequence. Applying [F3] gives the displayed exact sequence, including the indicated connecting maps. Its naturality follows from the naturality in [F3] for maps of these sequences. [F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 Let $r:\pi_iF^{j+1}E\to\pi_iF^jE$ be the transition homomorphism. Exactness at $\pi_iF^jE$ gives $\ker p=\operatorname{im}r$. Compatibility of the filtration maps gives $q\circ r:\pi_iF^{j+1}E\to\pi_iE$ as the structure homomorphism, and hence $q(\ker p)=F^{j+1}\pi_iE$. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 If a homomorphism $\bar p$ with $\bar p q=p$ exists on $\operatorname{im}q$, then $q(x)=0$ implies $p(x)=\bar p(0)=0$, so $\ker q\subseteq\ker p$. Conversely, under this inclusion define $\bar p(q(x))=p(x)$. If $q(x)=q(y)$, then $x-y\in\ker q\subseteq\ker p$, so $p(x)=p(y)$; thus the formula is independent of the lift. It defines a homomorphism because $p$ and $q$ are homomorphisms, and it is the unique such homomorphism because $q$ is onto its image. [F2, construct, step 2.1]

4.1 When $\bar p$ exists, an element $q(x)$ is in its kernel exactly when $p(x)=0$. Consequently $\ker\bar p=q(\ker p)=F^{j+1}\pi_iE$ by step 2.1. If $q$ is injective, $\ker q=0\subseteq\ker p$, so the projection exists; moreover $q$ restricts to an isomorphism from $\ker p$ onto $F^{j+1}\pi_iE$. This proves all assertions. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎



## Complex shifts and spectral homotopy indices

[Open item](item-lem-eilenberg-maclane-shift-index) · level 5

### Statement
Let $C$ be an unbounded cochain complex of abelian groups. Write $HC$ for the spectrum associated, through the stable spectra interface, to the Eilenberg–Mac Lane Omega spectrum of the chain complex $D_n=C^{-n}$. Then, naturally in $C$ and for all integers $i,j$,

$$\pi_i(HC)\cong H^{-i}(C),\qquad \pi_i(H(C[2j]))\cong H^{2j-i}(C),\qquad \pi_i((HC)[2j])\cong H^{2j-i}(C).$$

Here $C[2j]$ is the cochain shift, whereas $(HC)[2j]$ is spectral suspension by $2j$; the formulas do not identify these two objects by a specified equivalence. Consequently, a given equivalence $\operatorname{gr}^jE\simeq (HC_j)[2j]$ induces $\pi_i\operatorname{gr}^jE\cong H^{2j-i}(C_j)$. The unshifted realization of a support complex $C_{j,T}$ has $\pi_i=H^{-i}(C_{j,T})$; its $2j$-shift has the latter shifted index.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** $C$, $i$, and $j$ as stated; for the graded conclusion, a specified equivalence $\operatorname{gr}^jE\simeq(HC_j)[2j]$.

**Goal:** Establish the displayed natural group identifications and their graded and support consequences.

[F1] [lem-author-80e2d7bee57f-cochain-to-chain](item-lem-author-80e2d7bee57f-cochain-to-chain) identifies $H_i(D)$ with $H^{-i}(C)$.

[F2] [thm-author-80e2d7bee57f-eilenberg-maclane-input](item-thm-author-80e2d7bee57f-eilenberg-maclane-input) supplies the simplicial Omega spectrum of $D$ and its stable homotopy groups.

[F3] [lem-author-80e2d7bee57f-tower-group-index](item-lem-author-80e2d7bee57f-tower-group-index) compares a coherent Omega tower with its associated spectrum.

[F4] [lem-author-80e2d7bee57f-shift-cohomology](item-lem-author-80e2d7bee57f-shift-cohomology) computes cohomology after cochain shift, and [lem-author-80e2d7bee57f-chain-shift-reindex](item-lem-author-80e2d7bee57f-chain-shift-reindex) identifies the corresponding shifted chain complex.

[F5] [lem-author-80e2d7bee57f-spectral-integer-shift](item-lem-author-80e2d7bee57f-spectral-integer-shift) computes homotopy groups after spectral shift; [def-stable-spectra-interface](item-def-stable-spectra-interface) supplies the associated stable category and homotopy-group functors.

### Proof
1.1 Apply [F2] to $D_n=C^{-n}$. Its simplicial Omega spectrum defines a coherent Omega tower of pointed spaces and hence, by the stable spectra interface, an associated spectrum $HC$. By [F3], its enhanced homotopy groups agree with the stable groups in [F2]; by [F1] these are $H^{-i}(C)$. These identifications are natural in maps of complexes. [F1, F2, F3, F5, given]

2.1 Apply step 1.1 to $C[2j]$. By [F4], its associated chain complex is the corresponding chain shift and $H^{-i}(C[2j])\cong H^{2j-i}(C)$. Independently, [F5] gives $\pi_i((HC)[2j])\cong\pi_{i-2j}(HC)\cong H^{2j-i}(C)$. A specified equivalence of the graded object induces an isomorphism on homotopy groups, proving the graded formula. Applying the same two formulas to the support complex proves the final assertion, with its unshifted and shifted spectra kept distinct. [F4, F5, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Multiplicative filtrations and graded products

[Open item](item-def-multiplicative-filtered-spectrum) · level 5

### Definition
A **decreasing filtered spectrum** is a coherent diagram $F$ in spectra indexed by the integers, with a transition map $F^i\to F^k$ whenever $i\geq k$, as in [def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum). Write $\operatorname{FilSp}$ for the infinity-category of such diagrams and coherent natural transformations. A **multiplicative filtered spectrum**, written $F\in\operatorname{CAlg}(\operatorname{FilSp})$, is such a diagram equipped with coherently compatible symmetric, associative and unital multiplication data: for every finite ordered list $(i_1,\ldots,i_n)$, including the empty list, there is a map

$$\mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_n}:F^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge F^{i_n}\longrightarrow F^{i_1+\cdots+i_n}.$$

The empty smash product is the sphere spectrum $\mathbb S$, and the empty sum is $0$. The maps are compatible with all transition maps and permutations, with substitution of lists into lists, and with the unit, together with all higher homotopies required for a commutative algebra object. In particular, the one-input operation is the identity up to the specified coherent identification. Thus the notation specifies coherent data; unrelated binary pairings do not suffice.

A multiplicative filtration **on a commutative ring spectrum $E$** additionally has a coherent multiplicative augmentation $F\to\operatorname{const}(E)$: its component maps $F^i\to E$ form an augmentation of the underlying tower, and the $n$-input products commute with these maps and the $n$-fold product of $E$, coherently. A commutative ring spectrum means a commutative algebra object in spectra under smash product; $\operatorname{const}(E)$ is its constant filtered diagram.

Put $\operatorname{gr}^iF=\operatorname{cofib}(F^{i+1}\to F^i)$ and write $q_i:F^i\to\operatorname{gr}^iF$ for the canonical cofiber map. The **associated graded multiplication** is the coherent family

$$\overline\mu_{i,j}:\operatorname{gr}^iF\wedge\operatorname{gr}^jF\longrightarrow\operatorname{gr}^{i+j}F$$

induced by $\mu_{i,j}$. It satisfies $\overline\mu_{i,j}(q_i\wedge q_j)\simeq q_{i+j}\mu_{i,j}$. These are maps from filtration stages to graded pieces; the definition does not assert that there is a map from $E$ or from an image subgroup of $\pi_*E$ to a graded piece.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A coherent decreasing filtered spectrum $F$ with the specified commutative multiplication data, and, when a filtration on $E$ is discussed, a commutative ring spectrum $E$ and multiplicative augmentation as above.

**Goal:** Justify the indexing, the associated graded products and their compatibility with the cofiber maps.

[F1] [def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum) supplies the tower, its transition maps and the cofiber definition of the associated graded.

[F2] [def-stable-spectra-interface](item-def-stable-spectra-interface) supplies the symmetric monoidal stable infinity-category of spectra, the sphere unit, coherent diagrams and cofibers. Smash product preserves colimits separately in each variable.

### Justification

1.1 If $i_r\geq k_r$ for every $r$, then $\sum i_r\geq\sum k_r$, so the indicated target transition map exists. Addition is associative and commutative with identity $0$; consequently the stated compatibility, symmetry and substitution requirements have matching source and target indices. The augmentation is a coherent natural transformation to the constant tower, with additional compatibility with all products. These clauses specify structure and do not assert that every tower admits it. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 For fixed $i,j$, compatibility with transitions identifies the restriction of $\mu_{i,j}$ along $F^{i+1}\wedge F^j\to F^i\wedge F^j$ with a map factoring through $F^{i+j+1}\to F^{i+j}$; the same holds for $F^i\wedge F^{j+1}$. Hence their composites with $q_{i+j}$ have the canonical coherent nullhomotopies coming from the cofiber. Compatibility on their common corner follows from the coherent multiplication and transition data. [F1, F2, given, step 1.1]

3.1 Since smash preserves colimits separately, $\operatorname{gr}^iF\wedge\operatorname{gr}^jF$ is the iterated cofiber of the square with corners $F^{i+1}\wedge F^{j+1}$, $F^{i+1}\wedge F^j$, $F^i\wedge F^{j+1}$ and $F^i\wedge F^j$. The compatible nullhomotopies in step 2.1 therefore induce $\overline\mu_{i,j}$ by the universal property of that iterated cofiber, and its composite with $q_i\wedge q_j$ is $q_{i+j}\mu_{i,j}$. [F2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The same construction for any finite list uses the cube formed by replacing each $F^{i_r}$ by $F^{i_r+1}$ in every possible subset of inputs. Its iterated cofiber is the smash of the corresponding graded pieces, and every face with a raised index maps through $F^{\sum i_r+1}$. The coherent permutation, substitution and unit data of $F$ descend through these universal cofiber constructions. Thus the graded products are coherently commutative, associative and unital, with unit $\mathbb S\to F^0\xrightarrow{q_0}\operatorname{gr}^0F$. Together with step 3.1 this justifies the definition. [F1, F2, given, step 3.1] ∎

## Valuative dimension and degreewise bounded towers

[Open item](item-def-valuative-dimension-and-boundedness) · level 5

### Definition
All rings are commutative with identity. The **Krull dimension** of a nonzero ring is the supremum, in the nonnegative integers together with infinity, of the lengths $n$ of strict chains of prime ideals $\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_n$. The zero ring has dimension $-1$. A **domain** is a nonzero ring without zero divisors. Its fraction field is denoted $\operatorname{Frac}(D)$. A **valuation overring** of a domain $D$ is a subring $V$ of $\operatorname{Frac}(D)$ containing $D$ such that, for every nonzero element $x$ of that field, at least one of $x$ and $x^{-1}$ lies in $V$.

The **valuative dimension** $\dim_v D$ of a domain $D$ is the supremum of the Krull dimensions of its valuation overrings. For a ring $A$, put $\dim_v A=\sup_{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}A}\dim_v(A/\mathfrak p)$, with the supremum of the empty set equal to $-1$. For a scheme $X$, put $\dim_v X=\sup_{\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq X}\dim_v A$, over all affine open subschemes, again taking the empty supremum to be $-1$. The scheme has **finite valuative dimension** if this value is finite.

Let $F^jE$ be a decreasing filtration of a spectrum $E$, and let $S$ be a specified set of integers. It is **degreewise bounded above in filtration on $S$** if, for every $i\in S$, there is an integer $N(i)$ such that $\pi_iF^jE=0$ for all $j\geq N(i)$. If $S=\mathbb Z$, it is simply **degreewise bounded above in filtration**. The bound may depend on $i$. This is a condition on the homotopy groups of the stages; completeness is the separately defined condition that the inverse limit of the tower is the zero spectrum.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A scheme $X$, or a decreasing filtration $F^\bullet E$ and a set $S\subseteq\mathbb Z$.

**Goal:** Justify the quantities and conditions in the definition.

[F1] A scheme has a set of affine open subschemes and their coordinate rings; a decreasing filtration has stages $F^jE$, transition maps and functorial homotopy groups. The tower-vanishing definition of completeness is the one stated above. [math:def-scheme-over-base](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-scheme-over-base) [def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum)

### Justification
1.1 The fraction field of a domain is itself a valuation overring, so the supremum defining $\dim_v D$ is taken over a nonempty set. Prime quotients are domains. Prime ideals, subrings of a fixed field, affine opens and finite chains of ideals form sets; their suprema exist in $\{-1,0,1,\ldots,\infty\}$ with the stated empty convention. Isomorphisms of rings preserve prime chains, fraction fields and valuation overrings, so the scheme expression does not depend on the chosen presentation of any particular affine open. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 Each $\pi_iF^jE$ is a well-defined group, and the displayed quantifiers give a definite property of the tower and the specified set of degrees. The bound is chosen separately for each degree. Completeness is a condition on the inverse limit, so the two formulations are recorded separately; no uniform bound or injectivity of transition maps is included in either definition. [F1, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Support fibers commute with graded triangles

[Open item](item-lem-filtered-support-exactness) · level 5

### Statement
Let $U\subset X$ be an open immersion, write $T=X\setminus U$, and let $E$ be a presheaf of decreasing filtered spectra. Thus restriction gives a coherently compatible map of augmented towers $F^jE(X)\to F^jE(U)$ and a map $E(X)\to E(U)$. Here a presheaf means a contravariant coherent functor on a category containing this open immersion; no descent property is assumed. Put

$$F^j_T E(X)=\operatorname{fib}(F^jE(X)\to F^jE(U)),\qquad E_T(X)=\operatorname{fib}(E(X)\to E(U)).$$

The compatible maps make $F^\bullet_T E(X)$ a decreasing filtration on $E_T(X)$. For every integer $j$ there is a natural fiber sequence

$$\operatorname{gr}^j_T E(X)\longrightarrow \operatorname{gr}^jE(X)\longrightarrow \operatorname{gr}^jE(U),$$

where $\operatorname{gr}^j_T E(X)=\operatorname{cofib}(F^{j+1}_T E(X)\to F^j_T E(X))$. Consequently there is an exact sequence

$$\cdots\to\pi_{i+1}F^jE(U)\to\pi_iF^j_T E(X)\to\pi_iF^jE(X)\to\pi_iF^jE(U)\to\cdots.$$

In particular, every element in the kernel of the last displayed map lifts to $\pi_iF^j_T E(X)$. More specifically, if $\pi_iF^jE(U)\to\pi_iE(U)$ is injective, then every element of $\operatorname{im}(\pi_iF^jE(X)\to\pi_iE(X))$ whose restriction to $\pi_iE(U)$ is zero is the image of an element of $\pi_iF^j_T E(X)$ under the composite to $\pi_iE(X)$. Without such a condition, an ambient kernel condition alone does not identify a stage-level kernel.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A coherent presheaf of decreasing filtered spectra, an open immersion $U\subset X$, and integers $i,j$.

**Goal:** Construct the supported filtration and graded fiber sequence, and prove the exactness and lifting assertions with their stated hypotheses.

[F1] In [def-stable-spectra-interface](item-def-stable-spectra-interface), spectra form a stable infinity-category with zero object and coherent finite limits and colimits. A fiber is the pullback over zero, a cofiber is the pushout along zero, and a square is a pullback exactly when it is a pushout.

[F2] [def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum) defines an augmented decreasing filtration and its associated graded as the cofiber of the transition from stage $j+1$ to stage $j$.

[F3] [lem-fiber-sequence-homotopy-exactness](item-lem-fiber-sequence-homotopy-exactness) gives the natural long exact homotopy sequence of any fiber sequence of spectra.

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Apply the fiber construction to the diagram of filtration stages and use stability to compare its cofibers.

1.1 Restriction and the transition maps form a coherent diagram of arrows $F^jE(X)\to F^jE(U)$. Taking the pullback over zero at every stage is functorial, producing transition maps $F^{j+1}_T E(X)\to F^j_T E(X)$ with all composition coherences. The compatible augmentation maps to $E(X)\to E(U)$ likewise induce compatible maps $F^j_T E(X)\to E_T(X)$. This is the asserted augmented decreasing tower. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 For a coherent square of arrows of spectra, taking fibers preserves its finite limits: each fiber is itself a pullback, and the universal property of limits identifies an iterated finite limit with the limit over the corresponding product diagram. Limits of arrow diagrams are computed at their source and target. The zero arrow has zero fiber. In particular, if a square of arrows is pointwise a pushout, stability makes it pointwise a pullback; after taking fibers it is again a pullback and hence a pushout. Thus taking fibers carries pointwise cofiber squares of arrows to cofiber squares of spectra. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 Apply step 2.1 to the map of arrows from $F^{j+1}E(X)\to F^{j+1}E(U)$ to $F^jE(X)\to F^jE(U)$. Its pointwise cofiber is the arrow $\operatorname{gr}^jE(X)\to\operatorname{gr}^jE(U)$. The cofiber of its map of fibers is therefore naturally equivalent to the fiber of that graded arrow. By the definition of the supported graded spectrum, this is precisely the displayed graded fiber sequence. The construction uses the coherent diagram and universal properties, so it is natural in maps of such filtered presheaves and open pairs. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 The definition of $F^j_T E(X)$ gives a fiber sequence $F^j_T E(X)\to F^jE(X)\to F^jE(U)$. Applying [F3] yields the displayed long exact sequence. Exactness at $\pi_iF^jE(X)$ says that its restriction kernel is exactly the image of $\pi_iF^j_T E(X)$, proving the first lifting claim. [F1, F3, step 3.1]

5.1 Suppose the stated map on $U$ is injective. Choose a stage representative $a\in\pi_iF^jE(X)$ of an ambient element $x$ whose restriction to $\pi_iE(U)$ is zero. Compatibility of restriction with augmentation says that the image of $a|_U$ in $\pi_iE(U)$ is zero; injectivity therefore gives $a|_U=0$ in $\pi_iF^jE(U)$. Step 4.1 lifts $a$ to $\pi_iF^j_T E(X)$, whose image in $\pi_iE(X)$ is $x$. The argument explicitly uses injectivity to pass from the ambient kernel to the stage kernel. This proves all claims. [F2, step 1.1, step 4.1, given] ∎



## Images of filtration stages

[Open item](item-lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-image) · level 5


### Statement
Let $F$ be a coherently augmented decreasing filtration on a spectrum $E$. For integers $i,j$, the image of $\pi_iF^j\to\pi_iE$ is a subgroup of $\pi_iE$, and the same homomorphism, regarded as a map to this image, is surjective.

### Statement references

[def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum)

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A spectrum $E$, its augmented decreasing filtration $F$, and integers $i,j$.

**Goal:** Establish the subgroup and surjectivity assertions.

[F1] [def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum) supplies the structure map $F^j\to E$ and the induced homomorphism of abelian homotopy groups.

### Proof
1.1 Write $u$ for the homomorphism in [F1]. Its image consists precisely of the elements $u(x)$ with $x\in\pi_iF^j$. It contains zero and is closed under sums and negatives because $u$ is a homomorphism. [F1, given]

2.1 Every element of this image has a preimage by its definition. Thus $u$, with codomain restricted to its image, is surjective. This proves both assertions. [step 1.1] ∎


## Bockstein obstruction to prime torsion

[Open item](item-lem-author-c5b0693f4fc3-top-torsion-bockstein) · level 5

### Statement
For $C\in D(\mathbb Z)$ and a prime $\ell$, multiplication by $\ell$ on $H^6(C)$ is injective if and only if $H^5(C)\to H^5(C/\ell)$ is surjective. Here $C/\ell=C\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathbb Z/\ell$ and the map is the canonical reduction. In particular, $H^5(C/\ell)=0$ suffices.

### Facts & Assumptions
[F1] [lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-finite-coefficients](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-finite-coefficients) supplies the natural coefficient short exact sequence.

### Proof
**Given:** $C$ and $\ell$ as stated.

**Goal:** Prove the equivalence and sufficient vanishing.

1.1 Apply [F1] with $i=5$. The cokernel of the canonical reduction is $H^6(C)[\ell]$, the kernel of multiplication by $\ell$. [F1]

2.1 That cokernel is zero precisely when reduction is surjective, equivalently when multiplication is injective. A zero target makes reduction surjective. [step 1.1] ∎


## The selected zero fibers are finite etale schemes

[Open item](item-lem-author-fc2380accb47-finite-etale-zero-fibers) · level 5

### Statement
For every point $a\in T^\circ$, the zero scheme $S_a$ of the universal functional after base change to $L=\kappa(a)$ is a finite étale $L$-scheme, possibly empty. The same holds after every extension of $L$, so it is geometrically smooth of dimension zero. In particular for a chosen $a\in T^\circ(k)$ it is a finite disjoint union of copies of $\operatorname{Spec}k$, all in $X_{\mathrm{sm}/k}$. This also identifies the generic fiber over $k(T)$: it is finite étale, not merely a set of expected dimension. No dominance is needed or asserted in this argument.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The nonempty parameter open and the actual zero scheme, which is closed in the affine finite-type scheme $X_L$.

**Goal:** Prove geometric smoothness and finiteness with the correct scheme structure.

[F1] [lem-author-fc2380accb47-simultaneous-good-parameters](item-lem-author-fc2380accb47-simultaneous-good-parameters) makes the zero scheme lie in $W_L$ with derivative determinant invertible at every point, and retains this after field extension. [lem-regular-section-parameter-family](item-lem-regular-section-parameter-family) supplies the scheme-theoretic fiber description.

[F2] [thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input](item-thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input) supplies: a finite-type algebra over a field with zero differential module is étale, and an étale finite-type algebra over a field is a finite product of finite separable field extensions. These statements have no characteristic-zero restriction.

### Proof
1.1 Locally on $W_L$ trivialize the rank-three bundle and write the section coefficients $g_1,g_2,g_3$. On their zero scheme the conormal sequence gives a right-exact map $\mathcal O_{S_a}^{3}\xrightarrow{(dg_1,dg_2,dg_3)}\Omega^1_{W_L/L}|_{S_a}\longrightarrow\Omega^1_{S_a/L}\longrightarrow0.$ The middle bundle has rank three, and the first map has invertible determinant by [F1]. It is an isomorphism, so $\Omega^1_{S_a/L}=0$. The frame-independent determinant condition guarantees that this conclusion glues across charts. [F1]

2.1 As a closed subscheme of affine $X_L$, write $S_a=\operatorname{Spec}B_a$ with $B_a$ a finite-type $L$-algebra. Step1.1 gives $\Omega_{B_a/L}=0$, so [F2] makes $B_a$ a finite product of finite separable extensions of $L$. This is finite étale; the empty case is the zero algebra and empty product. After any extension these remain finite étale. For $L=k$ algebraically closed, every factor is $k$ itself. Apply [F1] to see all these points lie in the original smooth locus. The same argument applies to the generic point of $T^\circ$ and proves the claimed generic-fiber statement. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎


## Exact range of a cofiber connectivity bound

[Open item](item-lem-author-13e6fe931c45-cone-exact-range) · level 5

### Statement
If the cofiber of $f:A\to B$ in $D(\mathbb Z)$ is supported in degrees $>3$, meaning its cohomology vanishes in every degree at most three, then $H^i(f)$ is an isomorphism for every $i\leq3$.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $f$ and the stated cofiber bound.

**Goal:** Prove the isomorphism range.

[F1] The mapping-cone long exact sequence used in [lem-author-13e6fe931c45-cone-low-degrees](item-lem-author-13e6fe931c45-cone-low-degrees) contains $H^{i-1}(C)\to H^i(A)\to H^i(B)\to H^i(C)$.

### Proof

1.1 For each $i\leq3$, both $i-1$ and $i$ are at most three, so both adjacent groups in [F1] vanish. [F1, given]

2.1 Exactness makes $H^i(A)\to H^i(B)$ injective and surjective. Thus the stated range follows. [F1, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Perfect determinant with true-triangle additivity: precise external input

[Open item](item-thm-adjudicate-a8dfc5e2f7fe-perfect-determinant-true-triangle-input) · level 5


### Statement
Under AC and fixed universes for the sheaf-derived model, let $X$ be a scheme and let its perfect complexes mean objects locally represented by bounded finite locally free complexes. There is a global graded determinant functor on their derived isomorphisms. Its value is a line with locally constant integer Euler rank. For every actual short-exact complex diagram $0\to P\to Q\to R\to0$ with perfect terms, its true-triangle additivity supplies an isomorphism $\det(P)\otimes\det(R)\cong\det(Q)$. The determinant of zero is the trivial graded line. On a bounded finite locally free representative its underlying line is $\bigotimes_i(\det P^i)^{(-1)^i}$. It commutes with derived pullback, with the source's composition compatibility.

[def-exterior-determinant-bundles](item-def-exterior-determinant-bundles)
