Knudsen–Mumford Definition4 and Theorem2 are the external input, under the exact hypotheses and reading limits in the source record. Their perfect-complex definition agrees with the supplied local sheaf-derived definition. Their true triangles retain actual short-exact complex diagrams; one cannot replace all their morphisms by arbitrary commuting ordinary derived-triangle diagrams. The graded-line symmetry is retained before taking Picard classes.

For applications to cofiber classes, an actual complex map has the termwise split short-exact diagram from its target to its mapping cone to its shifted source. This is within the imported true-triangle contract even when no global bounded bundle representative exists. No resolution property, separatedness, regularity or finite-type condition is imposed on $X$. This input supplies the global line and its descent isomorphisms; it supplies no enhanced K-space map or unrestricted ordinary-triangle naturality. No local proof of the imported determinant theorem is claimed.


## Nisnevich covers and distinguished squares

[Open item](item-def-nisnevich-covering-interface) · level 6

### Definition
For a point $x$ of a scheme $X$, write $\kappa(x)$ for the residue field of the local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$. A family of scheme morphisms $\{f_i:U_i\to X\}_{i\in I}$ is a **Nisnevich covering family** if every $f_i$ is étale in the sense of [math:def-etale-morphism-schemes](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-etale-morphism-schemes) and, for every point $x\in X$, there are an index $i$ and a point $u\in U_i$ with $f_i(u)=x$ such that the induced field homomorphism $\kappa(x)\to\kappa(u)$ is an isomorphism. In this situation $u$ is called a residue-field-preserving lift of $x$.

On a specified small category of schemes in which these families are available, the **Nisnevich topology** is the Grothendieck topology generated by the sieves containing such families. A sieve and a Grothendieck topology have the meanings in [def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification](item-def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification). For the small Nisnevich site of a scheme $X$, take a suitably small category of étale $X$-schemes, closed under the relevant fibre products, with this topology; the big site requires a separately specified category of schemes over the base.

A **distinguished Nisnevich square** is a cartesian square of schemes

$$\begin{matrix} W&\longrightarrow&V\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow p\\ U&\xrightarrow{j}&X \end{matrix}$$

where $j$ is an open immersion, $p$ is étale, and, putting $Z=(X\setminus j(U))_{\mathrm{red}}$ for the closed complement with its reduced induced scheme structure, the base change $V\times_X Z\to Z$ is an isomorphism. Cartesian means that the displayed map $W\to U\times_X V$ is an isomorphism. The pair $\{U\to X,V\to X\}$ is its associated covering family.

For a set-valued presheaf $F$, the **distinguished-square excision conditions** are that $F(\varnothing)$ is a singleton and that, for every such square in the chosen category, the natural map

$$F(X)\longrightarrow F(U)\times_{F(W)}F(V)$$

is a bijection. Here the fibre product is the set of pairs whose restrictions to $W$ agree. These conditions describe the excision interface; no equivalence between them and the full sheaf condition is asserted here.

### Justification
The residue-field test is independent of a choice of representative of a point: a scheme morphism gives the indicated homomorphism of residue fields. The generated topology exists because the maximal topology is among the Grothendieck topologies containing the specified sieves, and their intersection is again a Grothendieck topology; the smallness convention makes this intersection legitimate.

For a distinguished square, the open immersion $U\to X$ is étale, as recorded in [math:def-etale-morphism-schemes](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-etale-morphism-schemes), and $V\to X$ is étale by hypothesis. If $x$ lies in $U$, its unique preimage under the open immersion has residue field $\kappa(x)$. Otherwise $x$ is a point of $Z$; the isomorphism $V\times_X Z\cong Z$ gives a point over $x$ with residue field $\kappa(x)$, whose image in $V$ is a residue-field-preserving lift. Thus the associated pair is a Nisnevich covering family. The empty family covers the empty scheme by the same pointwise definition. The restriction maps of the presheaf commute around the square, so they define the displayed natural map to the fibre product.

## Roots of unity and étale Tate twists

[Open item](item-def-etale-tate-coefficients) · level 6

### Definition
Let $n\geq 1$ be an integer invertible on a scheme $X$: its image in every local ring of $X$ is a unit. Work on a size-bounded small étale site of $X$ whose objects are étale $X$-schemes, whose covering families are jointly surjective étale families, and which includes the open restrictions and covers used below.

For an object $U$ put $P_n(U)=\{u\in\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)^\times:u^n=1\}$, with multiplication and restriction of functions. The **sheaf of $n$th roots of unity** $\mu_n$ is the sheafification of this presheaf. Its group law is written multiplicatively; multiplication by an integer means taking that power. As every section is annihilated by $n$, $\mu_n$ is a sheaf of $\mathbb Z/n$-modules. Here $\mathbb Z/n$ denotes both the quotient ring and, on the site, the constant sheaf obtained by sheafifying the constant presheaf with that value.

For $j\geq 1$, define the **Tate twist** $\mu_n^{\otimes j}$ to be the $j$-fold tensor product over the constant sheaf $\mathbb Z/n$: form the objectwise tensor product presheaf and sheafify it. Set $\mu_n^{\otimes 0}=\mathbb Z/n$. Only nonnegative twists are defined here.

If $X$ is a scheme over a field $k$ and a primitive $n$th root $\zeta\in k$ is chosen, meaning an element of multiplicative order exactly $n$, then necessarily $n$ is prime to the characteristic of $k$. The map $a\mapsto\zeta^a$ induces an isomorphism of $\mathbb Z/n$-sheaves $\mathbb Z/n\cong\mu_n$ and hence, for every $j\geq0$, an isomorphism $\mathbb Z/n\cong\mu_n^{\otimes j}$ sending $1$ to $\zeta^{\otimes j}$ when $j>0$ and to $1$ when $j=0$. For $n=1$ both sides are zero modules. These isomorphisms depend on the chosen root for positive $j$.

This definition alone asserts no motivic-to-étale comparison. In particular, in characteristic $p>0$ it does not treat $\mu_p$ as a prime-to-characteristic coefficient sheaf.

### Definition references
[def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification](item-def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification)

[math:def-etale-morphism-schemes](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-etale-morphism-schemes)

### Justification
The restriction maps preserve products and the equation $u^n=1$, so $P_n$ is a presheaf of abelian groups. The sheafification construction and its universal property are supplied by [def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification](item-def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification). Group operations and the $\mathbb Z/n$-action descend through sheafification: matching families can be added or multiplied after passing to a common covering sieve, and the relations hold locally and therefore in the sheafification. The same construction applied to objectwise tensor products gives the stated tensor sheaf; its universal property follows by applying the presheaf tensor universal property locally and gluing. Thus the constructions do not depend on representatives of local sections.

For the trivialization, if $n>1$ and the characteristic divided $n$, writing $n=p^r m$ would give $\zeta^m=1$ because in a field of characteristic $p$ the equation $t^{p^r}=1$ has only the root $1$; this contradicts the order $n$. Hence $n$ is invertible in $k$. The $n$ elements $1,\zeta,\ldots,\zeta^{n-1}$ are distinct, and their pairwise differences are units on every $k$-scheme. Consequently $T^n-1=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(T-\zeta^i)$ with pairwise comaximal factors. If $u\in P_n(U)$, apply the Chinese remainder idempotents to $u$ on each affine open of $U$: the resulting finite disjoint open decomposition has $u=\zeta^i$ on its $i$th part. Open restrictions are étale, and these decompositions cover $U$. Thus $a\mapsto\zeta^a$ is locally surjective. It is locally injective because distinct $\zeta^i-\zeta^h$ are units, so equality can occur only on the empty scheme. The sheafification universal property and the sheaf gluing condition therefore make the induced map an isomorphism. Tensoring this isomorphism $j$ times and using the canonical multiplication isomorphism $(\mathbb Z/n)^{\otimes j}\cong\mathbb Z/n$ gives the displayed twist trivialization. For $n=1$ the root and coefficient groups are trivial, giving the same conclusion.

## Spectral sequence of a tower

[Open item](item-prop-tower-exact-couple-interface) · level 6

### Statement
Let $E$ be a spectrum equipped with spectra $F^jE$ and compatible maps $F^{j+1}E\to F^jE\to E$, for all integers $j$. Put $\operatorname{gr}^jE=\operatorname{cofib}(F^{j+1}E\to F^jE)$ and $F^j\pi_nE=\operatorname{im}(\pi_nF^jE\to\pi_nE)$. The stage sequences form an exact couple and yield a cohomological spectral sequence, indexed from page 2, with

$$E_2^{a,b}=\pi_{-a-b}\operatorname{gr}^{-b}E,\qquad d_s:E_s^{a,b}\longrightarrow E_s^{a+s,b-s+1}\quad(s\ge2).$$

If specified equivalences $\operatorname{gr}^jE\simeq(HC_j)[2j]$ are given for cochain complexes $C_j$, then naturally

$$E_2^{a,b}\cong H^{a-b}(C_{-b}).$$

Suppose additionally that, for each integer $n$, there are integers $L_n\le U_n$ such that $\pi_nF^jE\to\pi_nE$ is an isomorphism for $j\le L_n$ and $\pi_nF^jE=0$ for $j\ge U_n$. Then every bidegree stabilizes after finitely many pages and there are natural isomorphisms

$$E_\infty^{a,b}\cong F^{-b}\pi_{-a-b}E/F^{-b+1}\pi_{-a-b}E.$$

Thus the spectral sequence converges to $\pi_{-a-b}E$ with its finite image filtration. Here $E_\infty$ denotes the eventual stable page in each bidegree; convergence includes the displayed associated-graded identification, not a canonical splitting of the filtration. The stated boundedness is a sufficient hypothesis; no convergence is asserted from the graded identifications alone.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The tower and compatible maps in the statement; for the indexed cohomology formula, the specified graded equivalences; for convergence, the stated degreewise bounds.

**Goal:** Construct the spectral sequence, calculate its indices, and prove its bounded convergence assertion.

[F1] For every $j,n$, [lem-filtered-stage-exact-sequence](item-lem-filtered-stage-exact-sequence) gives the natural long exact sequence containing $\pi_nF^{j+1}E\to\pi_nF^jE\to\pi_n\operatorname{gr}^jE\to\pi_{n-1}F^{j+1}E$.

[F2] [math:def-exact-couple](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-exact-couple) specifies the initial homological exact-couple degrees. [math:def-derived-exact-couple](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-derived-exact-couple) supplies the derived couple, its exactness, and its differential and homology construction. [math:def-cohomological-spectral-sequence](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-cohomological-spectral-sequence) specifies the cohomological differential degrees and page-to-page homology requirement.

[F3] Under a specified equivalence $\operatorname{gr}^jE\simeq(HC_j)[2j]$, [lem-eilenberg-maclane-shift-index](item-lem-eilenberg-maclane-shift-index) gives $\pi_n\operatorname{gr}^jE\cong H^{2j-n}(C_j)$.

### Proof

1.1 Set $D^1_{p,q}=\pi_{p+q}F^{-p}E$ and $E^1_{p,q}=\pi_{p+q}\operatorname{gr}^{-p}E$. Let $i$ be induced by $F^{-p}E\to F^{-p-1}E$, let $j$ be the stage projection, and let $k$ be the connecting homomorphism. Their respective degrees are $(1,-1)$, $(0,0)$ and $(-1,0)$. Exactness at all three vertices follows from the long exact sequences in [F1], so these maps form an initial exact couple. [F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Derive the couple repeatedly. At homological page $r\ge1$, its differential $d_r=jk$ has degree $(-r,r-1)$, squares to zero, and its homology is the next page. Define $E_s^{a,b}=E^{s-1}_{b,-a-2b}$ for $s\ge2$. A homological differential with $r=s-1$ changes $(b,-a-2b)$ to $(b-r,-a-2b+r-1)$, corresponding to $(a+s,b-s+1)$. Hence these reindexed pages satisfy the cohomological spectral-sequence convention. At $s=2$, their total homotopy degree is $b+(-a-2b)=-a-b$ and their filtration index is $-b$, proving the first displayed formula. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 With $j=-b$ and $n=-a-b$, [F3] gives $\pi_n\operatorname{gr}^jE\cong H^{2j-n}(C_j)=H^{a-b}(C_{-b})$. This proves the second displayed formula and its naturality for maps preserving the given graded equivalences. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Fix $j,n$. Iterating the derived-couple formulas shows the following two elementary lifting facts. A class on the initial graded term that survives through arbitrarily many differentials has connecting image in $\pi_{n-1}F^{j+1}E$ admitting lifts from arbitrarily high stages; the indeterminacies in choosing lifts are precisely the boundaries already factored out. Conversely, if its connecting image is zero, exactness writes it as the stage projection of an element of $\pi_nF^jE$, and that projected class survives every page. The first assertion follows inductively because passing to the next derived couple replaces the $D$-term by the image of the next transition map; the converse follows because a stage projection has zero connecting image and the same is true after each derivation. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 3.1]

5.1 The high-stage bound in degree $n-1$ makes the liftable subgroup in step 4.1 zero after finitely many stages. Thus every eventual class is represented by the stage projection of some $x\in\pi_nF^jE$. The derived-couple formulas also give the boundary test: such a projection is eventually zero exactly when the image of $x$ in a sufficiently low stage lies in the image there of $\pi_nF^{j+1}E$. Indeed, a boundary coming from a lower graded stage has connecting image in $\pi_nF^jE$ whose image in that lower stage vanishes; conversely, if $x$ differs by an element from $F^{j+1}$ by an element killed at a lower stage, repeated exactness lifts that difference through the intervening connecting maps and expresses its projection as an iterated boundary. These implications use only finitely many stages. [F1, F2, step 4.1]

6.1 Choose the low stage at or below $L_n$. Its map to $\pi_nE$ is an isomorphism, so the boundary test says precisely that the image of $x$ in $\pi_nE$ belongs to $F^{j+1}\pi_nE$. Consequently the projection induces an isomorphism from $F^j\pi_nE/F^{j+1}\pi_nE$ to the eventual graded term. The high- and low-stage bounds also bound the possible sources and targets of differentials at the fixed bidegree, so this eventual term is reached after finitely many pages. Finally $F^j\pi_nE=\pi_nE$ for $j\le L_n$ and $F^j\pi_nE=0$ for $j\ge U_n$; hence the image filtration is finite and the stated convergence follows. Substitution of $j=-b$ and $n=-a-b$ gives the displayed indexing. [given, step 2.1, step 5.1] ∎



## Products and projections on image filtrations

[Open item](item-lem-image-filtration-products) · level 6

### Statement
Let $F$ be a multiplicative decreasing filtration on a commutative ring spectrum $E$. For integers $i,j,a,b$, write
$$q_{i,a}:\pi_aF^i\longrightarrow\pi_aE,\qquad p_{i,a}:\pi_aF^i\longrightarrow\pi_a\operatorname{gr}^iF$$
for the maps induced by the augmentation and the cofiber projection, respectively, and set $F^i\pi_aE=\operatorname{im}q_{i,a}$. Then
$$F^i\pi_aE\cdot F^j\pi_bE\subseteq F^{i+j}\pi_{a+b}E.$$
For any stage lifts $x\in\pi_aF^i$ and $y\in\pi_bF^j$, their stage product $xy\in\pi_{a+b}F^{i+j}$ satisfies
$$p_{i+j,a+b}(xy)=p_{i,a}(x)\,p_{j,b}(y).$$
If, for the three pairs $(i,a)$, $(j,b)$ and $(i+j,a+b)$, one has $\ker q_{r,n}\subseteq\ker p_{r,n}$, the corresponding maps $p_{r,n}$ descend uniquely to homomorphisms $\bar p_{r,n}:F^r\pi_nE\to\pi_n\operatorname{gr}^rF$, and
$$\bar p_{i+j,a+b}(uv)=\bar p_{i,a}(u)\,\bar p_{j,b}(v)$$
for $u\in F^i\pi_aE$ and $v\in F^j\pi_bE$. Injectivity of each relevant $q_{r,n}$ is sufficient for these descent conditions; it is not needed for the containment or the formula for chosen stage lifts.

A decreasing filtration here is a coherent tower of spectra $F^r$ with maps $F^{r+1}\to F^r$ and compatible maps $F^r\to E$. Its graded piece is the cofiber $\operatorname{gr}^rF=\operatorname{cofib}(F^{r+1}\to F^r)$. Multiplicativity supplies compatible maps $F^i\wedge F^j\to F^{i+j}$ and $\operatorname{gr}^iF\wedge\operatorname{gr}^jF\to\operatorname{gr}^{i+j}$, and makes the augmentation compatible with multiplication on $E$. Products in homotopy groups are those induced by these maps and the canonical smash pairing of sphere spectra. An image filtration consists of the subgroups $F^r\pi_nE$ just defined; a stage lift of an element of one of these subgroups is a preimage under $q_{r,n}$.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A multiplicative decreasing filtration $F$ on a commutative ring spectrum $E$ and integers $i,j,a,b$.

**Goal:** Prove the product containment and the projection identity for stage lifts, and prove the stated conditional identity on image groups.

[F1] The stage multiplication is compatible with the augmentation to $E$, and the graded multiplication satisfies $\overline\mu_{i,j}(p_i\wedge p_j)\simeq p_{i+j}\mu_{i,j}$ for the cofiber maps $p_r:F^r\to\operatorname{gr}^rF$. These maps induce the corresponding pairings on homotopy groups. [def-multiplicative-filtered-spectrum](item-def-multiplicative-filtered-spectrum)

[F2] For each $(r,n)$, the stage projection $p_{r,n}$ factors uniquely through the image of $q_{r,n}$ exactly when $\ker q_{r,n}\subseteq\ker p_{r,n}$. In particular, injectivity of $q_{r,n}$ implies this condition. [lem-filtered-stage-exact-sequence](item-lem-filtered-stage-exact-sequence)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Apply the augmentation and cofiber compatibilities to representatives, then use the image-factorization criterion.

1.1 Let $u\in F^i\pi_aE$ and $v\in F^j\pi_bE$. By the definition of image, choose $x\in\pi_aF^i$ and $y\in\pi_bF^j$ with $q_{i,a}(x)=u$ and $q_{j,b}(y)=v$. The stage multiplication gives $xy\in\pi_{a+b}F^{i+j}$. Compatibility of multiplication with the augmentation gives $q_{i+j,a+b}(xy)=uv$. Hence $uv$ is in $F^{i+j}\pi_{a+b}E$, proving the containment. [F1, given, construct]

1.2 For any such stage classes $x,y$, the cofiber compatibility in [F1], applied to their representing sphere maps, gives $p_{i+j,a+b}(xy)=p_{i,a}(x)p_{j,b}(y)$. This equality concerns the chosen stage classes and does not require their images in $\pi_*E$ to determine them uniquely. [F1, given]

2.1 Assume the three kernel inclusions in the statement. By [F2], the three stage projections factor uniquely through their respective image groups. For the lifts chosen in step 1.1, the product $xy$ is a stage lift of $uv$. Therefore
$$\bar p_{i+j,a+b}(uv)=p_{i+j,a+b}(xy)=p_{i,a}(x)p_{j,b}(y)=\bar p_{i,a}(u)\bar p_{j,b}(v).$$
The factorization ensures that the displayed values are independent of the chosen lifts. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, assume-hyp]

3.1 An injective $q_{r,n}$ has zero kernel and thus satisfies the corresponding inclusion. Steps 1.1 through 2.1 prove all assertions, with no injectivity hypothesis used in the first two steps. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

## Extending a nonnegative filtration to integer indices

[Open item](item-lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-extension) · level 6

### Statement
Let $F$ be a coherent multiplicative decreasing filtration indexed by $\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$, with $F^0=E$ as commutative ring spectrum and with its maps to $F^0$ as multiplicative augmentation. It extends canonically to a multiplicative decreasing filtration indexed by $\mathbb Z$, by setting $\widetilde F^j=F^{\max(j,0)}$. Its stages and products in nonnegative degrees are the original ones, and every stage in nonpositive degree is $E$ with identity transition maps between such stages.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The specified coherent nonnegative multiplicative tower $F$.

**Goal:** Construct and justify the integer-indexed extension.

[F1] [def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum) specifies transition directions and augmentation; [def-multiplicative-filtered-spectrum](item-def-multiplicative-filtered-spectrum) specifies the coherent finite-input product data and their compatibility.

### Proof
1.1 Put $r(j)=\max(j,0)$. If $j\geq k$, then $r(j)\geq r(k)$, so the original transition $F^{r(j)}\to F^{r(k)}$ defines the extended transition. Monotonicity also gives all composition and identity compatibilities by restriction of the original coherent diagram. For $j\leq0$, $r(j)=0$, giving the asserted constant stages and identity transitions. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 For any finite list $(j_1,\ldots,j_n)$, the inequality $\sum r(j_t)\geq r(\sum j_t)$ holds, including the empty list. Compose the original $n$-input product into $F^{\sum r(j_t)}$ with the transition to $F^{r(\sum j_t)}$. Associativity of addition, monotonicity and functoriality of the original transitions ensure that all alternative composites use the same original product followed by the same transition. The original coherent permutation, substitution and unit data therefore give the corresponding coherent data for the extension. [F1, given, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The maps to $F^0=E$ provide the compatible multiplicative augmentation. When all indices are nonnegative, $r$ preserves their sum, so the construction recovers the original products and transitions. This proves the extension and its stated properties. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Nesting of image filtration groups

[Open item](item-lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-nesting) · level 6

### Statement
For a decreasing filtration $F$ on a spectrum $E$ and integers $i$ and $a\geq b$, the image of $\pi_iF^a\to\pi_iE$ is contained in the image of $\pi_iF^b\to\pi_iE$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** $F$, $E$, $i$, and $a\geq b$ as stated.

**Goal:** Prove the containment.

[F1] [def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum) gives a transition $F^a\to F^b$ compatible with the maps to $E$.

[F2] [lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-image](item-lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-image) identifies these images as subgroups.

### Proof
1.1 Applying $\pi_i$ to the compatible maps in [F1] shows that $\pi_iF^a\to\pi_iE$ factors through $\pi_iF^b\to\pi_iE$. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 Thus the image of the former lies in the image of the latter, as subgroups by [F2]. This is the desired containment. [F1, F2, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Naturality of image filtrations

[Open item](item-lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-naturality) · level 6

### Statement
Let $F$ and $G$ be decreasing filtrations on spectra $E$ and $D$. Suppose maps $F^j\to G^j$ and $E\to D$ form a coherent map of augmented towers: in particular each square with the maps to $E$ and $D$ commutes up to the specified homotopy. Then $\pi_iE\to\pi_iD$ carries the $j$th image subgroup of $E$ into that of $D$, for every $i,j\in\mathbb Z$. These restricted maps respect identity and composition whenever the original maps do.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The two augmented towers and compatible maps just specified.

**Goal:** Establish induced functorial maps on their image subgroups.

[F1] [def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum) supplies the induced homomorphisms on homotopy groups; homotopic maps induce the same homomorphism.

[F2] The image subgroups are defined and are subgroups by [lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-image](item-lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-image).

### Proof
1.1 Take an element in the image subgroup for $F^j$. Choose a preimage in $\pi_iF^j$. The homotopy-commutative square sends its image in $\pi_iE$ to the image in $\pi_iD$ of the chosen preimage under $\pi_iF^j\to\pi_iG^j$. Hence the element lands in the stated subgroup. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 The restricted map is the restriction of the given homomorphism on ambient homotopy groups. Therefore identity and composition hold on the image subgroups whenever they hold on the ambient groups. This proves the claim. [step 1.1] ∎

## Products of filtration images

[Open item](item-lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-products) · level 6

### Statement
Let $F$ be a multiplicative filtration on a commutative ring spectrum $E$, including its multiplicative augmentation as in [def-multiplicative-filtered-spectrum](item-def-multiplicative-filtered-spectrum). For integers $a,b,i,j$, multiplication on $\pi_*E$ sends the product of the image of $\pi_iF^a\to\pi_iE$ and the image of $\pi_jF^b\to\pi_jE$ into the image of $\pi_{i+j}F^{a+b}\to\pi_{i+j}E$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The multiplicatively augmented filtered spectrum $F\to E$ and the four integers.

**Goal:** Prove the containment of products.

[F1] [def-multiplicative-filtered-spectrum](item-def-multiplicative-filtered-spectrum) supplies $F^a\wedge F^b\to F^{a+b}$ and its compatibility with multiplication on $E$.

[F2] [lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-image](item-lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-image) supplies the image subgroups. Homotopy groups of spectra admit the pairing induced by smash product, in the convention used in [F1].

### Proof
1.1 Choose elements $x\in\pi_iF^a$ and $y\in\pi_jF^b$ lifting the two given image elements. Smashing representatives and applying the stage multiplication gives an element of $\pi_{i+j}F^{a+b}$. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 Multiplicative compatibility of the augmentation identifies its image in $\pi_{i+j}E$ with the product of the two original image elements. Thus that product belongs to the required image subgroup. This proves the statement. [F1, step 1.1] ∎

## A sheaf restricts injectively to a covering singleton

[Open item](item-lem-author-60d95bfb692a-cover-restriction-injective) · level 6

### Statement
Let $F$ be a set-valued sheaf on a scheme site, and suppose $u:U\to V$ generates a covering sieve. Then the restriction $F(V)\to F(U)$ is injective. A sheaf has unique amalgamations of compatible sections on each covering sieve.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $F$, $u$ and the covering sieve generated by $u$.

**Goal:** Prove injectivity of restriction.

[F1] Sections of a sheaf agreeing on every arrow in a covering sieve are equal, by uniqueness of amalgamation. [def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification](item-def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Restrict along the generated sieve.

1.1 If $a,b\in F(V)$ have equal restrictions to $U$, then their restrictions along any arrow factoring through $u$ are equal by functoriality. These arrows form the sieve generated by $u$. [given]

2.1 That sieve is covering, so [F1] gives $a=b$. Hence restriction is injective. [F1, step 1.1] ∎

## Filtered equivalences preserve image filtrations

[Open item](item-lem-author-91088613574d-filtered-images) · level 6


### Statement
Let $F^\bullet,G^\bullet$ be integer-indexed decreasing towers of spectra and $e:F^\bullet\simeq G^\bullet$ an equivalence compatible with their coherent transition maps. Identify $F^0$ and $G^0$ with the same spectrum $E$ so that $e^0$ becomes the identity. For every $j\geq0$ and $i\in\mathbb Z$, the isomorphism $\pi_i(e^j)$ identifies the images of the two transition maps to stage zero inside $\pi_iE$.

More generally, suppose the towers carry compatible augmentations $a_F^j:F^j\to E$ and $a_G^j:G^j\to E$, and $e$ respects them: $a_G^j e^j\simeq a_F^j$ for every integer $j$. Then their augmentation images agree for every $i,j\in\mathbb Z$. If the stage-zero augmentations are the chosen identifications, these are the transition-to-zero images for $j\geq0$. A decreasing tower supplies a transition $j\to k$ when $j\geq k$; it supplies no transition from a negative stage to zero.

### Statement references

[def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum)

[lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-image](item-lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-image)

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The towers, their equivalence and stage-zero identifications; for the second assertion, the specified compatible augmentations.

**Goal:** Compare the two image subgroups in the stated ranges.

[F1] An augmentation induces a homomorphism of abelian homotopy groups whose image is a subgroup. Transitions in a decreasing tower go from larger indices to smaller ones. [def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum](item-def-decreasing-filtered-spectrum), [lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-image](item-lem-author-98a750efd0cc-filtration-image)

### Proof
1.1 For $j\geq0$, the transition $j\to0$ exists. Compatibility of $e$ with this transition gives a commutative square on homotopy groups with left vertical isomorphism $\pi_i(e^j)$ and right vertical identity on $\pi_iE$. An element in the first image therefore lies in the second; conversely, lift its source along the inverse left isomorphism. The images agree. [F1, given]

2.1 Under the additional augmentation compatibility, the same commutative square exists with the augmentation maps for every integer $j$. The identical element argument proves equality of those images. For $j\geq0$, compatibility of each augmentation with the transition to zero and its stipulated stage-zero identification identifies the augmentation map with that transition followed by identification. Thus this general form includes the first form whenever these extra data are supplied. [F1, given, step 1.1] ∎


## External valuative dimension comparison on locally Noetherian schemes

[Open item](item-thm-author-0cc80c1b5792-valuation-input) · level 6

### Statement
The Jaffard valuative dimension of a domain is the supremum of the Krull dimensions of valuation overrings inside its fraction field. For an arbitrary ring it is the supremum of these dimensions over prime quotients; for a scheme take the supremum over affine opens. It is local on open covers. For every locally Noetherian scheme $X$ it equals its Krull dimension.

### Source contract
**Given:** Schemes and commutative rings with identity, in fixed universes.

**Goal:** Import the precise convention and Noetherian comparison required by the source filtration theorem.

[F1] EHIK §2.3 definitions and Proposition2.3.2(1),(9) supply the convention and comparison.

### External input
Import [F1] with the exact source record and reading limits. Its “rank of a valuation ring” is its Krull dimension; the equivalent chain-of-overrings definition is given on p9. The Noetherian comparison includes reducible and nonreduced schemes. It is not the false assertion that all valuation rings in arbitrary extension fields mapping to $X$ have bounded dimension.


## The source qcqs cdh site

[Open item](item-lem-author-dcdf962edbda-qcqs-site) · level 6

### Statement
Let $F=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_p$. Choose universes large enough to contain the schemes in use, and a suitably small skeleton $\mathcal C_F$ of the qcqs $F$-schemes in that universe. On $\mathcal C_F$ use the topology generated by Nisnevich covers and families $\{Y\to X,X'\to X\}$ from cartesian squares with $Y\to X$ a finitely presented closed immersion, $X'\to X$ finitely presented and proper, and $X'\setminus(X'\times_XY)\cong X\setminus Y$. This is the precise general cdh site used here. No separated finite-type hypothesis over $F$ or $k$ is imposed. Its evaluation object may be any qcqs $k$-scheme, viewed over its prime field $F$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The hypotheses in the statement.

**Goal:** Establish the displayed construction or conclusion with its actual maps.

[F1] The universe and generated-topology constructions are those of [def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification](item-def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification). EM §3.3 p.14 specifies the displayed generators.

### Proof
1.1 A topology with these generating sieves exists: intersect all Grothendieck topologies containing them. The topology axioms survive intersection, and the maximal topology belongs to the collection. This constructs the least such topology on the chosen small category. [F1, construct]

2.1 These are exactly the square and covering conventions specified in EM §3.3 p.14: in particular both finiteness conditions on the square are retained. A qcqs $k$-scheme is an object after composing its structure morphism with $\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}F$; quasi-compactness and quasi-separatedness here are properties of the underlying scheme. Thus the site supplies every evaluation object required. The previously completed separated finite-type site is a different specified site and is left unchanged; no equivalence between their cohomologies is asserted. [given, step 1.1] ∎

## Completely decomposed proper covers and the cdh topology

[Open item](item-def-cdh-topology-interface) · level 7

### Definition
Fix a field $k$ and a suitably small category equivalent to the category of separated schemes of finite type over $k$, with the indicated fibre products, closed subschemes and finite disjoint unions represented in it. Its morphisms are $k$-scheme morphisms. As usual, a morphism is **proper** if it is separated, of finite type and universally closed: every base change has closed image on every closed subset. For $x\in X$, $\kappa(x)$ denotes the residue field of the local ring at $x$.

A morphism $p:Y\to X$ is **completely decomposed** if, for every point $x\in X$, some $y\in Y$ maps to $x$ and the induced map $\kappa(x)\to\kappa(y)$ is an isomorphism. A **completely decomposed proper morphism**, or **cdp-morphism**, is one that is both proper and completely decomposed. Its singleton family $\{Y\to X\}$ is called a proper cdh covering family.

The **cdh topology** on this category is the least Grothendieck topology for which every Nisnevich covering family and every singleton family associated to a cdp-morphism generates a covering sieve. Thus a family is a **cdh covering family** when the sieve it generates is covering in this topology. A sieve is a collection of arrows into a fixed object closed under precomposition; a Grothendieck topology specifies covering sieves satisfying maximality, pullback stability and transitivity. A Nisnevich covering family consists of étale morphisms with a residue-field-preserving lift of every point. An arbitrary cdh covering family need not itself consist of proper morphisms.

An **abstract blowup square** is a cartesian square

$$\begin{matrix}E&\longrightarrow&Y\\\downarrow&&\downarrow p\\Z&\xrightarrow{i}&X\end{matrix}$$

in which $i$ is a closed immersion, $p$ is proper, $E=Y\times_X Z$, and $p$ restricts to an isomorphism $Y\times_X (X\setminus Z)\to X\setminus Z$. Here $X\setminus Z$ is the open complement of the underlying closed subset of $Z$, and cartesian means that the displayed $E$ is the fibre product. The associated family is $\{Z\to X,Y\to X\}$; it is a cdh covering family.

A statement that a presheaf or complex satisfies descent for abstract blowup squares is a statement about those squares. Applying it to all cdh covers requires a separate descent theorem with its hypotheses, including the relevant Nisnevich condition and the intended notion of descent or hyperdescent. This definition does not assert such a theorem.

### Definition references
[def-nisnevich-covering-interface](item-def-nisnevich-covering-interface)

[def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification](item-def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification)

### Justification
The residue-field homomorphism is induced by the local homomorphism of the scheme morphism, so complete decomposition is an intrinsic condition on points. The category is small, and the maximal topology contains the specified sieves. The intersection of all Grothendieck topologies containing them is again a Grothendieck topology, giving the least one. The meanings of Nisnevich covering family and generated topology are those of [def-nisnevich-covering-interface](item-def-nisnevich-covering-interface) and [def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification](item-def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification).

For an abstract blowup square, the map $Z\amalg Y\to X$ is proper: a closed immersion is proper, and a finite disjoint union of proper $X$-schemes is proper. Indeed, after any base change, a closed immersion remains a closed immersion, and the image of a closed subset of a finite disjoint union is the finite union of its closed component images; finite type and separatedness are likewise preserved by this finite union. If $x$ lies in the closed subset underlying $Z$, the unique point of $Z$ over $x$ has residue field $\kappa(x)$. If $x$ lies in its open complement, the assumed isomorphism gives a point of $Y$ over $x$ with that residue field. Hence $Z\amalg Y\to X$ is completely decomposed. Write $g:W=Z\amalg Y\to X$, let $R$ be the sieve generated by $g$, and let $S$ be the sieve generated by the two component maps. These sieves need not be equal, but $S$ is covering if and only if $R$ is covering in any topology containing the Nisnevich covers. Indeed, $S\subseteq R$, so covering of $S$ implies covering of $R$ by upward closure. Conversely, the pullback sieve $g^*S$ contains both open-and-closed inclusions $Z\to W$ and $Y\to W$. These inclusions form a Nisnevich covering family: they are étale and each point of $W$ lies in one summand with unchanged residue field. Thus $g^*S$ is covering. Every arrow $f:T\to X$ in $R$ factors as $g\circ h$ for some $h:T\to W$, so $f^*S=h^*(g^*S)$ is covering by pullback stability. If $R$ is covering, local character (the transitivity axiom for covering sieves) therefore implies that $S$ is covering. Here $g$ is completely decomposed proper, so $R$ is a generating cdh covering sieve, and the associated two-member family is consequently cdh covering. This argument uses only the existing Nisnevich and topology axioms, and neither equates these sieves nor assumes a later finite-refinement theorem.

## Degree zero and negative homology of the cycle complex

[Open item](item-lem-bloch-chow-and-negative-range) · level 7


### Statement
Let $k$ be a field, $X$ a smooth finite-type $k$-scheme and $r\geq0$. With ordinary Chow group $\mathrm{CH}^r(X)$ defined as codimension-$r$ cycles modulo principal-divisor rational equivalence as specified by the classical relation comparison, the identity on cycles induces $H_0z^r(X,\bullet)\cong\mathrm{CH}^r(X)$, and $H_nz^r(X,\bullet)=0$ for $n<0$. Consequently, if for every integer $p$ there is an isomorphism $H^{p,r}(X)\cong\mathrm{CH}^r(X,2r-p)$, then $H^{2r,r}(X)\cong\mathrm{CH}^r(X)$ and $H^{p,r}(X)=0$ for $p>2r$. The existence of the comparison isomorphisms is not asserted.

### Statement references

[lem-author-c8fb25136bd5-bloch-classical-comparison](item-lem-author-c8fb25136bd5-bloch-classical-comparison)

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $k$, $X$ and $r$ as in the statement; for the final conditional assertion, the stated comparison isomorphisms.

**Goal:** Identify degree-zero homology and derive the negative and reindexed vanishing statements.

[F1] Degree-zero homology is $Z^r(X)/B^r(X)$. [lem-author-c8fb25136bd5-zero-homology-quotient](item-lem-author-c8fb25136bd5-zero-homology-quotient)

[F2] The local graph-and-norm comparison identifies $B^r(X)$ with the subgroup of principal-divisor relations defining $\mathrm{CH}^r(X)$. [lem-author-c8fb25136bd5-bloch-classical-comparison](item-lem-author-c8fb25136bd5-bloch-classical-comparison)

[F3] Negative homology vanishes, and the stated higher-Chow comparison reindexes degree $2r$ to degree zero and $p>2r$ to negative homological degrees. [lem-author-c8fb25136bd5-negative-homology](item-lem-author-c8fb25136bd5-negative-homology), [lem-author-c8fb25136bd5-comparison-reindexing](item-lem-author-c8fb25136bd5-comparison-reindexing)

[F4] Higher Chow groups are defined as homology of the Bloch complex. [def-bloch-higher-cycle-complex](item-def-bloch-higher-cycle-complex)

### Proof

1.1 The two relation subgroups agree by [F2], so the identity on $Z^r(X)$ identifies the quotient in [F1] with the ordinary Chow group. This identification commutes with open restriction: a cycle restricts to its intersection with the open, and the face-length coefficients are unchanged there, so the common boundary/relation subgroup is preserved and the induced quotient maps agree. [F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Negative homology vanishes by [F3]. Under the additional comparison isomorphisms, [F3] identifies the degree-$2r$ group with degree-zero homology and gives zero for $p>2r$; composing the former identification with step 1.1 gives the asserted Chow-group isomorphism. [given, F3, F4, step 1.1] ∎


## Cycle complexes with fixed support

[Open item](item-def-supported-higher-cycle-complex) · level 7

### Definition
Let $k$ be a field, $U$ a smooth finite-type $k$-scheme, $T\subset U$ a closed subset, $V=U\setminus T$, and $r\geq0$. In the unnormalized Bloch complex $z^r(U,\bullet)$, define $z_T^r(U,n)$ to be the free subgroup generated by admissible integral cycles contained in $T\times\Delta^n$, with differential induced from $z^r(U,\bullet)$. Put $\mathrm{CH}_T^r(U,n)=H_n(z_T^r(U,\bullet))$ and $\mathrm{CH}_T^r(U)=\mathrm{CH}_T^r(U,0)$. Its cohomological indexing is $H_T^{p,r}(U;z)=\mathrm{CH}_T^r(U,2r-p)$.

The restriction $j^*:z^r(U,\bullet)\to z^r(V,\bullet)$ has homotopy-fiber model $F_n=z^r(U,n)\oplus z^r(V,n+1)$, with differential $(a,b)\mapsto(\partial a,j^*a-\partial b)$. The inclusion $z_T^r(U,\bullet)\to F$ is a quasi-isomorphism, so the displayed supported groups are also the homology groups of this derived restriction fiber, with the same indexing. A quasi-isomorphism is a chain map inducing isomorphisms on all homology groups.

[lem-author-75596422a482-face-support](item-lem-author-75596422a482-face-support), [lem-author-75596422a482-open-restriction](item-lem-author-75596422a482-open-restriction), [lem-author-75596422a482-restriction-kernel](item-lem-author-75596422a482-restriction-kernel)

[F3] The quotient by that kernel embeds into the target with the same cokernel as restriction. [lem-author-75596422a482-quotient-inclusion](item-lem-author-75596422a482-quotient-inclusion)

[F4] The restriction cokernel is acyclic by the imported localization theorem, and an acyclic cokernel makes the kernel a model for the homotopy fiber. [thm-author-75596422a482-bloch-localization-input](item-thm-author-75596422a482-bloch-localization-input), [lem-author-75596422a482-kernel-homotopy-fiber](item-lem-author-75596422a482-kernel-homotopy-fiber)

### Justification
By [F1] and [F2], the displayed groups form a subcomplex, so its homology quotient is defined. The hypotheses of [F4] hold for the stated field, smooth finite-type scheme and open complement; [F2] identifies the kernel, and [F3] records the quotient used in the comparison. Thus [F4] gives the stated quasi-isomorphism. The cohomological notation is a reindexing of these homology groups. This construction depends only on the closed subset $T$ and does not identify the whole support fiber with the image of ordinary Chow groups of $T$ in those of $U$. A comparison with a separately defined motivic cohomology theory requires its own compatible comparison theorem.


## Milnor K symbols and the Nisnevich sheaf

[Open item](item-def-milnor-k-sheaf-interface) · level 7

### Definition
All rings here are commutative and unital, and ring homomorphisms preserve the unit. For a ring $A$, let $A^\times$ be its abelian group of units under multiplication. Regard it as a $\mathbb Z$-module, and form its tensor algebra $T_{\mathbb Z}(A^\times)=\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}(A^\times)^{\otimes n}$, with degree-zero summand $\mathbb Z$. Let $I_A$ be the two-sided homogeneous ideal generated by $a\otimes(1-a)$ for all $a$ such that both $a$ and $1-a$ are units. The **naive Milnor K-ring** is $K_*^{M,\mathrm{naive}}(A)=T_{\mathbb Z}(A^\times)/I_A$; its degree-$d$ abelian group, for an integer $d\geq 0$, is $K_d^{M,\mathrm{naive}}(A)$. The image of $a_1\otimes\cdots\otimes a_d$ is written $\{a_1,\ldots,a_d\}$ and called a **Milnor symbol**. Thus symbols are additive in each entry with respect to multiplication of units, and $\{a,1-a\}=0$ whenever both entries are units. In degree zero the group is $\mathbb Z$.

Fix a scheme $X$ and the suitably small Nisnevich site of étale $X$-schemes specified in [def-nisnevich-covering-interface](item-def-nisnevich-covering-interface), with the size convention of [def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification](item-def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification). For an object $U$ put $P_d(U)=K_d^{M,\mathrm{naive}}(\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U))$; for a morphism $V\to U$ use restriction of global functions. The **naive Milnor K-sheaf** $\mathcal K_d^{M,\mathrm{naive}}$ is the Nisnevich sheafification $aP_d=(P_d^+)^+$, with its induced abelian-group structure. Here the plus construction and its sheafification unit are those defined in [def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification](item-def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification). In particular, degree-zero sheafification is the sheafification of the constant presheaf $\mathbb Z$; its sections are not asserted to be $\mathbb Z$ on every object.

This specifies the naive convention only. In particular, the name $\mathcal K_d^M$ in a comparison must be accompanied by its intended convention; no identification with the separately constructed improved Milnor K-theory, including for local rings with finite residue fields, is asserted here. No comparison with motivic cohomology is asserted by this definition.

### Justification
A unital ring homomorphism sends units to units and sends each generator $a\otimes(1-a)$ of $I_A$ to the corresponding generator for the target ring. It therefore induces a graded ring homomorphism on the quotients. Identities and composition are preserved, so restriction of global functions makes $P_d$ a presheaf of abelian groups. The ideal is homogeneous and has no degree-zero generators, giving the stated degree-zero group.

By [def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification](item-def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification), applying plus twice produces a sheaf of sets with the stated universal property. Its group operations are induced by the presheaf operations: matching families can be added, negated and given zero componentwise. Families on two covering sieves can be compared on a common covering subsieve, and agreement after restriction is preserved by these operations. Hence the operations are well-defined on plus classes and satisfy the group laws locally, and therefore on the classes. Applying the same argument a second time gives an abelian-group sheaf. The degree-zero assertion follows because sheafification is applied to the presheaf with value $\mathbb Z$ and identity restrictions, rather than being evaluated before sheafification.

### Reading limits
Remark 6.8 of the article uses $K_d^M$ in a reported comparison; the passage does not specify the naive or improved convention. This item fixes a usable naive convention and does not attribute that choice to the article.

## Elmanto–Morrow motivic complex input

[Open item](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-elmanto-morrow-complexes) · level 7

### Statement
Let $F$ be a prime field, namely $\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_p$ for a prime $p$. For each integer $j\geq0$, Elmanto and Morrow construct a finitary Nisnevich sheaf $\mathbb Z(j)_{\mathrm{mot}}$ on the category of quasi-compact quasi-separated $F$-schemes, valued in the derived category $D(\mathbb Z)$ of complexes of abelian groups. Finitary means compatibility with the filtered inverse limits to which the cited theorem applies. The sheaf is understood in the derived, homotopy-coherent sense of the cited source.

For a field $k$ with prime subfield $F$, restriction along the forgetful functor from qcqs $k$-schemes to qcqs $F$-schemes supplies the corresponding contravariant complex-valued functor on $\mathrm{Sch}_k$ of [def-article-conventions](item-def-article-conventions), with Nisnevich descent for covers in that category. Nisnevich covers are as in [def-nisnevich-covering-interface](item-def-nisnevich-covering-interface).

### External input
The existence and Nisnevich descent of the prime-field sheaves are imported from the opening assertion of Elmanto–Morrow, Theorem 1.1, under its stated hypotheses. This item does not reconstruct their construction or import the filtration, spectral sequence, or comparison theorems.

### Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The cited external input gives the prime-field functor and its Nisnevich descent.

[F2] A qcqs $k$-scheme is a qcqs $F$-scheme by composition with $\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}F$; Nisnevich covering families are defined by their underlying étale morphisms and residue-field maps ([def-article-conventions](item-def-article-conventions), [def-nisnevich-covering-interface](item-def-nisnevich-covering-interface)).

### Proof

**Given:** A field $k$, its prime subfield $F$, and $j\geq0$.

**Goal:** Obtain the stated restricted functor and descent from the external input.

1.1 Apply [F1] to $F$ and $j$. Composition with the forgetful functor in [F2] gives a contravariant $D(\mathbb Z)$-valued functor on qcqs $k$-schemes. [F1, F2]

2.1 Every Nisnevich covering family and its fibre-product descent diagram in the chosen qcqs $k$-site is also such a diagram after forgetting to $F$. The descent equivalence supplied by [F1] therefore applies to the restricted diagram. This proves the stated restriction and descent; existence itself remains the external input. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## The local valuative convention matches the source convention

[Open item](item-lem-author-0cc80c1b5792-valuative-conventions) · level 7

### Statement
The completed local valuative dimension is exactly the valuative dimension used in the source filtration bounds. The equality is used for domains, nonzero rings and nonempty schemes. The empty scheme is handled separately, without identifying unstated source conventions for an empty supremum. In particular a finite-dimensional locally Noetherian scheme has finite source valuative dimension equal to its Krull dimension.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The local definition using valuation overrings, prime quotients and affine opens.

**Goal:** Match actual conventions before applying an external boundedness assertion.

[F1] [def-valuative-dimension-and-boundedness](item-def-valuative-dimension-and-boundedness) is the completed local convention.

[F2] [thm-author-0cc80c1b5792-valuation-input](item-thm-author-0cc80c1b5792-valuation-input) gives EHIK’s convention and its locally Noetherian comparison.

### Proof
1.1 For a domain $A$, both [F1] and [F2] take the supremum of the dimensions of valuation rings $A\subseteq V\subseteq\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. The source equivalently describes the rank by chains of such overrings. Thus the domain numbers agree. Taking the same supremum over all prime quotients gives the same number for nonzero rings. No source convention for the empty prime spectrum is needed. [F1, F2]

2.1 For a nonempty scheme, both scheme conventions take that same invariant over nonempty affine opens, so their values agree. The open-local property and the locally Noetherian equality in [F2] therefore apply directly to the local invariant as well. This proves the stated finite-dimensional consequence without any finite-type-over-a-field assumption. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎


## The actual big cdh slice over a field

[Open item](item-lem-author-2ac325480ae8-slice-site) · level 7

### Statement
Assume AC and compatible universe bounds. Fix a prime $p$, $S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z[1/p]$, and let $\mathcal C=\mathrm{Sch}^{\rm qcqs}_S$ with BEM’s big cdh topology: finite Nisnevich covers and finitely presented abstract blowup covers generate it. For a field $k$ with $p$ invertible, put $U=\operatorname{Spec}k$. The slice $\mathcal C/U$ is exactly the category of qcqs $k$-schemes with the restricted BEM big cdh topology. The covering sieves of an object $(V,f)$ correspond to the covering sieves of $V$ in $\mathcal C$. For presheaves with values in $D(\mathbb Z)$, both restriction $j^*$ along $j:\mathcal C/U\to\mathcal C$ and the functor $j_*Q(V)=Q(V\times_S U\to U)$ preserve cdh sheaves.

### Facts & Assumptions
[F1] [thm-author-2ac325480ae8-bem-finite-comparison](item-thm-author-2ac325480ae8-bem-finite-comparison) specifies BEM’s big site and cover generators. [def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification](item-def-scheme-sites-and-sheafification) fixes the size convention and meaning of a site. All schemes and necessary products lie in the chosen enlarged universe.

[F2] A complex-valued sheaf here means a presheaf satisfying derived Čech descent for every covering family (limits in $D(\mathbb Z)$); $L_{\mathcal C}$ below is its reflective sheafification. These are BEM’s ordinary sheaf conventions, not an unasserted identification with the separately fixed hypercomplete finite-type site.

### Proof
**Given:** $S,k,U,\mathcal C$ as stated.

**Goal:** Identify the slice site and prove both descent-preservation assertions.

1.1 A map $V\to U$ in $\mathcal C$ is precisely a qcqs $k$-scheme. Every arrow $W\to V$ acquires the unique structure map $W\to V\to U$, and any composite into $(V,f)$ remains over $U$. Thus $(\mathcal C/U)/(V,f)\cong\mathcal C/V$, identifying their sieves. Each Nisnevich or abstract blowup covering of $V$ has this unique lift over $U$; conversely forgetting a lifted generator gives such a generator. The generated topologies therefore agree under that identification. This establishes the asserted big-site convention. [F1, construct]

2.1 A sheaf $P$ on $\mathcal C$ satisfies descent for each covering Čech diagram over $V$. That same diagram is the underlying diagram for a cover of $(V,f)$, so $j^*P$ is a sheaf. For a sheaf $Q$ on the slice, a cover of $V$ pulls back to a cover of $V\times_SU$, with its Čech nerve equal to the pulled-back nerve. Evaluating $Q$ on this nerve proves descent for $j_*Q$. Both functors are the displayed actual functors; this does not compare with the older separated finite-type site. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎


## Every qcqs cdh generator is an arc covering family

[Open item](item-lem-author-7113c087ecba-generators-arc) · level 7

### Statement
On the completed qcqs prime-field category every Nisnevich covering family and every abstract blowup family $\{Z\to X,Y\to X\}$ is an arc cover. Here $Z\to X$ is a finitely presented closed immersion, $Y\to X$ is finitely presented proper and an isomorphism outside $Z$. Consequently the source cdh topology is coarser than the arc topology, including on arbitrary nonnoetherian objects.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The hypotheses in the statement.

**Goal:** Establish the stated exact map or descent conclusion.

[F1] [thm-author-7113c087ecba-valuative-input](item-thm-author-7113c087ecba-valuative-input) supplies the exact valuative facts. [F2] [lem-author-dcdf962edbda-qcqs-site](item-lem-author-dcdf962edbda-qcqs-site) fixes the cdh generators; the arc definition is recorded in that input.

### Proof
1.1 For a Nisnevich family and a rank-at-most-one valuation ring $V$ mapping to $X$, choose a member with a point over the image of the closed point; its pullback to $\operatorname{Spec}V$ is étale and has a point over the closed point. Choose an affine neighborhood $\operatorname{Spec}B$ of that point. By the exact valuation input [F1], its local ring $W=B_{\mathfrak m}$ is an extension of valuation rings with the same value group as $V$. It therefore has the same rank, and $\operatorname{Spec}W$ supplies the required lift into that cover member. For a family on a qcqs object take a finite subfamily, which exists since étale images are open. [F1, F2]

1.2 For an abstract blowup family, if the generic point of $\operatorname{Spec}V$ maps into $Z$, the pulled-back ideal is zero in $\operatorname{Frac}V$ and therefore zero in the domain $V$, so the entire map factors through $Z$. Otherwise the generic point has the unique lift to $Y$ over the open complement. Properness and the valuative criterion in [F1] extend it to $\operatorname{Spec}V\to Y$. Thus the abstract family even permits the identity extension $V\to V$. [F1, F2]

2.1 These valuation tests are the defining tests for arc covers; the source topology is generated by the listed families. Both tests are stable under the source base changes, so every generated cdh covering sieve is arc covering. No finite-type or dimension bound on $X$ was used. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎


## The actual smooth open pair and its Nisnevich square

[Open item](item-lem-author-8a080e7d9445-geometry) · level 7


### Statement
Let $X$ be an affine finite-type threefold over algebraically closed $k$, let $U=X_{\mathrm{smooth}}$, and let $T\subset X$ be closed with $T\subset U$. Put $V=U\setminus T$ and $W=X\setminus T$. All four schemes are qcqs and $U,V$ are smooth separated finite type over the perfect field $k$. They are regular Noetherian as schemes over the prime field. The two opens $U,W$ cover $X$ and their intersection is $V$, giving a Nisnevich two-open covering square. If $T$ is an integral curve, it is affine; it lies in one of the open-and-closed relative-dimension strata of $U$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The geometric hypotheses in the statement, with fixed universe bounds.

**Goal:** Construct the stated actual maps and prove their consequence.

[F1] [def-article-conventions](item-def-article-conventions) and [def-nisnevich-covering-interface](item-def-nisnevich-covering-interface) fix the finite-type and two-open conventions. Basic smoothness here includes its regularity over a perfect field and locally constant relative dimension.

### Proof
1.1 Finite-type affine $X/k$ is Noetherian and separated. Every open is quasi-compact in a Noetherian space, and its induced scheme is separated finite type. Thus the four objects lie in $\mathrm{Sch}_k$. The smooth locus and its open $V$ are smooth over $k$, hence regular Noetherian. An algebraically closed field is perfect: in positive characteristic each polynomial $t^p-a$ has a root, so Frobenius is surjective; characteristic zero is perfect. Forgetting the map to $k$ does not change regularity or Noetherianness. [F1]

2.1 The inclusion $T\subset U$ gives $X=U\cup W$ and $U\cap W=V$. Open immersions are étale, and each point has a residue-preserving lift to one of these opens, so the family is Nisnevich. A closed subscheme of affine $X$ is affine, giving the curve assertion. For a smooth morphism to a field the relative dimension is locally constant; the finitely many dimension strata of $U$ are open and closed. The connected integral curve lies in one such stratum. These are component/dimension bookkeeping facts, with no new comparison theorem assumed. [F1, step 1.1] ∎


## Motivic complexes and cohomology

[Open item](item-def-motivic-cohomology) · level 8

### Definition
Let $k$ and $\mathrm{Sch}_k$ have the conventions of [def-article-conventions](item-def-article-conventions): objects of $\mathrm{Sch}_k$ are quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes over $k$. For an integer $j\geq0$, the **motivic complex of weight $j$** is the restriction to $\mathrm{Sch}_k$ of the Elmanto–Morrow Nisnevich sheaf $\mathbb Z(j)_{\mathrm{mot}}$ supplied by [lem-author-b747b28c359f-elmanto-morrow-complexes](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-elmanto-morrow-complexes). It is a contravariant functor with values in $D(\mathbb Z)$, the derived category of complexes of abelian groups.

For $X\in\mathrm{Sch}_k$ and $i\in\mathbb Z$, its **motivic cohomology group of degree $i$ and weight $j$** is
$$H^{i,j}_{\mathrm{mot}}(X,\mathbb Z):=H^i\bigl(\mathbb Z(j)_{\mathrm{mot}}(X)\bigr).$$
For a positive integer $n$, define finite coefficients objectwise by
$$H^{i,j}_{\mathrm{mot}}(X,\mathbb Z/n):=H^i\bigl(\mathbb Z(j)_{\mathrm{mot}}(X)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n\bigr).$$
The derived tensor product here is equivalently the mapping cone of multiplication by $n$. A morphism $X\to Y$ of $k$-schemes induces pullback from the group of $Y$ to that of $X$.

### Justification
The external input [lem-author-b747b28c359f-elmanto-morrow-complexes](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-elmanto-morrow-complexes) supplies the specified complex-valued functor and its Nisnevich descent on the stated category. By [lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-cohomology](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-cohomology), $H^i$ is a functor on $D(\mathbb Z)$, so the integral group and pullback are independent of representatives and respect identities and composition. [lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-finite-coefficients](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-derived-finite-coefficients) supplies the derived quotient, its equivalence with the cone, and its functoriality; applying cohomology gives the finite-coefficient group and its pullback. Evaluation in this definition is evaluation of the supplied complex-valued sheaf; no identification with derived sections on a separately chosen site is assumed.

### Reading limits
The article's Definition 2.2 and the introduction and opening statement of Elmanto–Morrow Theorem 1.1 were read. The construction is used through the explicitly marked external input; its proof is not reconstructed here.

## Finite subintegral maps are cdh covers

[Open item](item-lem-author-60d95bfb692a-finite-subintegral-cdh-cover) · level 8

### Statement
Let $p:T\to X$ be a finite subintegral morphism between separated finite-type schemes over a field. Then the singleton $\{p\}$ is a cdh covering family. Here finite means affine with finite-module coordinate rings; subintegral means integral, bijective on points and inducing isomorphisms on all residue fields. A cdh covering family generates a covering sieve for the topology of [def-cdh-topology-interface](item-def-cdh-topology-interface).

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite subintegral morphism $p:T\to X$ in the indicated scheme category.

**Goal:** Show that $p$ is a completely decomposed proper morphism and hence a cdh cover.

[F1] A finite morphism is proper: it is separated, of finite type and universally closed. This follows affine-locally from integral maps being closed, a property preserved by base change. [def-cdh-topology-interface](item-def-cdh-topology-interface)

[F2] A completely decomposed proper morphism is a cdh covering singleton. Complete decomposition means that every target point has a preimage with isomorphic residue field. [def-cdh-topology-interface](item-def-cdh-topology-interface)

### Proof

**Proof technique:** Apply the definitions.

1.1 By finiteness and [F1], $p$ is proper. By subintegrality, every $x\in X$ has a preimage $t$ and $\kappa(x)\to\kappa(t)$ is an isomorphism. Thus $p$ is completely decomposed. [F1, given]

2.1 By [F2], the singleton $\{p\}$ is a cdh cover, as required. [F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Huber–Kelly representable cdh sheafification input

[Open item](item-thm-author-60d95bfb692a-huber-kelly-representable-input) · level 8


### Statement
Let $S$ be noetherian and Nagata, and let $X,Y$ be separated finite-type $S$-schemes. The canonical map identifies the cdh sheafification of the presheaf $h_Y(Z)=\operatorname{Hom}_S(Z,Y)$, evaluated at $X$, with $\operatorname{Hom}_S(X^{\mathrm{sn}},Y)$, naturally in $X$ and $Y$. Here noetherian means admitting a finite affine cover by spectra of noetherian rings; Nagata means that the normalization of every finite-type $S$-scheme is finite over that scheme. The notation $X^{\mathrm{sn}}\to X$ denotes the seminormalization of the reduction, with its canonical map to $X$.

For this statement, use a suitably small category equivalent to the category of separated finite-type $S$-schemes, with all $S$-morphisms. Its **cdh topology** is the least Grothendieck topology in which Nisnevich covering families and singleton proper completely decomposed morphisms generate covering sieves. A Nisnevich family consists of étale morphisms such that every target point has a lift inducing an isomorphism of residue fields. A morphism is completely decomposed if it has such a lift at every target point, and proper means separated, of finite type and universally closed. On a field base this is the supplied field-site topology.

### Statement references

[def-seminormal-scheme-interface](item-def-seminormal-scheme-interface)

[def-cdh-topology-interface](item-def-cdh-topology-interface)

### External input
The formula is the cdh case of Huber–Kelly Theorem 1.4: its rh formula (2) and rh-to-cdh comparison (3) give the stated identification. The source includes the spectrum of a perfect field as an example of a noetherian Nagata base. Its general-base site convention is Section 2A and Remark 2.2(1), using the cdp-morphisms of Definition 2.1; the statement above supplies that convention explicitly rather than extending the field-only interface by reference. The source's Proposition 2.8 also places $X^{\mathrm{sn}}$ in this finite-type site under the Nagata hypothesis. These are precise external inputs; their proofs are not reconstructed here. The local finite-subintegral descent lemmas do not by themselves prove this representable-sheaf formula.


## Finite subfamilies of Nisnevich covers on the finite-type site

[Open item](item-lem-author-5bfbe3ebf14f-finite-nisnevich-subfamily) · level 8

### Statement
In the specified category of separated finite-type schemes over a field $k$, every Nisnevich covering family $\{U_i\to X\}_{i\in I}$ contains a finite subfamily which is still Nisnevich. The empty family suffices if $X=\varnothing$. This does not assert that the residue-field-lifting locus of a given étale map is Zariski open.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The site above and the pointwise residue-field-lifting definition of a Nisnevich family.

**Goal:** Obtain a finite subfamily with that same pointwise lifting property.

[F1] The completed interfaces specify these schemes and étale covering morphisms. Finite-type schemes over a field are Noetherian of finite dimension; closed reduced subschemes have finitely many irreducible components. [def-cdh-topology-interface](item-def-cdh-topology-interface), [def-nisnevich-covering-interface](item-def-nisnevich-covering-interface)

[F2] On an integral affine scheme $Z=\operatorname{Spec}A$, a morphism from its generic point into a finite-type $Z$-scheme extends over a nonempty open: choose an affine target neighbourhood over $Z$, write its coordinate ring using finitely many $A$-algebra generators and relations, and clear the finitely many denominators of their images in $\operatorname{Frac}A$. The resulting homomorphism into $A[1/a]$ is the required extension. Relations hold there because $A[1/a]\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Frac}A$ is injective. This argument proves the fact rather than importing a rational-section theorem.

### Proof
1.1 For a nonempty reduced closed subscheme $Z\subset X$ and each of its finitely many generic points $\eta$, choose a residue-preserving lift in one of the $U_i$. This gives a generic section of $U_i\times_X Z_\eta\to Z_\eta$, where $Z_\eta$ is the corresponding integral component. By [F2] it extends over a dense open of that component. Shrink this open to avoid the other components. It is then open also in $Z$. Finitely many such opens have union $O\subset Z$ containing all generic points of $Z$; the finitely many chosen maps provide residue-preserving lifts over $O$. A section preserves residue fields because the induced field maps $\kappa(z)\to\kappa(u)\to\kappa(z)$ have composite identity, so the middle field is the base field. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 The closed reduced complement $Z\setminus O$ has strictly smaller dimension than $Z$. Repeat step 1.1 there. Induction on the finite dimension terminates, and at each stage only finitely many original indices are selected. Thus their union is finite and provides residue-preserving lifts at every point of $X$. Each selected original map remains étale, so it is a Nisnevich subfamily. Nilpotents do not change points or residue fields; starting with $X_{\mathrm{red}}$ therefore proves the claim for $X$ as well. No lifting-locus openness has been asserted. [F1, step 1.1] ∎


## Pullback and composition of the cdh generating families

[Open item](item-lem-author-5bfbe3ebf14f-cdh-generators-pullback-composition) · level 8

### Statement
On this finite-type site, Nisnevich families and singleton completely decomposed proper (cdp) morphisms contain identities and are stable under arbitrary base change. Finite compositions of such families are stable under base change and composition. Every resulting composite family is completely decomposed in the pointwise sense: each target point has a lift with identical residue field. Finite disjoint unions of Nisnevich maps forming a cover give a Nisnevich covering morphism; finite disjoint unions over the disjoint union of their targets of cdp morphisms give a cdp morphism.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The pointwise definitions from [def-nisnevich-covering-interface](item-def-nisnevich-covering-interface) and [def-cdh-topology-interface](item-def-cdh-topology-interface).

**Goal:** Verify the closure properties used for a finite pretopology.

[F1] Étale and proper morphisms are preserved by base change and composition; finite disjoint unions have those same properties componentwise. Properness means separated, finite type, universally closed, and these conditions verify the stated proper assertions directly. The corresponding closure properties for étale morphisms are those of [math:def-etale-morphism-schemes](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-etale-morphism-schemes).

### Proof
1.1 If $y\in Y$ over $x\in X$ has $\kappa(y)=\kappa(x)$, then over any $x'\in X'$ above $x$, the fiber of $Y\times_X X'$ contains the point specified by the $\kappa(x')$-valued base change of $y$. Its residue field is exactly $\kappa(x')$. Thus complete decomposition survives every base change. Combining this with [F1] proves base-change stability of both sorts of generating families. Identity maps plainly have the lifting property. [F1, given]

2.1 To lift a point through a composite family, lift it through the first family with unchanged residue field, then through the covering family above that chosen object, again with unchanged residue field. Composing the two residue-field isomorphisms proves complete decomposition of the composite. A pullback of such a composite is the composite of its pulled-back families by the fiber-product associativity isomorphism. This proves the asserted finite-composition and pullback closure. [step 1.1, given]

3.1 A point of a finite disjoint union lies in exactly one component. For covers over disjoint target components apply the required lifting property on that component. For a Nisnevich family over a common target apply its lifting property to one summand of its source coproduct. Étaleness and properness are supplied by [F1]; for the proper assertion the targets are disjoint, so properness is checked on those open-and-closed pieces. This proves the stated coproduct assertions. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎


## External MVW proper-cover identification and two-stage refinement

### Statement
Fix a prime field $F$ and $j\geq0$. The actual EM functor $M_{j,F}=\mathbb Z(j)_{\mathrm{mot}}$ on qcqs $F$-schemes has a natural comparison $\alpha_{j,F}:M_{j,F}\to C_{j,F}$, where
$$C_{j,F}=\mathbb Z(j)_{\mathrm{cdh}}=L_{\mathrm{cdh}}L_{\mathrm{Kan}}\mathbb Z(j)_{\mathrm{cla}}.$$
Here $L_{\mathrm{Kan}}$ extends the classical smooth-$F$ motivic complex to qcqs $F$-schemes and $L_{\mathrm{cdh}}$ is derived cdh sheafification. The comparison identifies $C_{j,F}$ with $L_{\mathrm{cdh}}M_{j,F}$. For every Noetherian $F$-scheme $X$ of finite dimension $d$, $H^i(C_{j,F}(X))=0$ for $i>j+d$.

[F2] The p.56 paragraph following Remark8.8 explicitly states $C_{j,F}(X)\in D(\mathbb Z)^{\leq j+d}$ in the Noetherian dimension-$d$ context, invoking Theorem3.5(1).
