Wedge bases give $\det(L^\vee\oplus\mathcal O_X^N)\cong L^\vee$ and $\det(\mathcal O_X^{N+1})\cong\mathcal O_X$; the usual wedge-of-summands map is canonical and glues. Hence $L^\vee\cong\mathcal O_X$, and dualizing gives $L\cong\mathcal O_X$ by local double-dual evaluation. [F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 Conversely, if $L$ is trivial, its dual is trivial and the two terms of $1-[L^\vee]$ cancel. This proves the equivalence with the precise spectral class. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎


## Murthy top Chow cycle comparison with its actual exterior-dual map

[Open item](item-thm-author-394a5b71198d-murthy-chow-to-k-input) · level 14


### Statement
Assume AC. Let $A$ be a regular integral affine algebra of dimension $n\geq2$ over an algebraically closed field of arbitrary characteristic, and put $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$. Write $K_0^{\mathrm{proj}}(A)$ for the Grothendieck group of finite projective modules, with exact-sequence relations. Let $F^nK_0^{\mathrm{proj}}(A)$ be its subgroup generated by the classes $[A/\mathfrak m]$ of the residue fields of smooth maximal ideals of height $n$; a finite projective resolution defines each such class. Then this subgroup has no $(n-1)!$ torsion, meaning that $(n-1)!x=0$ forces $x=0$. The natural cycle map $\phi:\mathrm{CH}^n(X)\to F^nK_0^{\mathrm{proj}}(A)$ sending each closed-point cycle $[x]$ to $[k(x)]$ is an isomorphism. For a rank-$n$ finite projective module $P$ and associated bundle $E$, the actual equality is $\phi(c_n(E))=C^K_n(P)=\sum_i(-1)^i[\Lambda^iP^*]$. Thus this class belongs to $F^n$, and $c_n(E)=0$ exactly when $C^K_n(P)=0$.

### External input
This is an explicitly imported established primary-source statement. The additional regular-ring finite-resolution input in [F5] is imported from the two precise Stacks statements cited above. The local steps check its hypotheses and translate its map; they do not reprove the zero-cycle theorem or its source proof. The map used is the closed-point cycle map phi, not a group isomorphism chosen without a map, and not the nth Chern operation on an arbitrary virtual K-class (whose composite with the cycle map carries a factorial). The degree-one interface and degree-zero boundary are proved independently in local prerequisites; no dimension-at-least-two hypothesis is silently applied there.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The hypotheses and data in the statement, with AC and the article's fixed universes wherever perfect K-theory is used.

**Goal:** Establish the asserted conclusion.

[F1] Theorem 2.14(i) supplies absence of factorial torsion for $n=2$, or for $n\ge 3$ when A is regular in codimension one. Its part (ii) supplies the natural cycle isomorphism for regular A.

[F2] Definition 3.5 and Remark 3.6(i)–(ii) identify the class with the exterior powers of the dual and with the usual top Chow Chern class under the cycle isomorphism.

[F3] The affine spectral/module interface for this actual alternating class is supplied by [lem-author-394a5b71198d-exterior-dual-interface](item-lem-author-394a5b71198d-exterior-dual-interface).

[F4] A projective module lifts maps through surjections. [math:def-projective-module](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-projective-module) The resolution comparison is verified below using this property. Weibel II, Theorem 7.6 and Corollary 7.7.2, pp.65–67, give the established general comparison; their role here is source documentation, not a replacement for the local relation checks. Murthy's Section 1 opening convention, printed p.3 / PDF p.5, defines the group using all finitely generated modules and identifies it with the group of finite modules of finite projective dimension. The all-finite-module group is denoted $G_0(A)$ here to distinguish the presentations. That source identification is justified in the present regular scope by [F5], but is not valid for arbitrary singular Noetherian rings.

[F5] The imported regular-ring resolution facts are Stacks Lemma 10.110.8 (Tag 00OE) and Lemma 10.109.6 (Tag 0CXE): a regular Noetherian ring of finite dimension $n$ has global dimension $n$, and every finite module of projective dimension at most $n$ admits a resolution of length at most $n$ by finite projectives. These are cited established premises; the comparison of exact-relation groups in steps 1.1–2.1 is supplied locally.

### Proof
1.1 Write $\mathcal P$ for finite projective $A$-modules and $\mathcal H$ for finite modules admitting finite resolutions by objects of $\mathcal P$. Give both groups short-exact-sequence relations. The latter category is extension closed: for $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ and finite projective resolutions of the end terms, lift the map $P''_0\to M''$ to $M$ by projectivity and combine it with $P'_0\to M'$. This gives a surjection $P'_0\oplus P''_0\to M$ whose kernel sits in an exact sequence between the two first syzygies. Repeating, with resolutions padded by zeros, gives a resolution of $M$ with terms $P'_i\oplus P''_i$; the last extension of projective syzygies splits by the lifting property. Thus the inherited exact structure is defined, and inclusion induces $j:K_0^{\mathrm{proj}}(A)\to K_0(\mathcal H)$. [F4, construct]

1.2 For $M\in\mathcal H$, choose a finite resolution $P_\bullet\to M$ and put $\chi(M)=\sum_i(-1)^i[P_i]$. Given two resolutions, lift the identity of $M$ to a chain map by lifting successively through the surjections onto kernels in the target resolution. It induces the identity on degree-zero homology and both resolutions have zero higher homology, so its finite mapping cone is acyclic. Every bounded acyclic complex of projectives is split exact: in its lowest nonzero degree the preceding differential surjects onto a projective term and splits; remove that contractible pair and continue. The alternating projective class of the cone is zero, while its termwise alternating sum is the difference of the two resolution sums. Hence $\chi(M)$ is independent of the chosen resolution. [F4, construct, algebra]

2.1 The resolution in step 1.1 gives $\chi(M)=\chi(M')+\chi(M'')$ for every defining exact relation, using independence from step 1.2. Hence $\chi$ induces a homomorphism $K_0(\mathcal H)\to K_0^{\mathrm{proj}}(A)$. Length-zero resolutions give $\chi j([P])=[P]$. Each successive syzygy of a finite projective resolution is in $\mathcal H$, because the tail is its finite resolution. The corresponding short exact sequences telescope to $(M)=\sum_i(-1)^i(P_i)$ in $K_0(\mathcal H)$, so $j\chi((M))=(M)$. These are mutually inverse group maps, respecting every exact relation. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The affine algebra $A$ is Noetherian, regular and of finite dimension $n$. By [F5] every finite $A$-module has a resolution by finite projectives of length at most $n$. Hence $\mathcal H$ is the whole category of finite $A$-modules, with exactly the same short exact sequences, so its exact-relation group is $G_0(A)$, the all-finite-module group in the source convention [F4]. Step 2.1 therefore makes $j:K_0^{\mathrm{proj}}(A)\to G_0(A)$ an isomorphism with inverse $\chi$. Write $(M)$ for the source class of a finite module; its image under $\chi$ is the resolution Euler class, and length-zero resolutions identify projective classes by $j$. This establishes the comparison with the source's full category, rather than only its finite-projective-dimension subcategory. For the subgroup $F^n_H$ generated by the selected $(A/\mathfrak m)$, $\chi$ restricts to an isomorphism onto the stated $F^nK_0^{\mathrm{proj}}(A)$, since it takes each residue module to its resolution Euler class and $j$ is its inverse. For the actual source cycle map $\phi_H$, the composite $\chi\phi_H$ sends $[x]$ to that same Euler class of $k(x)$; therefore it is the stated map $\phi$, with rational-equivalence descent inherited from $\phi_H$. The algebra is regular and integral, so Theorem 2.14(ii) applies. In part (i), use its $n=2$ alternative or its $n\geq3$ regular-in-codimension-one alternative. Thus [F1] gives the source cycle isomorphism and absence of $(n-1)!$ torsion in arbitrary characteristic, and the subgroup isomorphism transfers both assertions to the stated target. The comparison with $G_0(A)$ has used regularity and finite dimension explicitly; it asserts nothing analogous for a singular ring. [F1, F4, F5, step 2.1, given]

4.1 Apply [F2] to $P$ in the same presentation: $\phi_H(c_n(E))=\sum_i(-1)^i(\Lambda^iP^*)$. Every exterior term is finite projective, so its length-zero resolution gives $\chi((\Lambda^iP^*))=[\Lambda^iP^*]$. Applying $\chi$ proves exactly $\phi(c_n(E))=C_n^K(P)$, including membership in $F^n$. Injectivity of $\phi$ proves the asserted equivalence of vanishings. Finally [F3], under its inherited AC and universe assumptions, takes this actual projective-module alternating class to $\varepsilon(E)$ in the article's perfect group. The factorial in the distinct nth-Chern-operation composite has not replaced the actual point-cycle map. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

### Source notes

The locally checked Euler comparison supplies the presentation translation; it does not reconstruct Murthy's deep zero-cycle inputs. The retained earlier source check reports visual reading of the cached scan's cover and printed pp.1–2, 13–14 and 17 (PDF pp.1, 3–4, 15–16 and 19). This round additionally visually read printed p.3 / PDF p.5 and authenticated the same cached PDF digest stated above. A fresh web request to the ICTP PDF timed out. Cached download provenance and correspondence with the final Annals wording remain unattested; journal bytes and the deep results cited within Murthy's short proofs were not read. The article passage maintained here is its Introduction, PDF p.1, citing Remark 3.6 and Theorem 3.7. The low-dimensional exclusions and all ordinary integral Chow and characteristic qualifications are unchanged.

The preliminary scan's Section 1 convention on printed p.3 is a separate consulted-literature defect outside the present regular scope. For $B=k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$, finite projectives are free, so $K_0^{\mathrm{proj}}(B)=\mathbb Z[B]$, whereas composition length gives $G_0(B)=\mathbb Z[k]$. The exact sequence $0\to k\to B\to k\to0$ makes the natural map send $[B]$ to $2[k]$; it is not an isomorphism. Steps 1.1–2.1 still compare projectives with finite-projective-resolution modules, so the scan cannot identify that category's group with all-finite-module $G_0$ in this singular example. In the assigned theorem, [F5] supplies precisely the missing regularity argument; no source error is attributed to the unread final journal version.

Retain the consulted-literature error in Weibel II, Lemma 7.7.1, p.67: its kernel projective-dimension bound prints a minimum where a maximum is required. For $R=k[t]$, the split exact sequence with kernel and quotient $R/(t)$ and middle term $(R/(t))^2$ has middle and quotient projective dimension one, but nonprojective kernel. The printed minimum would make that kernel projective. The local comparison above uses no such estimate; neither Murthy's results nor the resolution comparison is refuted by this source typo.


## A common-core zero curve exists on a nonempty parameter open

[Open item](item-lem-author-27d786ff4d27-common-core-nonempty) · level 14

### Statement
For the family just constructed, let $O$ be any nonempty smooth open subset of $U$. There is a nonempty open $T_O\subset T$ such that each $k$-parameter in $T_O$ has a nonempty zero scheme on $O$. At the generic parameter this zero scheme is nonempty as well. This conclusion uses an actual smooth point of the incidence projection, rather than an inference from its total dimension.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The integral threefold, rank-two section family, and $O$ as above.

**Goal:** Ensure nonemptiness on a common open core before asserting irreducibility by charts.

[F1] [lem-author-27d786ff4d27-dual-global-controls](item-lem-author-27d786ff4d27-dual-global-controls) gives first-jet surjectivity and value generation. [lem-regular-section-parameter-family](item-lem-regular-section-parameter-family) gives the actual universal zero-incidence $I_O\subset O\times T$ and its fibers.

[F2] [thm-author-27d786ff4d27-relative-jacobian-openness](item-thm-author-27d786ff4d27-relative-jacobian-openness) supplies the relative Jacobian criterion and openness of smooth maps. [thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input](item-thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input) supplies rational closed points and dimension conventions.

### Proof
1.1 Choose a closed $x\in O$, whose residue field is $k$. First-jet surjectivity gives a $k$-parameter $a$ with value zero at $x$ and derivative $T_xO\to E(x)$ of rank two. On a local smooth presentation of $O$ and a frame of $E$, $I_O$ is defined in $O\times T$ by two coefficients. Their derivatives in the $O$ directions are independent at $(x,a)$. Augmenting the smooth presentation's Jacobian by these two rows produces an invertible maximal minor, so the relative Jacobian criterion makes $I_O\to T$ smooth of relative dimension one near $(x,a)$. This argument is valid in all characteristics. [F1, F2]

2.1 Choose that smooth open neighbourhood in $I_O$. Its image is a nonempty open $T_O$ by [F2]. Every point of $T_O$ has a preimage in the incidence, so its actual zero fiber on $O$ is nonempty, including the generic point of the irreducible parameter space. In particular its closed $k$-parameters have a zero there. This proves the asserted dominance on an actual incidence open and the needed nonempty fibers. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎


## A rank-two family avoids each prescribed codimension-two locus

[Open item](item-lem-author-27d786ff4d27-fixed-locus-avoidance) · level 14

### Statement
Fix a closed subset $Z\subset U$ of codimension at least two before choosing the functional. Set $B=Z\cup U_{\mathrm{sing}}$ with reduced structure. Then $\dim B\leq1$, and a nonempty open $T_{\mathrm{av}}\subset T$ consists of parameters whose zero schemes are disjoint from $B$. The allowed open may depend on $Z$; this is $\forall Z\,\exists t$, not $\exists t\,\forall Z$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The integral normal threefold and fixed $Z$; the globally value-generating family of [lem-author-27d786ff4d27-dual-global-controls](item-lem-author-27d786ff4d27-dual-global-controls).

**Goal:** Combine the prescribed avoidance with all later generic conditions.

[F1] [thm-author-fc2380accb47-normal-geometric-input](item-thm-author-fc2380accb47-normal-geometric-input) gives normality's $(R_1)$ and the smooth/regular equality over the perfect field. [thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input](item-thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input) gives dimension and image-closure bounds.

[F2] [lem-regular-section-parameter-family](item-lem-regular-section-parameter-family) and [lem-surjection-kernel-bundle](item-lem-surjection-kernel-bundle) identify zero incidence over $B$ with the total space of the rank-$(N-2)$ value kernel.

### Proof
1.1 Codimension at least two in the integral threefold gives $\dim Z\leq1$. By [F1] the singular locus is closed of dimension at most one. Hence their union $B$ is a closed finite-type subset of $U$ with $\dim B\leq1$. The restricted evaluation surjection $\mathcal O_B^N\to E|_B$ has locally free kernel of rank $N-2$, even if $B$ is singular. Thus its total space, the actual zero incidence $I_B$, has dimension at most $1+N-2=N-1$. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 The closure of the image of $I_B$ in $T$ has dimension at most $N-1$ by [F1]. Its complement $T_{\mathrm{av}}$ is nonempty open. Its inverse image in $I_B$ is empty and remains empty after every field extension. Hence all its zero fibers avoid $B$. Intersecting this open with any finitely many nonempty parameter opens retains a nonempty open since $T$ is irreducible. The construction starts with the chosen $Z$, giving exactly the stated quantifier order. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎


## Cohomology of shifted Nisnevich units

[Open item](item-lem-author-13e6fe931c45-shifted-units) · level 14

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the size bounds in [def-derived-sections-on-sites](item-def-derived-sections-on-sites). For a scheme $X$, put $A=R\Gamma_{\rm Nis}(X,\mathbb G_m)[-1]$, using the small Nisnevich site and the sheaf of units of [lem-nisnevich-line-bundle-torsors](item-lem-nisnevich-line-bundle-torsors). Then $H^i(A)=H^{i-1}_{\rm Nis}(X,\mathbb G_m)$ for every integer $i$; these groups are zero for $i\leq0$, the global units for $i=1$, and $\operatorname{Pic}(X)$ for $i=2$.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $X$, the stated site, Choice, and the size bounds.

**Goal:** Compute the indicated cohomology groups.

[F1] Derived sections of an abelian sheaf concentrated in degree zero have no negative cohomology ([def-derived-sections-on-sites](item-def-derived-sections-on-sites)).

[F2] Degree-zero Nisnevich cohomology of $\mathbb G_m$ is $\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)^\times$, and degree one is $\operatorname{Pic}(X)$, the group of line bundles under tensor product ([lem-nisnevich-line-bundle-torsors](item-lem-nisnevich-line-bundle-torsors)).

### Proof

1.1 For the cohomological shift, a complex $C[-1]$ has $C[-1]^i=C^{i-1}$, with the corresponding signed differential. Its cycles and boundaries in degree $i$ are those of $C$ in degree $i-1$, so $H^i(C[-1])=H^{i-1}(C)$. Apply this to the derived-sections complex. [given, algebra]

2.1 If $i\leq0$, then $i-1<0$, so [F1] gives zero. For $i=1,2$, [F2] gives global units and the Picard group respectively. These identifications use the specified small site and retain the Choice and size hypotheses. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## External actual EM graded algebra, Picard class and complex PBF

[Open item](item-thm-author-4f94f7982b0d-em-graded-input) · level 14

### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the fixed compatible site and universe bounds of the supplied constructions. On qcqs schemes over a prime field, $A_n=\mathbb Z(n)_{\rm mot}[2n]$ forms a natural unital commutative graded algebra in spectra. Put $A_n=0$ for $n<0$. There is the actual natural complex map $R\Gamma_{\rm Nis}(\mathbb G_m)[-1]\to\mathbb Z(1)_{\rm mot}$ of Definition5.2; after shifting by2 and taking Ω∞ this is the pointed Picard class. Its restriction to $(\mathbb P^1,\infty)$ is $b=c_1(\mathcal O(1))$ with the trivial-line nullhomotopy at infinity. Multiplication by its powers and pullback give the actual complex equivalences
$$\bigoplus_{m=0}^{d}\mathbb Z(j-m)_{\rm mot}(Y)[-2m]\xrightarrow{\sum c_1(\mathcal O(1))^m\pi^*}\mathbb Z(j)_{\rm mot}(\mathbb P^d_Y).$$
These hold for $j\geq0$, and also for $j<0$ with all terms zero. The general bundle version holds with the stated line/quotient convention conversion by dual bundle. All structures restrict naturally to smooth schemes over any qcqs $S/k$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The qcqs prime-field schemes, weights and supplied local constructions in the statement, with the stated Choice and size premises.

[A1] The assumed [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice) and fixed size bounds discharge the premise of [prop-motivic-projective-bundle-formula](item-prop-motivic-projective-bundle-formula) when using its supplied projective-bundle contract and quotient-convention conversion. [def-motivic-cohomology](item-def-motivic-cohomology) fixes the actual coefficient functor. This records the chosen local supplier contract; it makes no foundational necessity claim about the published EM constructions.

### External input
Import the stated EM constructions and actual maps, with the completed projective-bundle supplier’s quotient convention. No A¹-invariance is imported. The Picard map is a map of complexes and hence supplies its coherent pointed class, rather than a choice made from an identification of groups.

## Excision and the exact fixed-support cycle fiber

[Open item](item-lem-author-8a080e7d9445-support-fiber) · level 14


### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the fixed universe and site-size bounds of the supplied comparisons. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, let $X$ be an affine finite-type $k$-scheme of dimension three, put $U=X_{\mathrm{smooth}/k}$, and let $T\subset X$ be a closed subset contained in $U$. Use the reduced structure on $T$ when a scheme structure is needed. Put $V=U\setminus T$ and $W=X\setminus T$. There is an actual equivalence of support fibers
$$\mathbb Z(3)_{\mathrm{mot},T}(X)\simeq\operatorname{fib}(\mathbb Z(3)_{\mathrm{mot}}(U)\to\mathbb Z(3)_{\mathrm{mot}}(V))\simeq z_T^3(U,\bullet)[-6].$$
Here support complexes are unshifted cohomological fibers, so $H^{a,3}_{\mathrm{mot},T}(X,\mathbb Z)\cong H_{6-a}z_T^3(U,\bullet)$. These maps respect the support-to-global maps, followed by restriction to $U$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** $k,X,U,T,V,W$ and the choice and size assumptions of the statement.

**Goal:** Construct the stated actual maps and prove their consequence.

[F1] [lem-author-8a080e7d9445-geometry](item-lem-author-8a080e7d9445-geometry), [def-cohomology-with-support](item-def-cohomology-with-support), [lem-author-b747b28c359f-elmanto-morrow-complexes](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-elmanto-morrow-complexes) and [lem-open-excision-for-support-fibers](item-lem-open-excision-for-support-fibers).

[F2] [lem-author-8a080e7d9445-restriction-diagram](item-lem-author-8a080e7d9445-restriction-diagram) and [def-supported-higher-cycle-complex](item-def-supported-higher-cycle-complex).

[F3] The assumed Axiom of Choice, [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice), discharges the foundational hypotheses of the support definition in [F1] and the diagram comparison in [F2] when they are invoked in steps 1.1 and 2.1. The excision and fiber arguments use no additional choice.

### Proof
1.1 The completed EM complex supplier gives derived Nisnevich descent. The geometry lemma supplies the actual two-open cover and its restriction square, so that square is homotopy cartesian. Apply the completed open-excision supplier to obtain the first support equivalence, with its support-to-global compatibility. All these objects are qcqs, so the arbitrary-open extension convention is unnecessary here. [F1, F3]

2.1 Taking homotopy fibers is a functor on coherent arrow diagrams. Apply it to the preceding restriction-diagram equivalence. The completed fixed-support cycle definition gives the quasi-isomorphism from $z_T^3(U,\bullet)$ to the homotopy fiber of the actual unshifted homological cycle restriction. Reindex to cochains and shift by $-6$, which commutes with fibers. This gives the second equivalence and $H^a=H_{6-a}$, with the indicated projection maps. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎


## The actual smooth open pair and its choice scope

[Open item](item-lem-author-149a02132c3b-geometry) · level 14

### Statement
Assume AC. Let $X$ be an affine finite-type threefold over algebraically closed $k$, let $U=X_{\mathrm{smooth}}$, and let $T\subset X$ be closed with $T\subset U$. Put $V=U\setminus T$ and $W=X\setminus T$. All four schemes are qcqs and $U,V$ are smooth separated finite type over the perfect field $k$. They are regular Noetherian as schemes over the prime field. The two opens $U,W$ cover $X$ and their intersection is $V$, giving a Nisnevich two-open covering square. If $T$ is an integral curve, it is affine; it lies in one of the open-and-closed relative-dimension strata of $U$.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The hypotheses in the statement, with the Axiom of Choice and fixed universe bounds.

**Goal:** Construct the stated actual maps and prove their consequence.

[F1] [def-article-conventions](item-def-article-conventions), [def-cohomology-with-support](item-def-cohomology-with-support) and [def-nisnevich-covering-interface](item-def-nisnevich-covering-interface) fix the finite-type, size, AC and two-open conventions. Basic smoothness here includes its regularity over a perfect field and locally constant relative dimension.

### Proof
1.1 Finite-type affine $X/k$ is Noetherian and separated. Every open is quasi-compact in a Noetherian space, and its induced scheme is separated finite type. Thus the four objects lie in the completed qcqs category. The smooth locus and its open $V$ are smooth over $k$, hence regular Noetherian. An algebraically closed field is perfect: in positive characteristic each polynomial $t^p-a$ has a root, so Frobenius is surjective; characteristic zero is perfect. Forgetting the map to $k$ does not change regularity or Noetherianness. [F1]

2.1 The inclusion $T\subset U$ gives $X=U\cup W$ and $U\cap W=V$. Open immersions are étale, and each point has a residue-preserving lift to one of these opens, so the family is Nisnevich. A closed subscheme of affine $X$ is affine, giving the curve assertion. For a smooth morphism to a field the relative dimension is locally constant; the finitely many dimension strata of $U$ are open and closed. The connected integral curve lies in one such stratum. These are component/dimension bookkeeping facts, with no new comparison theorem assumed. [F1, step 1.1] ∎


## A smooth point has the exact finite-type excision pair

[Open item](item-lem-author-59b1a831fe59-neighborhood) · level 14

### Statement
Assume AC and the completed universe bounds. Let $X$ be a qcqs $k$-scheme of pure finite dimension $d$, where $k$ is perfect, and let $x$ be a closed point at which $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth. There is an affine smooth separated finite-type neighbourhood $V$ of $x$, pure of dimension $d$. Its residue field $L=\kappa(x)$ is finite separable over $k$, and $\operatorname{Spec}L\hookrightarrow V$ has pure codimension $d$. Both $X\setminus\{x\}$ and $V\setminus\{x\}$ are qcqs. For every $j\geq0$, actual EM Nisnevich descent gives the support-excision equivalence $C_{j,x}(X)\simeq C_{j,x}(V)$, compatibly with support-to-global maps. Here $C_{j,x}$ is the unshifted cohomological restriction fiber, not its $[2j]$ spectral shift.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** Exactly the hypotheses above; smooth at $x$ means smooth on some open neighbourhood, with the usual locally finite-presentation condition.

**Goal:** Verify the actual geometric and descent hypotheses before applying a classical purity theorem.

[F1] [def-article-conventions](item-def-article-conventions) and [def-cohomology-with-support](item-def-cohomology-with-support) give qcqs and support conventions. [lem-author-b747b28c359f-elmanto-morrow-complexes](item-lem-author-b747b28c359f-elmanto-morrow-complexes) gives derived Nisnevich descent on this category. [lem-open-excision-for-support-fibers](item-lem-open-excision-for-support-fibers) is the conditional excision theorem.

[F2] [thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input](item-thm-author-fc2380accb47-finite-type-geometric-input) supplies finite-type dimensions, transcendence-degree dimensions of domains, and finite closed-point residue fields. Smooth finite-type schemes are regular Noetherian, with locally constant relative dimension.

### Proof
1.1 Choose an affine open in the smooth neighbourhood containing $x$ and shrink within its relative-dimension stratum. It is smooth separated finite type over $k$, pure of some dimension $e$. In the usual finite-type setting, purity of $X$ and [F2] give $e=d$. The same conclusion holds if only qcqs $X$ is assumed: let $T$ be the reduced irreducible component through the chosen local smooth component, with function field $K$. Its finite-type nonempty open has dimension $e=\operatorname{trdeg}_kK$. Every affine coordinate domain on $T$ is a subalgebra of $K$; any finite strict prime chain in it remains strict in some finitely generated $k$-subalgebra, by choosing one witness for each strict inclusion. That subalgebra has dimension at most $\operatorname{trdeg}_kK=e$. Every finite specialization chain in $T$ lies in an affine open containing its most special point. Hence $\dim T\leq e$, while its open of dimension $e$ gives the reverse inequality. Purity of $X$ gives $\dim T=d$, so $e=d$. Denote the resulting neighbourhood by $V$. [F2, given, construct]

2.1 Since $x$ is closed in $V$, [F2] gives finite $L/k$; perfectness makes it separable. Thus both $V$ and $\operatorname{Spec}L$ belong to the smooth separated finite-type category, and the dimension formula gives codimension $d$. The open $V\setminus\{x\}$ is quasi-compact because $V$ is Noetherian. To prove $X\setminus\{x\}$ quasi-compact without imposing global Noetherianness, take any open cover of it. Together with $V$ it covers quasi-compact $X$, so finitely many members plus $V$ suffice. Finitely many members also cover quasi-compact $V\setminus\{x\}$. These two finite selections cover $X\setminus\{x\}$. Quasi-separatedness is inherited by open subschemes. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The two opens $V$ and $X\setminus\{x\}$ cover $X$, with intersection $V\setminus\{x\}$. They form a Nisnevich two-open cover, and all four objects are qcqs by step 2.1. Apply the actual derived Nisnevich descent of [F1] and then its conditional excision theorem. This supplies exactly the claimed restriction-induced support equivalence and support-to-global compatibility for every nonnegative weight. [F1, step 2.1] ∎


## Generic rank and point-supported classes on a curve

[Open item](item-lem-curve-generic-rank-localization) · level 15


### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $C$ be an integral Noetherian scheme of dimension one, with generic point $\eta$ and function field $k(\eta)=\mathcal O_{C,\eta}$. The generic-rank homomorphism
$$\operatorname{rk}_\eta:G_0(C)\longrightarrow K_0(k(\eta))\cong\mathbb Z$$
sends the class of a coherent sheaf $F$ to $\dim_{k(\eta)}F_\eta$. Its kernel is generated by classes of coherent sheaves supported at closed points. In fact it is generated by the residue-field sheaves $\kappa(x)$ at closed points $x$.

For every nonempty open subscheme $V\subseteq C$, restriction defines a directed system as opens shrink, and the natural homomorphism
$$\varinjlim_{\eta\in V\subseteq C}G_0(V)\longrightarrow K_0(k(\eta))\cong\mathbb Z$$
is an isomorphism. Thus the displayed kernel is the kernel of localization at the generic point, computed as this filtered limit.

For the following additional supported comparison, fix the compatible site and universe bounds of the supplied perfect-$K$-theory construction. If $i:C\hookrightarrow U$ is a closed immersion into a regular Noetherian finite-dimensional scheme, the supported comparison $K_0^{|C|}(U)\cong G_0(C)$ identifies generic rank with the alternating generic length of a supported perfect complex $E$:
$$[E]\longmapsto\sum_n(-1)^n\operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_{U,\eta}}H^n(E)_\eta.$$
The sum and each length are finite. No regularity or smoothness of $C$ is assumed.

Here $G_0(X)$ is the abelian group generated by coherent $\mathcal O_X$-modules, with relation $[F]=[F']+[F'']$ for every short exact sequence $0\to F'\to F\to F''\to0$. An integral scheme is reduced and irreducible; its generic point has dense closure and its local ring there is a field. The dimension is the supremum of lengths of chains of strict specializations. The sheaf $\kappa(x)$ is the pushforward of the residue field along the closed immersion of the point. A sheaf is supported at $x$ if its stalks vanish away from $x$. Length is the number of simple factors in a finite composition series, independent of the series. A perfect complex is locally quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex of finite locally free sheaves, and support in $|C|$ means that its cohomology sheaves vanish away from $C$.

### Statement references
[math:lem-coherent-devissage-one-generic-generator](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/lem-coherent-devissage-one-generic-generator)

[prop-supported-k-zero-devissage](item-prop-supported-k-zero-devissage)

### Facts & Assumptions
[A1] The assumed [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice) discharges the coherent dévissage and associated-sheaf premises in [F1]–[F2]. For step 5.1, the additional fixed site and universe bounds discharge the selected supported perfect-$K$ comparison in [F3]. No such supported-model premise is needed for the preceding coherent generic-rank and filtered-colimit assertions.

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and $C,\eta$ as in the Statement. For the final supported assertion, also fix the stated closed immersion, a supported perfect complex $E$, and the compatible site and universe bounds of that comparison.

**Goal:** Compute generic localization and its filtered limit, and identify it under supported dévissage with alternating generic length.

[F1] The coherent one-generic-generator dévissage theorem says that on a Noetherian scheme a property of coherent sheaves holds for all coherent sheaves if it holds for zero, is two-out-of-three in coherent short exact sequences, and has a coherent witness of generic length one supported on each integral closed subscheme. It assumes AC. [math:lem-coherent-devissage-one-generic-generator](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/lem-coherent-devissage-one-generic-generator)

[F2] Coherent sheaves on a Noetherian scheme form an abelian category; kernels, cokernels and finite direct sums are coherent, and coherence is local. The residue-field supplier establishes coherence on a Noetherian affine neighbourhood of a closed point. Step 2.1 extends this to the global point sheaf by the local criterion. [math:thm-coherent-sheaves-abelian-noetherian-scheme](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-coherent-sheaves-abelian-noetherian-scheme) [math:ex-skyscraper-coherent-closed-point](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/ex-skyscraper-coherent-closed-point)

[F3] For a regular Noetherian finite-dimensional ambient scheme and any closed subscheme, supported perfect-complex $K_0$ is identified with the coherent $G_0$ of the closed subscheme by the coherent-cohomology Euler class followed by the finite filtration by powers of the defining ideal. [prop-supported-k-zero-devissage](item-prop-supported-k-zero-devissage)

### Proof
**Proof technique:** Apply coherent dévissage using only points distinct from the generic point, then localize on shrinking opens and compute supported ideal-filtration lengths.

1.1 Every nonempty open $V\subseteq C$ is integral and Noetherian, has dimension at most one, and contains $\eta$. Every point $x\neq\eta$ of $V$ is closed in $V$: a further proper specialization would give a chain of length at least two starting at $\eta$. Hence every proper nonempty integral closed subscheme of $V$ is the reduced point at such an $x$. The whole integral closed subscheme is $V$ itself. The possibility that $V=\{\eta\}$ is open is allowed; then $V=\operatorname{Spec}k(\eta)$ and there are no points $x\neq\eta$ in $V$. [given]

2.1 Let $H_V\subseteq G_0(V)$ be generated by $[\mathcal O_V]$ and $[\kappa(x)]$ for $x\in V\setminus\{\eta\}$. These point sheaves are coherent: on an affine neighbourhood $W=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $x$, the global closed-point direct image restricts to $\widetilde{A/\mathfrak m_x}$, which is coherent by [F2]; on $V\setminus\{x\}$ it is zero. These two opens cover $V$, so locality of coherence gives the global assertion. Apply [F1] under [A1] to the property $P(F):[F]\in H_V$. It holds for zero and is two-out-of-three by the exact relations in $G_0(V)$. For the integral closed subscheme $V$, the witness is $\mathcal O_V$, with generic stalk $k(\eta)$ annihilated by the zero maximal ideal of $\mathcal O_{V,\eta}$. For each proper integral closed subscheme from step 1.1, use $\kappa(x)$; its stalk at $x$ is one-dimensional over the residue field and annihilated by the maximal ideal. All witness hypotheses hold, so $H_V=G_0(V)$, including when $V=\{\eta\}$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Taking stalks at $\eta$ is exact and gives finite-dimensional $k(\eta)$-vector spaces. Dimension therefore defines the generic-rank homomorphism. It sends $[\mathcal O_V]$ to $1$ and each $[\kappa(x)]$ with $x\neq\eta$ to zero. By step 2.1, an element of its kernel is an integral linear combination of precisely these point classes. Conversely all such point classes have generic rank zero. For $V=C$, the generic point is not closed because $\dim C=1$, so these are exactly the closed-point classes in the Statement. Coherent sheaves supported at closed points have generic rank zero, and each residue sheaf is such a sheaf. Finally dimension identifies the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional vector spaces with $\mathbb Z$, giving the stated $K_0(k(\eta))$ normalization. [A1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The nonempty opens are filtered under reverse inclusion, since every finite intersection contains $\eta$. Restriction is exact and preserves the generic stalk and structure-sheaf class. For $x\in V\setminus\{\eta\}$, the open $V\setminus\{x\}$ still contains $\eta$ and kills the residue-sheaf class. Each element in step 2.1 involves only finitely many such points, so one nonempty open removes them all. Thus every colimit element is an integer multiple of the compatible structure-sheaf class, and generic rank sends that class to $1$. This proves the colimit isomorphism. If $V=\{\eta\}$, its only generator in this argument is $[\mathcal O_V]$; the generic point is never treated as a removable point class. For $V=C$, step 3.1 identifies the kernel of localization with the stated point-supported subgroup. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Under the additional bounds in [A1], apply [F3] and let $\mathcal I$ define $C$ in $U$. The image of $[E]$ in $G_0(C)$ is the finite sum of the classes of $\mathcal I^rH^n(E)/\mathcal I^{r+1}H^n(E)$ with signs $(-1)^n$. At $\eta$ each quotient is a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathcal O_{U,\eta}/\mathcal I_\eta=k(\eta)$, so its dimension is its length as an $\mathcal O_{U,\eta}$-module. The finite exhaustive filtration and additivity of length identify the sum of these dimensions, for each $n$, with the length of $H^n(E)_\eta$. Only finitely many $n$ contribute. Applying generic rank gives exactly the alternating generic-length formula, without requiring regularity or smoothness of $C$. [A1, F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎


## Classical smooth critical-rank classifications

[Open item](item-thm-smooth-critical-rank-classifications) · level 15

### Statement
Assume AC and the article\'s universes. Over an algebraically closed field $k$ of arbitrary characteristic, the ordinary integral Chow Chern maps are bijections $C_2:\mathrm{Vect}_2(X)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{CH}^1(X)\times\mathrm{CH}^2(X)$ for every smooth affine surface $X$, and $C_3:\mathrm{Vect}_3(Y)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{CH}^1(Y)\times\mathrm{CH}^2(Y)\times\mathrm{CH}^3(Y)$ for every smooth affine threefold $Y$. In each case every tuple is realized, and its realizing bundle is unique up to isomorphism. These are the classical surface classification of Murthy–Swan and threefold classification of N. Mohan Kumar–M. P. Murthy. Here $\mathrm{Vect}_r$ denotes bundle isomorphism classes, and $c_i$ is the coefficient of the standard quotient-projective-bundle Chern relation, with $c_1(\mathcal O(D))=[D]$.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data and hypotheses in the statement.

**Goal:** Establish the stated conclusion.

[F1] The exact all-characteristic rank-three classification is imported in [thm-author-f08c343a07fc-local-kumar-murthy-chow-input](item-thm-author-f08c343a07fc-local-kumar-murthy-chow-input).

[F2] The ordinary Chow Chern interface, cylinder geometry and stabilized Chern data are supplied by [lem-author-f08c343a07fc-local-chern-interface](item-lem-author-f08c343a07fc-local-chern-interface), [lem-author-f08c343a07fc-local-cylinder-geometry](item-lem-author-f08c343a07fc-local-cylinder-geometry), [lem-author-f08c343a07fc-local-stabilized-chern](item-lem-author-f08c343a07fc-local-stabilized-chern).

[F3] The local cylinder reductions establish surface uniqueness subject to line cancellation and surface existence subject to cylinder rank-three existence. [lem-author-f08c343a07fc-local-surface-uniqueness-reduction](item-lem-author-f08c343a07fc-local-surface-uniqueness-reduction), [lem-author-f08c343a07fc-local-surface-existence-reduction](item-lem-author-f08c343a07fc-local-surface-existence-reduction)

[F4] The module cancellation theorem and its local bundle/K-zero interface establish cancellation on any affine surface at rank two. [thm-author-f08c343a07fc-cancel-suslin-module-input](item-thm-author-f08c343a07fc-cancel-suslin-module-input), [lem-author-f08c343a07fc-cancel-cancellation-interface](item-lem-author-f08c343a07fc-cancel-cancellation-interface)

### Proof

1.1 The threefold assertion, including both realization of every tuple and uniqueness for that tuple, is exactly [F1] with its actual Chern map as in [F2]. [F1, F2, given]

1.2 Let $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ be a smooth affine surface. Its cylinder is a smooth affine threefold by [F2], so [F1] supplies every rank-three Chern triple there. The surface-existence reduction in [F3] consequently realizes every pair on $X$ by a rank-two bundle. [F1, F2, F3]

1.3 For rank-two $E,F$ on $X$ with identical pairs, the surface-uniqueness reduction in [F3] reduces their isomorphism to cancellation of a common trivial line. The algebra $A$ has dimension two and is finite type over algebraically closed $k$; [F4] therefore gives cancellation at rank two. More explicitly a common line stabilization gives equal K-zero classes, and the local interface applies the module theorem to produce $E\cong F$. Thus $C_2$ is injective. [F3, F4, given]

2.1 Steps 1.2 and 1.3 prove surface bijectivity; step 1.1 proves threefold bijectivity. In both cases isomorphisms preserve Chern tuples by [F2], so these bijections have exactly the existence and uniqueness interpretation asserted. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

### Source notes

Math. 36 (1976), 125–165, DOI 10.1007/BF01390007. The original Murthy–Swan proof was not read. The local proof uses a cylinder, the completed Serre splitting supplier and a separately namespaced cancellation import. Consequently the patch is independent of the uncompleted native cancellation target. Ordinary Chow classes are the interface here; no unnamed motivic comparison is assumed. The two smooth schemes are understood equidimensional, as surfaces and threefolds in the article; finitely many disjoint equidimensional components can equally be handled componentwise.


## Rank-two uniqueness on singular threefolds

[Open item](item-op-rank-two-threefold-uniqueness) · level 15


### Open problem
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the suitable universes used by the supplied constructions. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $X$ be a normal singular affine threefold of finite type over $k$. For rank-two vector bundles $E$ and $F$ on $X$, do the equalities $c_1(E)=c_1(F)$ in $H^{2,1}_{\mathrm{mot}}(X,\mathbb Z)$ and $c_2(E)=c_2(F)$ in $H^{4,2}_{\mathrm{mot}}(X,\mathbb Z)$ imply $E\cong F$?

Here an affine threefold of finite type over $k$ is a scheme $\operatorname{Spec}A$, with $A$ a finitely generated commutative $k$-algebra, of Krull dimension three. Normal means that every local ring is an integrally closed domain; singular means that at least one local ring is not regular. A rank-two vector bundle is an $\mathcal O_X$-module locally isomorphic to $\mathcal O_X^2$, and $E\cong F$ means an invertible $\mathcal O_X$-linear map. The supplied construction assigns to such a bundle its first and second integral motivic Chern classes in the indicated motivic cohomology groups, invariant under isomorphism. Equivalently, the question asks whether the map $(c_1,c_2)$ from the set of isomorphism classes of rank-two bundles to the product of these two groups is injective.

### Open problem references
[def-vector-bundle-classes](item-def-vector-bundle-classes)

[def-motivic-chern-classes](item-def-motivic-chern-classes)

[math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

### Status
Fasel and Yakerson state this uniqueness question as open immediately after Corollary D. At that location they state surjectivity of $(c_1,c_2)$ for normal affine threefolds over algebraically closed fields; surjectivity alone does not settle injectivity. This entry records the article's status as of its cited 2026 version, not an exhaustive assessment of subsequent work. No solution is asserted.

The Choice assumption is inherited from the supplied bundle-class and motivic Chern-class constructions used to formulate the question.


## Excision and K theory purity at a smooth closed point

[Open item](item-prop-smooth-point-excision-purity) · level 15


### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme over a perfect field $k$, and let $x$ be a closed point at which $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth. Write $S=X_{\mathrm{smooth}}$ for the open locus where this morphism is smooth and $U=X\setminus\{x\}$. The square of open immersions
$$\begin{matrix}S\cap U&\longrightarrow&U\\\downarrow&&\downarrow\\S&\longrightarrow&X\end{matrix}$$
is both cartesian and cocartesian in schemes. With $K$ on arbitrary opens interpreted by the quasi-compact-open homotopy-limit convention of the support definition, its restriction square is homotopy cartesian. Restriction and dévissage give canonical isomorphisms
$$\pi_0K(X/U)\xrightarrow{\sim}\pi_0K(S/(S\cap U))\xrightarrow{\sim}K_0(\kappa(x))\xrightarrow{\dim_{\kappa(x)}}\mathbb Z.$$
Here $K(A/B)$ denotes the fiber of $K(A)\to K(B)$ for an open immersion $B\subseteq A$, and $K_0(\kappa(x))$ is the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional vector spaces over the residue field. The inverse image of $1$ is the supported class of the residue sheaf $i_*\kappa(x)$, for $i:\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\hookrightarrow X$; its image in $K_0(X)$ is the ordinary perfect-complex class of that sheaf. Neither support-to-global map is asserted to be injective.

### Statement references
[def-cohomology-with-support](item-def-cohomology-with-support)

### Facts & Assumptions
[A1] The already assumed [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice) and fixed suitable universes are inherited by the support, localization, local perfect-complex and dévissage constructions in [F1]–[F4]. They are used to invoke those selected constructions in the annotated steps below.

**Given:** AC, $X,k,x,S,U$ as in the statement. Smooth at $x$ means that $x$ has an open neighbourhood on which the structure morphism is smooth; a perfect field is a field all of whose algebraic extensions are separable.

**Goal:** Prove the scheme and K-theory squares, the supported degree-zero identifications and the normalization of the generator, without requiring $S$ to be quasi-compact.

[F1] [def-cohomology-with-support](item-def-cohomology-with-support) defines $K$ on an arbitrary open as the homotopy limit of its values on quasi-compact opens, with restriction maps, and defines $K(A/B)$ as the indicated fiber. The value on a quasi-compact open is its supplied K-spectrum.

[F2] [prop-perfect-k-localization-input](item-prop-perfect-k-localization-input) gives localization, two-open Mayer–Vietoris and supported open excision for quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes and the stated quasi-compact opens. Its localization identifies the supported perfect-category K-spectrum with the corresponding restriction fiber, naturally for open restriction and support-to-global maps.

[F3] [lem-koszul-point-support-class](item-lem-koszul-point-support-class) supplies, under AC, a smooth affine finite-type neighbourhood of a smooth closed point on a finite-type scheme, the perfect residue sheaf and its supported class. A smooth morphism is locally of finite presentation; thus a smooth point on $X$ has a smooth affine neighbourhood $V$ of finite type over $k$, to which that supplier applies. On $V$ it also gives a regular-sequence ideal for $x$ after shrinking. [prop-supported-k-zero-devissage](item-prop-supported-k-zero-devissage) identifies the supported $K_0$ of a regular Noetherian finite-dimensional scheme with $G_0$ of the closed subscheme, with inverse given by coherent pushforward; its proof carries AC. A smooth finite-type scheme over a field is regular, Noetherian and finite-dimensional.

[F4] [def-scheme-perfect-complexes](item-def-scheme-perfect-complexes) defines perfectness by local representation as a bounded complex of finite locally free modules. It defines the supported perfect category by vanishing of cohomology stalks outside the specified support. In particular, perfectness of a fixed derived object can be checked on an open cover; the zero complex is perfect.

### Proof
1.1 Choose a smooth affine finite-type neighbourhood $V$ of $x$ and shrink it as in [F3] so that the ideal of $x$ in $V$ is finitely generated by a regular sequence. The point is closed in $V$, and $V\setminus\{x\}$ is quasi-compact: it is the finite union of the principal opens where the chosen generators are nonzero. The empty sequence gives the empty complement when $V$ is the point. [A1, F3, given]

2.1 If $Z$ is any quasi-compact open of $X$ containing $V$, then $Z\setminus\{x\}$ is quasi-compact. Indeed, cover $Z$ by finitely many affine opens. An affine open $A$ not containing $x$ needs no removal. If $x\in A$, choose a principal neighbourhood $D(f)$ of $x$ contained in $A\cap V$. The closed set $A\setminus D(f)$ is quasi-compact and avoids $x$, so finitely many principal opens in $A$ avoiding $x$ cover it. Inside $D(f)$ the complement of $x$ is quasi-compact: it is the intersection of $D(f)$ and $V\setminus\{x\}$, hence quasi-compact because $X$ is quasi-separated and both are quasi-compact opens of $X$. These finite covers prove the claim. In particular $U$ is quasi-compact by taking $Z=X$. Every such $Z$ is quasi-separated as an open subscheme of $X$. [step 1.1, given]

3.1 The displayed scheme square is cartesian because intersections of open subschemes are their fiber products. It is cocartesian because $S\cup U=X$: $x\in S$, and $U$ contains every other point. Morphisms from $S$ and $U$ to any scheme that agree on $S\cap U$ glue uniquely over this open cover. [given, step 2.1]

4.1 Let $\mathcal C$ be the poset of quasi-compact opens $Z$ of $S$ containing $V$. It is cofinal among quasi-compact opens of $S$, since any such open $B$ is contained in the quasi-compact open $B\cup V$. By step 2.1, each $Z\setminus\{x\}$ is quasi-compact. These complements are cofinal among quasi-compact opens of $S\setminus\{x\}$: a quasi-compact open $B$ there is contained in $(B\cup V)\setminus\{x\}$. Consequently [F1], cofinality of homotopy limits, and preservation of limits by fibers give $K(S/(S\cap U))\simeq\operatorname*{holim}_{Z\in\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}}\operatorname{fib}\bigl(K(Z)\to K(Z\setminus\{x\})\bigr).$ The comparison is induced by restriction, not merely an abstract equivalence. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 For each $Z\in\mathcal C$, localization and supported excision in [F2] identify its displayed fiber, naturally in $Z$, with $K_{\{x\}}(V)$. The indexing poset has the least element $V$, so its nerve is contractible; the homotopy limit of this coherent constant diagram is $K_{\{x\}}(V)$. Applying the same localization and excision to $V\subseteq X$, using the quasi-compact complement from step 2.1, identifies $K(X/U)$ with $K_{\{x\}}(V)$ compatibly with restriction. Thus restriction induces an equivalence $K(X/U)\simeq K(S/(S\cap U))$. [A1, F2, step 2.1, step 4.1]

6.1 The restriction square on $X,S,U,S\cap U$ is coherent. Its horizontal fibers, taken over $K(U)$ and $K(S\cap U)$, are equivalent by step 5.1. In spectra a square with equivalent corresponding fibers is homotopy cartesian: compare its upper-left corner with the homotopy pullback of the other three corners and use the fiber sequences over the common base. This proves the K-theory square, including when $S$ is not quasi-compact. [F1, step 5.1]

7.1 The scheme $V$ is regular, Noetherian and finite-dimensional, and the closed subscheme $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)$ has underlying set $\{x\}$. By [F3], supported dévissage gives $\pi_0K_{\{x\}}(V)\cong G_0(\kappa(x))$. Every finite-dimensional vector space over a field is a finite direct sum of copies of the field, and dimension is additive in short exact sequences. Hence dimension gives $G_0(\kappa(x))\cong\mathbb Z$, with inverse $1\mapsto[\kappa(x)]$. Combining this with step 5.1 gives the asserted isomorphisms. [A1, F3, step 5.1, step 6.1]

8.1 The inverse in dévissage sends $[\kappa(x)]$ to the class of the residue sheaf on $V$. Let $E=i_*\kappa(x)[0]$ be the globally defined residue sheaf in degree zero. Its restriction to $V$ is perfect by the Koszul resolution in [F3], applied only to the smooth finite-type scheme $V$. Its restriction to $U=X\setminus\{x\}$ is zero, hence perfect. Since $V\cup U=X$, the local definition in [F4] makes $E$ perfect on $X$; its cohomology stalks vanish away from $x$, so it belongs to the supported perfect category on $X$. Naturality of localization and restriction in [F2] identifies the supported class of this object with that of its restriction to $V$. Its image under support-to-global is the class of the same perfect object on $X$. Thus it is the inverse image of $1$ under the displayed isomorphisms. The image in global $K_0$ can vanish, so no injectivity is used. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 7.1] ∎

## The product on graded motivic groups is the source cup product

[Open item](item-lem-author-74a9c17e63f1-graded-products) · level 15


### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Under the actual graded comparison, the filtered multiplication induces the source cup product on the page2 groups. Explicitly it gives
$$E_2^{a,b}\otimes E_2^{c,e}\longrightarrow E_2^{a+c,b+e}$$
corresponding to the motivic product of degree/weight $(a-b,-b)$ and $(c-e,-e)$. The commutativity sign is $(-1)^{(a+b)(c+e)}$, equivalently the usual cohomological cup-product sign $(-1)^{(a-b)(c-e)}$.

### Facts & Assumptions
[A1] The Axiom of Choice and the fixed size conventions of the cited constructions are inherited through [thm-author-74a9c17e63f1-source-multiplicative-input](item-thm-author-74a9c17e63f1-source-multiplicative-input). They discharge that supplier’s local-realization premise at its first application below. [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice)

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and the fixed size conventions of the cited constructions, together with the actual filtered algebra and its source-induced graded algebra.

**Goal:** Identify products by actual multiplication maps, not by a coincidence of additive groups.

[F1] [def-motivic-filtration](item-def-motivic-filtration) gives coherent filtered products. [thm-author-74a9c17e63f1-source-multiplicative-input](item-thm-author-74a9c17e63f1-source-multiplicative-input) makes associated graded strong symmetric monoidal and supplies its actual source comparison.

[F2] [lem-author-74a9c17e63f1-graded-comparison](item-lem-author-74a9c17e63f1-graded-comparison) specifies that comparison; [lem-author-74a9c17e63f1-index-calculation](item-lem-author-74a9c17e63f1-index-calculation) gives its page2 degree labels.

### Proof
1.1 Use the supplied realization under [A1]. Associated graded in [F1] sends filtered multiplication to actual maps $Q_r\wedge Q_t\to Q_{r+t}$. Transport these maps along the source $\gamma_r,\gamma_t,\gamma_{r+t}$; the resulting maps on the shifted motivic complexes are their specified source products by [F1], not independently chosen pairings. After taking homotopy groups the degrees add: $r=-b,t=-e$ and homotopy degrees $-a-b,-c-e$ give target weight $-b-e$ and degree $-a-b-c-e$, namely the page2 group at $(a+c,b+e)$. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 Symmetry of sphere smash in homotopy degrees $-a-b$ and $-c-e$ contributes $(-1)^{(a+b)(c+e)}$. The shifts $2r$ and $2t$ are even, and $a+b$ has the same parity as $a-b$, likewise for $c,e$. Hence the transported sign is exactly the displayed cohomological sign. Associativity and unit maps are those of the actual graded algebra in [F1], so these are the source cup products with all indicated laws. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎


## Degreewise boundedness and finite collections of eventual vanishings

[Open item](item-lem-author-0cc80c1b5792-finite-degrees) · level 15


### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice. The actual motivic filtration of every finite-dimensional Noetherian equicharacteristic scheme is degreewise bounded above in filtration on all integer homotopy degrees. For any finite set $S\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and any anchor $t$, one may choose a common sufficiently large $\ell$ making every $\pi_qF^{t+\ell}$ with $q\in S$ zero. The same holds for their image subgroups in $K_q(X)$. No threshold independent of an unbounded set of degrees is asserted.

### Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and the general source filtration or its actual standing-field restriction.

**Goal:** Express the stagewise result in the completed local boundedness language and in the form used by finite exact-sequence arguments.

[F1] For nonempty $X$, [lem-author-0cc80c1b5792-threshold](item-lem-author-0cc80c1b5792-threshold) supplies an actual zero-group threshold for each fixed degree and anchor.

[F2] [def-valuative-dimension-and-boundedness](item-def-valuative-dimension-and-boundedness) defines degreewise boundedness; [def-motivic-filtration](item-def-motivic-filtration) defines the image subgroups.

[F3] The assumed [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice) discharges the inherited Choice premises of the threshold supplier in [F1] and the selected filtration in [F2]. The finite maximum in the proof introduces no stronger choice assumption.

[F4] [lem-adjudicate-5eb16844831b-empty-motivic-stages](item-lem-adjudicate-5eb16844831b-empty-motivic-stages) proves that every actual stage on the empty scheme is zero, independently of any dimension convention.

### Proof
1.1 If $X$ is empty, [F4] gives all stage and image vanishings, with threshold zero for any anchor. Suppose henceforth that $X$ is nonempty. Under the inherited Choice premise in [F3], take anchor $t=0$ in [F1]. For every fixed $q$, all stages beyond $\ell_0(q,0)$ have zero $\pi_q$. These are exactly the quantifiers in [F2]. If a stage group is zero, its image under the augmentation to $K_q(X)$ is zero as well. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 For a finite nonempty $S$, take the maximum of the finitely many $\ell_0(q,t)$; the empty set is vacuous. Every larger $\ell$ satisfies every individual threshold in [F1], proving simultaneous vanishing for that finite set. This construction leaves the dependence on $S$ and $q$ explicit and makes no assertion of a universal bound for all integer homotopy degrees. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎


## The actual first Chern map is the Picard isomorphism on an affine curve

[Open item](item-lem-author-394a5b71198d-curve-picard) · level 15

### Statement
Assume AC. Let $C$ be a smooth integral affine curve over an algebraically closed field. The actual first Chern map $\operatorname{Pic}(C)\to\mathrm{CH}^1(C)$, $[L]\mapsto c_1(L)$, is an isomorphism. In particular $c_1(L)=0$ if and only if $L\cong\mathcal O_C$, and this is equivalent to $\varepsilon(L)=0$. Since $\det L=L$, this is the determinant/line-bundle interface in dimension one.

### Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and data in the statement, with AC and the article's fixed universes wherever perfect K-theory is used.

**Goal:** Establish the asserted conclusion.

[F1] The local rings of a smooth scheme over the perfect base field are regular. A one-dimensional regular local ring is a DVR, and a DVR is a PID and hence a UFD under AC. [math:thm-regular-equals-smooth-over-perfect-field](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-regular-equals-smooth-over-perfect-field), [math:thm-one-dimensional-regular-local-rings-are-dvrs](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-one-dimensional-regular-local-rings-are-dvrs), [math:cor-dvr-is-a-pid](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/cor-dvr-is-a-pid), [math:thm-principal-ideal-domains-are-unique-factorisation-domains](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-principal-ideal-domains-are-unique-factorisation-domains)

[F2] On a locally factorial noetherian integral scheme Cartier and Weil divisors agree, compatibly with principal divisors; Cartier divisors modulo principal ones give the Picard group. [math:thm-cartier-weil-isomorphism-locally-factorial](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-cartier-weil-isomorphism-locally-factorial), [math:thm-cartier-divisors-mod-principal-to-picard](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/thm-cartier-divisors-mod-principal-to-picard)

[F3] On a curve rational equivalence of codimension-one cycles is generated by principal divisors of rational functions on the curve itself. The actual first Chern class of a line bundle is the divisor of a nonzero rational section, modulo these relations. [math:def-chow-group-of-cycles-mod-rational-equivalence](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-chow-group-of-cycles-mod-rational-equivalence), [math:def-intersection-with-a-cartier-divisor-and-first-chern-class](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-intersection-with-a-cartier-divisor-and-first-chern-class)

[F4] For a line bundle, vanishing of the exterior-dual class is equivalent to triviality. [lem-author-394a5b71198d-line-determinant](item-lem-author-394a5b71198d-line-determinant)

### Proof

1.1 The noetherian integral curve has a field as its generic local ring, and every other local ring is a one-dimensional regular local ring. By [F1] these rings are UFDs, so the curve is locally factorial. By [F2], Cartier divisors modulo principal divisors identify with Picard classes and with Weil divisors modulo principal divisors. By [F3] the latter quotient is precisely $\mathrm{CH}^1(C)$. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 This is the actual first Chern map: a rational section of $L$ defines a Cartier divisor $D$ with $\mathcal O_C(D)\cong L$, and [F3] sends $L$ to the Weil divisor cycle of $D$. Thus the composed quotient isomorphism carries $[L]$ to $c_1(L)$, fixing the sign and the map, rather than identifying only groups. Its kernel is the trivial line class. Combining with [F4] gives the asserted equivalences; $\Lambda^1L=L$ gives the determinant statement. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1] ∎


## Murthy splitting criterion for the exterior-dual obstruction

[Open item](item-thm-author-394a5b71198d-murthy-module-splitting-input) · level 15



### Statement
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the fixed compatible site and universe bounds of the supplied constructions. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of arbitrary characteristic and $A$ a reduced affine $k$-algebra of dimension $n\geq2$. Suppose the subgroup $F^nK_0^{\mathrm{proj}}(A)$, generated by residue-field classes of height-$n$ smooth closed points, has no $(n-1)!$ torsion. For a finite projective $A$-module $P$ of constant rank $n$, put $P^*=\operatorname{Hom}_A(P,A)$ and $C^K_n(P)=\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^i[\Lambda^iP^*]$. Then $C^K_n(P)=0$ if and only if $P\cong A\oplus Q$ for a finite projective module $Q$ of constant rank $n-1$.

### External input
Murthy's Theorem 3.7 is imported in its algebraically closed branch. Its short proof uses a generic dual section, the Koszul class, Corollary 3.4 and Corollary 1.9; those deep suppliers are not reproved here. The introduction writes the image of a finite-projective-dimension module in ordinary $K_0(A)$ and refers classical K-theory to Bass. It does not explicitly define an inequivalent group.

To make the resolution notation precise, also import Weibel's Resolution Theorem 7.6 and Corollary 7.7.2 in the stated finite-resolution scope. Let $\mathcal P(A)$ be the finite projective modules and $\mathcal H(A)$ the modules with finite resolutions by such projectives, with inherited short exact sequences. Inclusion induces $j:K_0^{\mathrm{proj}}(A)\longrightarrow K_0(\mathcal H(A))$. Its inverse is $\chi([M]_{\mathcal H})=\sum_i(-1)^i[P_i]$ for a finite projective resolution $P_\bullet\to M$. The imported theorem supplies independence of resolution and compatibility with exact relations. For this noetherian algebra, finite modules of finite projective dimension admit such finite resolutions by taking finite free surjections and their finite syzygies. This identifies precisely the resolved-module notation in the scan. No identification of singular-ring $K_0$ with the group of all coherent modules is used.

### Facts & Assumptions
[A1] The assumed [math:def-axiom-of-choice](https://alphabetamath.cc/item/def-axiom-of-choice) and fixed universes discharge the exterior-dual and split-vanishing suppliers [F2] when their actual module/perfect-class comparisons are invoked. These are inherited local-realization premises; the imported Murthy and resolution statements and their source-reading limits remain unchanged.


**Given:** The hypotheses and data in the statement, with AC and the article's fixed universes wherever perfect K-theory is used.

**Goal:** Establish the asserted conclusion.

[F1] The imported primary statement is Theorem 3.7, using the exterior-dual definition in Definition 3.5 and the subgroup fixed in the introduction and Remark 3.6(i).

[F2] The local exterior-dual convention and necessary vanishing direction are established by [lem-author-394a5b71198d-exterior-dual-interface](item-lem-author-394a5b71198d-exterior-dual-interface) and [lem-author-394a5b71198d-split-vanishing](item-lem-author-394a5b71198d-split-vanishing).

[F3] The external resolution comparison just specified gives mutually inverse group maps $j$ and $\chi$, with $\chi([M]_{\mathcal H})$ the actual finite-resolution Euler class and $j([T])=[T]_{\mathcal H}$ for every finite projective $T$. This is Weibel II, Definition 7.7 and Corollary 7.7.2, using the inverse described in the proof of Theorem 7.6.

### Proof
1.1 Apply [F3] to the affine algebra $A$. The height-$n$ smooth residue modules $A/\mathfrak m$ are precisely the finite-projective-dimension point modules whose resolved classes generate the source subgroup in [F1]. By the formula for $\chi$, their classes in the statement are exactly $\chi([A/\mathfrak m]_{\mathcal H})$. Thus $\chi$ and $j$ restrict to mutually inverse maps on the subgroups generated by the height-$n$ smooth points. In particular the stated factorial-torsion condition holds in either presentation. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 Each $\Lambda^iP^*$ is finite projective, so $\chi(\sum_i(-1)^i[\Lambda^iP^*]_{\mathcal H})=C^K_n(P)$. Since $\chi$ is an isomorphism, this identifies the actual exterior-dual classes and their vanishing, as well as the point subgroups from step 1.1. In ordinary projective $K_0$ notation this is simply the canonical interpretation of the source's resolved-module classes. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The reduced affine algebra, algebraically closed field, dimension, module rank and factorial-torsion hypothesis now match the algebraically closed branch of [F1]. With the actual class identified in step 2.1, Theorem 3.7 gives $C^K_n(P)=0$ if and only if $P$ has a free direct summand of rank one. This is the imported converse; the local Koszul calculation in [F2] is not a replacement proof of it. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, given]

4.1 A free line summand gives $P\cong A\oplus Q$. The complementary summand $Q$ is finite projective, and localization gives its constant rank $n-1$. Conversely this decomposition is a free line summand. The exterior convention and necessary vanishing direction agree with [F2]. Together with step 3.1 this proves the stated equivalence. [A1, F2, step 3.1] ∎

The source criterion retains its reduced affine and arbitrary-characteristic scope. Weibel II, Lemma 7.7.1 has a separate quantitative typo: its printed $\min\{m,n-1\}$ must be replaced by $\max\{m,n-1\}$, with the nonnegative-length boundary convention. Over $R=k[t]$, the split sequence with kernel and quotient $R/(t)$ and middle term $(R/(t))^2$ has all three projective dimensions one; the printed minimum would make the kernel projective. This error does not invalidate the finite-resolution comparison: the displayed truncated-cone construction still has finite length and supplies the required kernel closure. The false bound is not used here.

### Source qualification
